“Everyone, this is Mr.
Choi, who leads the Peace Guild and Ares Guild.
And this is Mr.
Jin, whom you all know.
As for the people here...”
Jack.
Philip.
Joey.
Liam.
Isabella.
Names and titles I’d heard in Hollywood war movies flew past me.
Team Leader Choi seemed to know every face and name, as usual.
I just stared and nodded.
How many departments and titles are there?
The only people who stuck in my mind were the directors of the CIA and FBI.
Probably because those organizations showed up in movies so often.
“Now that we’ve made the introductions, I should tell you why we brought you here so suddenly.”
Snap.
Fwoosh!
The instant President Doramp snapped his fingers, the holograms that had briefly disappeared filled the room in every direction.
This is...
A map.
Not of the whole Earth, but a detailed map of one region.
Coordinates hovered over countless buildings and stretches of terrain.
Markers whose meaning I couldn’t guess glittered here and there like stars.
Oh.
The place names.
The deserts scattered across the map.
And what President Doramp had been saying when we arrived.
I put it together and muttered, “The Middle East?”
“It’s a tactical map showing the locations of the terrorist groups.
The sparkling markers are probably Gates or their bases.”
Team Leader Choi had spoken almost at the same time as me.
President Doramp nodded to us both.
“You’re both right, though Mr.
Choi’s answer is more detailed and closer to the mark.
The lights indicate suspected terrorist bases.
Hologram, zoom out.”
Whoosh.
The enlarged map shrank into a globe.
It turned slowly at President Doramp’s gesture, lights large and small scattered across its surface.
“All of those are terrorist groups?”
“When my late father was president, there were already more than a hundred Islamic terrorist organizations alone.
After the Great Cataclysm, of course, they multiplied at a frightening rate.”
That was news to me.
More than a hundred Islamic terrorist organizations before the Great Cataclysm.
Who knew how many there were now?
Sure, some were probably little groups that operated on the scale of clubs.
The problem was, they weren’t meeting to talk about comics.
They carried out attacks to kill people.
Seriously, why are there so many?
I knew the world had plenty of lunatics.
I’d never imagined there were this many.
Team Leader Choi watched the hologram, his gaze dark.
“Does that exclude the rebel forces scattered across Africa?”
“A good question, Mr.
Choi.
Fortunately, the rebels are included.”
“Just as you said, Mr.
President, that truly is fortunate.
And I think I understand why you went out of your way to invite us.”
His voice dropped.
“You’re planning to launch an operation to wipe out the terrorist groups, aren’t you?”
“That’s right.”
President Doramp gave a grave nod.
“As both of you know, the United States is still the world’s greatest power, but that also means we face an equal amount of opposition.
Therefore, we have no choice but to act cautiously, both militarily and diplomatically.”
The United States might have a long history as the world’s bully, but even it couldn’t push around every country on Earth.
That was especially true after it had suffered the worst losses in the Great Cataclysm.
“But the terrorist groups and rebels operating around the world must be eliminated as soon as possible.
I’m sure you both know why.”
Of course I did.
As Magic Johnson had told us, the terrorist groups and African rebels had begun experimenting with Gates and Magic Gems.
I didn’t know what those experiments would produce, or whether they would succeed.
But the experiments alone were dangerous enough.
Like nuclear tests.
The whole world paid attention whenever North Korea tested a missile.
Koreans, of course, just thought, Those bastards are at it again, and got on with their day.
But that was because we knew they weren’t going to fire at us.
Terrorist groups were as crazy as North Korea.
Crazier, even.
“You must have heard from Mr.
Johnson.
Today alone, terrorist groups carried out the same kind of attack simultaneously in California, Arizona, and Texas.
And this isn’t happening only in the United States.”
President Doramp swept a hand through the hologram.
The globe vanished.
Dozens of small windows took its place.
“Surrender!
Put down your weapons now, and...!” “God is great!” “R-run!” “BOOM!”
Dozens of languages, translated for me by the System, mingled in a deafening clamor.
People of different appearances and skin colors fled explosions or screamed as human bone and flesh sprayed over them.
“There have been thirty-two attempted attacks around the world today alone.
Fortunately, as with the incident in Texas that made the news, the damage so far has been minor.
But if the terrorist groups complete their experiments with the Gates and Magic Gems in their possession...”
Chuck Hagel, fiddling with his cigar, cut in.
“Fuck.
Everything goes to shit.
Monster Waves will break out at any time, anywhere, just like what happened in South Korea.”
Magic Johnson spoke with a sigh.
“And the rebels won’t stay quiet, either.
They’re just as dangerous as the terrorist groups.
They kidnap even children, brainwash them, and use them as soldiers.
If it meant taking over a country, they wouldn’t bat an eye even if tens or hundreds of thousands of people died.”
Why did that remind me of the saying that human beings were capable of both the greatest good and the greatest evil?
The bodies of the people who had died before my eyes only weeks ago came back to me.
So did their screams.
A weight settled in my chest.
“Hmm.”
I glanced sideways at Team Leader Choi with a low hum.
His gaze was deeply sunken as he remembered someone who had left his side not long ago.
That can’t happen again.
I didn’t know how cruel people could become, or how many had to die or be hurt before this insane wheel stopped turning.
But at the same time, I felt relieved.
I possessed enough power to stop that endlessly turning wheel, even if only for a moment.
And if I couldn’t stop it...
I’ll break it.
Having already made up my mind, I looked at President Doramp and suddenly spoke.
“When will the operation to wipe them out begin?”
He understood what I meant.
A smile spread across his face, and at his signal, someone at the pentagonal table stood.
“Assuming the entire UN Security Council agrees, we estimate that it will take two months at the earliest to complete all preparations.
At the longest, it may take more than six months.”
“Two months at the earliest?”
Slow.
Far slower than I’d expected.
I frowned.
“Considering how dangerous you’ve said the situation is, doesn’t that seem like an awfully long time?”
“International law leaves us little choice.
Deploying troops to countries in the Middle East and Africa without their consent would be a clear violation of their sovereignty.”
“Funny.
My modern history textbooks made it look like you fought in the Middle East just fine.
I watched a documentary criticizing the oil money involved, too.”
The key government official who had been listening suddenly lost his ability to speak and cleared his throat.
“Ahem...
That was because of the 9/11 attacks.
Under the new international agreements made after the Great Cataclysm—”
“Never mind.
Two months really is the absolute earliest?”
“Ahem.
Yes.”
I thought for a moment, then leaned close to President Doramp and whispered.
“Can I ask you something?”
“Anything.”
“Suppose someone nobody could identify—some mysterious stranger, for example—wiped out the African rebels or the terrorist groups in the Middle East.
Would that break international law?”
“Pardon?”
“Batman.
Spider-Man.
Someone like that.
And lower your voice before you answer.”
President Doramp stared blankly at me.
When he finally caught on, he struggled to get the words out.
“So you’re saying that Mr.
Jin would hide his identity and launch an operation against the terrorist groups...?”
“Me?
Why would I?”
“But what you just said—”
“I never said that.
It was an example.”
“W-wait, Mr.
Jin.”
“This man is going to cause a disaster.
Why would I do something like that alone?
Unless I were some lunatic who stormed into Ares Guild headquarters by himself.”
A suffocating silence filled the room.
President Doramp stared at me as if I were insane.
At last, he spoke.
“It seems I misunderstood.
What an absurd thought.”
“Right?”
“Yes.
In that case, we’ll end today’s meeting here.
I’m going to leave the holographic tactical map behind by accident.”
“Ah.
An accident.”
“Yes.
It’s top-secret—more secret than any other classified information—so it must never be leaked outside.
Especially since it contains the precise locations of rebel forces in the Middle East and Africa.”
“Anything else?”
“Everything necessary is in the materials.
Not that you’ll have any opportunity to obtain them, Mr.
Jin.
You’ll be heading straight back to Korea, won’t you, Mr.
Johnson?”
Magic Johnson had caught on.
He nodded.
“Of course, Mr.
President.
Though Jin likes to travel.
I wonder if it would be all right for me to take a few days off and spend some time with him.”
“Is that so?
Is there anywhere you particularly like to—”
“Africa and the Middle East,” I said without drawing breath.
“I go crazy for deserts.
My dream is to pee in an oasis and give the Sphinx some Churu.”
Team Leader Choi added calmly, “I was born in summer, so I like hot places.”
“Well.
What a coincidence.”
“Ready, Choi?”
“Of course, Johnson...
No, that sounds a little strange.”
The conversation was bewildering, yet somehow going remarkably smoothly.
Chuck Hagel clamped his cigar between his teeth and put an end to it.
“A lunatic is going to kill lunatics.”
He was right.
Lunatics ought to die at the hands of a lunatic.
It was an ordinary day.
Muhammad Saladir ad-Din, leader of an armed Islamic terrorist group, had interrogated a foreign prisoner and killed a subordinate who’d gotten mouthy.
Then he returned to his bedroom.
Before he could take off his outer clothes, he found an uninvited guest waiting for him.
“Stand up straight, Hassan.”

chapters.title: Chapter 609
paragraphs: “Stand up straight, Hassan.”
Muhammad Saladir ad-Din, leader of a massive Islamic terrorist group, was momentarily taken aback.
Who the hell was Hassan? And whose voice had just spoken in his bedroom, where no one else should have been?
But if something this minor could make him lose his composure, he never would have risen to his current position.
Muhammad answered calmly.
“Sorry, but I’m not Hassan. I don’t know who you are, but you seem to have mistaken me for someone else.”
“I don’t think so.”
Step.
The uninvited guest emerged from the darkness, speaking flawless Arabic without a syllable out of place. When Muhammad saw the intruder’s face, he narrowed his eyes.
What the hell? Who is this strange bastard?
The man’s features were impossible to make out, but the mask covering his face was bizarre enough on its own.
It wasn’t a turban or a strip of cloth. It was made of thick red yarn, with gaping holes for his eyes and mouth.
Calling it a mask was strange enough. Muhammad had never seen a lunatic wear anything like it in the scorching desert.
“Who are you?” he asked.
The man, who appeared to be an assassin, answered.
“I’m Mami...”
“Mami?”
“No, I’m a back scratcher.”
A filial son was one thing, and a hand was another. What the hell was a “filial son’s hand” supposed to be?
One thing was certain: the man hadn’t come to practice filial piety.
“Who sent you?”
“Allah.”
“Allah?”
“Yeah. That Allah you’re always sucking off.”
Muhammad saw the corner of the man’s mouth lift through the hole in his mask.
“He told me to tell you he never ordered any of that shit, so stop interpreting the scripture however the fuck you want.”
“You insane bastard.”
“I never thought I’d live to hear a terrorist leader call me an insane bastard. What a shitty life.”
Muhammad considered when to draw the scimitar at his waist, then spoke with an air of authority.
“You fool. Do you really think you’ll get away with this?”
“Yep. I think I’ll be fine.”
“You seem eager to die. If you surrender now...”
“Yeah, I think I heard that a minute ago. Hang on.”
The man rummaged through his clothes, then pulled something from his sleeve and tossed it.
Thud. Roll...
A round object landed with a heavy thud and rolled to Muhammad’s feet.
Healthy bronze skin, like a desert warrior’s. Eyes frozen wide open. Not a drop of blood stained the cleanly severed neck.
“K-Kasim?”
“Why are you so surprised? Know him?”
Muhammad froze solid.
Kasim was the bodyguard and assassin he trusted more than anyone.
An S-rank Hunter unknown to the world, Kasim was an Awakened assassin whose victims were too numerous to count.
He killed Kasim? So quickly and quietly that no one noticed?
Allah help me. This is real.
Fear gripped Muhammad’s entire body, and his voice trembled.
“I-I’ll give you one last chance. Leave now, and I’ll forget what happened today. There’ll be no retaliation.”
“N-No, dumbass. Why bother with all that when I can just kill you?”
“T-Then I’ll give you as much wealth as you want! Diamonds! What about diamonds?”
His ultimate diamond attack!
“Diamonds? The ones in the safe under your desk? I already took those. They were pretty.”
But it had no effect! Muhammad’s world went dark!
“Bodyguards! Bodyguarrrds! Omari! Sadat! Nasser! Where are you all?”
Muhammad had lost his composure. As he screamed their names, the intruder called along with him.
“Omari! Sadat! Nasser! Right here!”
Thud. Thud. Thud.
“Woohoo! Bodyguard heads acquired!”
How had all those heads come out of that narrow sleeve?
Muhammad stared in horror at the three heads that had fallen one after another. Then—
Bang!
The door, which had remained firmly shut despite the commotion in the bedroom, flew open. A huge man wearing the same kind of mask walked in.
“Is this terrorist asshole still alive?”
Blood soaked his hands. Muhammad froze like a statue, and the intruder raised a hand in greeting.
“There’s still work to do. Are you finished cleaning up?”
“More or less. The other two are downstairs looking around. By the way, can’t I take off this shitty mask? I’ve been suffocating in it.”
“No.”
“Damn it. Then at least let me smoke a cigar. My face is covered by illusion Magic anyway.”

“Why not hang your ID around your neck? Anyone with half a brain would account for illusion Magic. You’re already huge, and with your skills, smoking a cigar would practically advertise that you’re Chuck Hagel.”
Muhammad’s eyes widened as he realized something.
“C-Chuck Hagel? You bastards! You’re from the United States!”
“Gasp. How did this bastard figure that out? Chuck, there must be a spy among the U.S. leadership.”
As the intruder recoiled in surprise, Chuck Hagel put a cigar between his teeth and muttered,
“...Crazy Korean.”
“No, Chuck. Are you insane? If you say Korean here, he’ll understand us.”
“I think I’m going to lose my mind. I think I’m going to lose my mind. I think I’m going out to eat lunch...”
But Chuck Hagel wasn’t the one on the verge of losing his mind. Muhammad was.
As if the name Chuck Hagel hadn’t been enough, now he’d heard Korean.
He couldn’t help thinking of the most famous Korean in the world right now.
“J-Jin Taekyung?”
“No, I’m a back scratcher.”
“D-Don’t give me that bullshit. Who do you think you’re fooling—”
Whoosh! Slash!
Muhammad’s jeweled turban flew off. Even the few strands of hair left on his head were cut away as if erased.
The strange man—or rather, Jin Taekyung—asked the frozen Muhammad, who had forgotten how to breathe.
“I’ll ask again. Who am I?”
“A-A back scratcher.”
“You said Jin Taekyung a moment ago.”
“I-I was mistaken. I must have mistaken you!”
“Really? Can you swear to God?”
“I-I swear by mighty Allah and the Prophet Muhammad! You’re a back scratcher!”
“How dare you swear by God and lie? I’m Jin Taekyung, you apostate bastard!”
“Gyaaaaaah!”
Muhammad, seized by terror, screamed with all his strength. But the sound vanished without ever leaving the bedroom.
A barrier of qi, formed from powerful internal energy, sealed the space without the slightest gap.
“W-Why the hell are you doing this to me?”
Muhammad was crying now. Chuck Hagel let out a quiet laugh.
“Don’t ask us. Ask the god whose name you’ve been peddling. You’ll meet him soon enough anyway.”
“Oh. Of course, there’s something you need to do first.”
Muhammad didn’t hear Chuck Hagel’s last words. What he’d said before filled Muhammad’s mind to bursting.
Meet God? I’m going to die? Me?
Death.
Every human being thought about that word, but not Muhammad. He had always been the one who dealt death, never the one on the receiving end.
A shrill voice slipped between his trembling lips.
“T-That can’t be. It can’t.”
He had joined an armed terrorist organization as a boy. Instead of a pen, he’d held an automatic rifle; after awakening, he’d taken up a sword.
He had risen through the ranks to lead a terrorist organization, kidnapping, imprisoning, and brutally executing countless people.
Muhammad shared a name with the prophet of old. He believed himself a new prophet and leader.
But then... why?
“I-I’m under God’s protection. How could this...”
“It’s simple.”
The corners of Jin Taekyung’s mouth, which had been raised through the holes in his mask, slowly sank.
When Jin Taekyung spoke, his voice had turned cold.
“You’re a fucking lunatic who’s used God’s name to do every kind of insane shit. That’s why you’re dying.”
“Attacking civilians. Kidnapping kids and brainwashing them. Strapping bombs to their bodies for suicide attacks... I can’t even list everything. There’s too much.”
Hack. Ptooey.
Chuck Hagel spat, and the phlegm landed thickly on Muhammad’s face. His rough voice followed, cutting into Muhammad’s ears.

“So I’ll give you one last chance. You’re a fucking terrorist bastard who’d have no right to complain if Johnson tormented you all week. But cooperate, and maybe you’ll have something to say for yourself before God.”
“W-What does that mean?”
“It doesn’t mean we’re letting you live. But you might die with a little less pain.”
“W-What the hell do you want?”
“Orders.”
“What?”

“We know you have countless branches under your command. We also know about the other armed terrorist organization at odds with you. The problem is that wiping them out one by one would never end. So give them orders.”
Hoo...
Chuck Hagel exhaled acrid cigar smoke and grinned.
“Start an all-out offensive against your enemies. Right now. Keep fighting until one side crumbles into the desert sand. Got it, you son of a bitch?”
Facing Muhammad, whose eyes were wide with terror, Jin Taekyung pressed his hands together as if in prayer and added one more thing.
“From now on, kill each other.”
Muhammad finally understood. He had no choices left.
If he refused this final offer, all that awaited him was an agonizing, brutal death.
If I’d been a reasonably popular webnovel author, I could’ve gotten at least five episodes out of this.
Power struggles between terrorist groups large and small, political scenes, a few other ingredients thrown in for flavor—I could probably have stretched it to ten.
But I wasn’t a webnovel author, and there were plenty of terrorist groups and rebel forces we needed to deal with right away.
In short, we had to run our asses off.
Kaboom!
Boom-boom-boom!
At first, we tried to handle things quietly. But the territory was vast and there were too few of us to cover it. Before long, we started getting a warm welcome.
And the single word enemy included a hail of gunfire and artillery shells, along with Awakened who called themselves “warriors of God.”
“Kill them!”
“They’re the ones who wiped out the mujahideen!”
“Thirty million dollars, paid immediately, to whoever captures or kills them!”
Shishshishshishk!
Dodging attacks raining down from every direction, I shouted in amazement.
“Wow, our bounty went up!”
“Shut up and dodge!”
“I think it was ten million yesterday. So this is why Luffy goes pirating!”
“Fucking shut up! Motherfuckeeer!”
“Fifty million! Let’s hit fifty million! The Grand Line is just ahead!”
Sometimes we fought pitched battles. Other times, we slipped in like thieves in the night and wiped out a terrorist group or rebel force.
And when we reached the Grand Line—no, the desert—a living treasure was waiting for us.
“Leader of the Sooni faction. Omar al-Hussein, right?”
“It’s Sunni, not Sooni.”
“What are you talking about, you bastard who looks like Jeomsoon from the land steward’s house?”
“Bastard...!”
“Hey, kid. Spring fists taste best in spring.”
Crack!
We didn’t stop. We fought across dozens of regions every day, capturing the leaders of terrorist groups and rebel forces or controlling them with Magic Johnson’s custom brainwashing Magic.
And just like that... a week passed in the blink of an eye.

Chuck Hagel spat, and the phlegm landed thickly on Muhammad’s face.
His rough voice followed, cutting into Muhammad’s ears.
“So I’ll give you one last chance.
You’re a fucking terrorist bastard who’d have no right to complain if Johnson tormented you all week.
But cooperate, and maybe you’ll have something to say for yourself before God.”
“W-What does that mean?”
“It doesn’t mean we’re letting you live.
But you might die with a little less pain.”
“W-What the hell do you want?”
“Orders.”
“What?”
“We know you have countless branches under your command.
We also know about the other armed terrorist organization at odds with you.
The problem is that wiping them out one by one would never end.
So give them orders.”
Hoo...
Chuck Hagel exhaled acrid cigar smoke and grinned.
“Start an all-out offensive against your enemies.
Right now.
Keep fighting until one side crumbles into the desert sand.
Got it, you son of a bitch?”
Facing Muhammad, whose eyes were wide with terror, Jin Taekyung pressed his hands together as if in prayer and added one more thing.
“From now on, kill each other.”
Muhammad finally understood.
He had no choices left.
If he refused this final offer, all that awaited him was an agonizing, brutal death.
If I’d been a reasonably popular webnovel author, I could’ve gotten at least five episodes out of this.
Power struggles between terrorist groups large and small, political scenes, a few other ingredients thrown in for flavor—I could probably have stretched it to ten.
But I wasn’t a webnovel author, and there were plenty of terrorist groups and rebel forces we needed to deal with right away.
In short, we had to run our asses off.
Kaboom!
Boom-boom-boom!
At first, we tried to handle things quietly.
But the territory was vast and there were too few of us to cover it.
Before long, we started getting a warm welcome.
And the single word enemy included a hail of gunfire and artillery shells, along with Awakened who called themselves “warriors of God.”
“Kill them!”
“They’re the ones who wiped out the mujahideen!”
“Thirty million dollars, paid immediately, to whoever captures or kills them!”
Shishshishshishk!
Dodging attacks raining down from every direction, I shouted in amazement.
“Wow, our bounty went up!”
“Shut up and dodge!”
“I think it was ten million yesterday.
So this is why Luffy goes pirating!”
“Fucking shut up!
Motherfuckeeer!”
“Fifty million!
Let’s hit fifty million!
The Grand Line is just ahead!”
Sometimes we fought pitched battles.
Other times, we slipped in like thieves in the night and wiped out a terrorist group or rebel force.
And when we reached the Grand Line—no, the desert—a living treasure was waiting for us.
“Leader of the Sooni faction.
Omar al-Hussein, right?”
“It’s Sunni, not Sooni.”
“What are you talking about, you bastard who looks like Jeomsoon from the land steward’s house?”
“Bastard...!”
“Hey, kid.
Spring fists taste best in spring.”
Crack!
We didn’t stop.
We fought across dozens of regions every day, capturing the leaders of terrorist groups and rebel forces or controlling them with Magic Johnson’s custom brainwashing Magic.
And just like that... a week passed in the blink of an eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 610
paragraphs: While dealing with armed terrorist groups and rebel forces in the Middle East, I came to realize two things.
First, there was no end to human malice.
Second, this horrific wheel would keep turning.
There were just too many bad people in the world.
They were weeds, plain and simple—viruses found everywhere on Earth. No matter how many you pulled out, more would grow somewhere else and make the world sick.
There was no way to stop this damn wheel forever.
Still, one thing is certain.
Even if I couldn’t stop it forever, I could break it and bring it to a halt for a while.
And the old man sitting in front of me was one of the biggest parts keeping that enormous wheel turning.
“Hey there, young man in the strange mask.”
The old man spoke calmly, stroking a teacup that gave off a strange scent with his wrinkled hand.
“Finding me was impressive, but... the world doesn’t change that easily.”
Al Diab Jawahiri—a man with a name as long as any other Arab’s—remained calm despite the thunderous noises outside and the uninvited guest who had barged in.
He’s clearly nothing more than a powerless old man.

I didn’t know whether that remarkable composure came from more than a century of experience, or from the fact that he was the leader of Al-Qaeda, a colossal terrorist organization that divided control of the Middle East with ISIS.
What mattered was that he was wrong.
“It does change. People change, and someday the world will, too.”
“Do you know how many Muslims bow before mighty Allah?”
“No. Other than the one sitting in front of me.”
“Twenty-five percent, they say. Twenty-five percent of the entire world. That’s over a billion people.”
Al Diab smiled faintly and continued.
“You’re fighting more than a billion Muslims. You’ve made mighty Allah and His servants your enemies.”
The ramblings of a crazy old man weren’t going to shake me. I smiled back.
“Not Muslims. Terrorists like you.”

“I won’t deny that some of them still do not sympathize with us. It is a truly regrettable thing. But in the end, we are brothers. Bound together in the name of Allah, we will eventually gather beneath a single flag.”
“Is that why your ‘brothers’ split into Shiites and Sunnis and have spent centuries beating the hell out of each other?”
Al Diab answered without batting an eye.
“There is nothing strange about it. Husbands and wives. Brothers and sisters. Even within one household, people quarrel endlessly.”
“That’s because your family’s a complete mess. Mine isn’t.”
“What can one do? The conflict has been passed down from our ancestors. It is only a small dispute born of trivial misunderstandings and differences of opinion—a step on the way to becoming one.”
Al Diab didn’t understand. No, he didn’t want to understand in the slightest.
He didn’t understand how much suffering innocent people had endured because of those trivial misunderstandings and conflicts, and that hollow word unity.
Or how many countless people would suffer in the future.
Monster.
The old man before me was a monster, too. One consumed by twisted beliefs and stubborn conviction.
Then I saw a broad smile spread across his face, and a chill ran through me.
“What do you say, misguided young man? Why not put an end to this foolishness and join me?”
“Your eyes are wavering. Your heart is shaken. Do not suffer while trapped by countless afflictions. Enter the warm embrace of Allah.”
His voice was perfectly serene as his deeply wrinkled hand reached slowly toward me.
I watched him with a faint tremor in my eyes, then let out a small sigh.
“Has living this long driven you out of your mind, old man...? What kind of shit are you trying to pull?”
Shock flashed in his eyes.
“If you get caught trying something, you pay in blood. Pick one: neck or wrist.”
The instant our eyes met—
Shk! Bang!
Everything happened in an instant.

The slender old man’s wrist shot into the air, severed by the short sword I swung at the speed of a ray of light. At the same time, a bullet fired from a special firearm hidden deep inside his dark, voluminous sleeve pierced somewhere beyond my shoulder.
In short, I dodged. He didn’t.
“Aaaaaaargh!”
Quite a set of lungs on the old man.
The scream was impossibly loud for someone well over a hundred years old. Clutching the stump of his cleanly severed wrist, Al Diab collapsed onto the carpet.
And then... another group moved even faster.
Shishshishshishk!
They emerged like ghosts from the ceiling, the walls, and beneath the carpet-covered floor. Beams of light and gusts of wind swirled from their hands.
Front, back, left, right—they surrounded me from all thirty-six directions and unleashed a terrifying assault.
But instead of dodging, I chose to attack.
Inventory open. Equip Fire Dragon Armor.
At the same instant—
Kakak! Ting-ting!
Aura tore through the air and struck the reddish armor, only to vanish. Blackened arrowheads bounced off it harmlessly.
Of course they did. Nothing short of the concentrated energy called Force or an Aura Blade could pierce the Fire Dragon Armor.
The men had the air of Murim assassins about them. I had no idea who had trained them, or how, but they realized the same thing immediately.
Whoosh!
No orders. Not even an exchanged glance.
The men in black turbans moved like machines following a programmed command. They abandoned my armored upper body and aimed for the exposed areas, including my lower body.
But the Fire Dragon Armor was a divine weapon capable of changing the course of a fight.
Against someone stronger than me, it could let me hold my own for a while. Against someone my equal, it could give me an overwhelming advantage.
And against people far weaker than me?
Thirty men? Even if ten times as many rushed me, they would be the ones to fall.
“Come on in, you crow bastards.”
With that short taunt, I brought down the short sword in my hand.
Whoosh!
One horizontal strike was enough.
Kabooooom!
Superheated air erupted along the blade, melting Magic and weapons alike. The space around me warped.
As the mighty power that had lain dormant stretched and woke, the underground hideout shook from top to bottom.
Rumble-rumble-rumble!
The ground and ceiling weren’t the only things shaking.
Several pairs of eyes visible between the black turbans quivered faintly.
Maybe it was because the men caught in my sword’s path had died without so much as a final cry. Maybe they had felt the unbelievable gap in our strength.
Maybe it was both.
Either way, it was too late to retreat.
“Not coming? Then I’ll come to you.”
The word outnumbered had long since lost its meaning for me.
I had occasionally fought dozens of people, sometimes hundreds, and rarely even thousands—and I had survived every time.
The battle about to unfold here was nothing more than an extension of all the battles that had come before.
Shing!
A blade shot up from the ground and grazed my chin.
The patient one had never revealed himself, even while his comrades appeared one after another. But his attack had failed, and the price was death.
Crack!
I unleashed a grappling technique at lightning speed.
Before the man who had performed the bizarre feat of rotating his neck several times could collapse, I thrust out one hand.
Shishshik! Puk!
Five streams of Finger Qi cut through the air. Some of the crows launching themselves off the ceiling and walls fell.
The others who rushed in while leaving behind their comrade, whose neck had been pierced clean through, met much the same fate.
Fwoooooosh! Slash!
Their One Strike carried desperate resolve.
But the gap between will and ability was vast and deep.
My short sword split one man in two along with his sword. His body fell like a kite with its string cut.
Fwoosh! Boom!

I drove a palm strike at the blood spraying through the air. It evaporated in the terrible heat, and another attacker coming at me from beyond it flew backward even faster than he’d approached, slamming into the wall.
Boom!
The impact shook the room.
But even if the whole world had been turned upside down, their attacks wouldn’t have stopped.
Whoosh!
Neck. Calf. Hand.
Three attacks whistled through the air at once, each aimed at a different target.
Instead of dodging, I stepped forward and swung the short sword in my hand.
No. I threw it.
Fwoooooosh! Crunch!
No one could survive with a Force-infused sword embedded in their heart.
The hilt slipped from its owner’s hand as he died.
I reached for the two blades already closing in on me.
Grab!
Aura was an incredibly sharp and destructive concentration of energy. Cutting through bare hands imbued with Force was another matter.
I tightened my grip on the blades.
Grnk. Crack!
Two swords broke in half. Two pairs of eyes went wide with shock.
I said goodbye without a trace of emotion.
“Go.”
“W-Wait...!”
“Oh, take these with you.”
Had they ever given the people they killed time to say even one last word?
Maybe they had. I wasn’t going to.
Puk!
“Guh!”
They let out gurgling cries as I drove their own broken blades into their chests. The light faded from their eyes.
Thud.
The two bodies fell like rotten logs. I looked around.
No one else came at me. There was no more sound of attacks cutting through the air, no more death.
Only one man remained, staring at me in terror.
“Satan. You... you’re Satan.”
“Maybe. At least to people like you.”
Satan. I’d first heard the word from a deacon at church when I was little. By now, it felt almost as familiar as my own name.
I pulled the short sword from a corpse and approached Al Diab, muttering,
“Funny, isn’t it? The people who act more like demons than anyone else keep calling me Satan.”
“Y-You devil! Stay away from me! Evil Satan! Demon! In God’s name, begone!”
“...I’ve heard that a lot on Line 1. I’m suddenly getting homesick for a place I’ve never even missed.”
I was briefly wondering whether Al Diab had studied in Korea when the iron door leading outside opened. The noise beyond it had died away, and the Skeleton King appeared, covered in dust.
“Vile human. Are you finished?”
“Yeah. You?”
“I finished a little while ago. I’m getting ready to work. There’s no shortage of usable material, and I certainly have no objection, but... are you sure about this?”
“About what?”
“They’re human, like you. Your own kind. Using them for my Skeleton army might bother you...”
“They’re not my kind. Besides, this way I can go back to Korea with peace of mind.”
I answered without hesitation, then introduced the Skeleton King to Al Diab, who had frozen with his eyes wide open.
“Oh. This one’s an actual demon.”
Fight barbarians with barbarians.
Barbarians should be dealt with by barbarians. Terrorists should be dealt with by what used to be terrorists.
I jabbed the Skeleton King in the side.
“Hey. Do it.”
“...I don’t want to.”
“Come on, don’t be like that. Do it already.”
Looking less than pleased, he gave Al Diab a thumbs-up.
“Don’t worry! The undead army will take care of those piece-of-shit terrorists!”
Oh, I couldn’t resist that.

chapters.title: Chapter 611
paragraphs: “Allah! O great Allah!”
“Deal with him, Satan.”
“Goodbye, vile human.”
I left Al Diab, who was screaming loud enough to split the heavens, in the Skeleton King’s hands and turned away. Whatever happened after that was no longer my concern.

If he had been the leader of some run-of-the-mill terrorist organization, there would have been nothing left to discuss—I would have executed him on the spot. But the leader of Al-Qaeda was another matter entirely. Magic Johnson or the Skeleton King would probably find a way to put him to good use. Whether through Magic or some kind of divine power.
Maybe I should have learned the Soul-Seizing Technique.
I felt a twinge of regret.

The Soul-Seizing Technique bewitched and controlled people. It was classified among the demonic, heterodox arts, but there were people in the orthodox faction who had learned it. The same went for the disguise technique.
I hadn’t learned either one. Not because I didn’t need them—I’d just been too busy putting on a tearful shitshow trying to stay alive.
Come to think of it, there’s a practitioner of demonic, heterodox arts nearby...
I wasn’t sure whether that guy had learned the Soul-Seizing Technique. If I got the chance, maybe I could learn a few techniques from him that might prove useful in the future.
While I was thinking about matters in the Murim, the enormous underground hideout, which resembled a giant anthill, finally came to an end. An endless sandy desert filled my field of vision.
Beneath the glittering stars, a man puffing thick clouds of cigar smoke opened his mouth in a rough voice.
“Back already? That was quicker than I expected. Did you catch Al Diab?”
I looked over the bodies of the terrorists scattered around him and answered.
“Yes. I left him with the Skeleton King.”
“Allah’s faithful servant, in the hands of a monster. Good. Damn old bastard. I’d have liked to see his face.”
“He didn’t seem to like it very much. He’s probably still screaming and calling him Satan.”
Chuck Hagel laughed with satisfaction.
He’d learned the Skeleton King’s true identity three days ago. In the short conversation that followed, he’d proved that he thought nothing like an ordinary person.
“Undead?”
“Yes.”
“Is Undead his last name? Because I could’ve sworn you called him Stone King earlier.”
“No. Undead is his gender. Wait, not gender—species.”
“You said he was from Georgia.”
“Surprise. He’s actually the Skeleton King from the Demon Realm.”
“So he’s a monster.”
“Yes.”
“Hey, motherfucker. Are you kidding me? Why is there a monster here—”
“Technically, an undead monster. A named undead monster, to be even more precise.”
“...Are you people out of your minds? What the hell are you doing?”
“He’s a monster, but he saved my life from an Arch Lich during the Small Cataclysm.”
“What?”
“Oh, and he helped suppress more than ten Mutated Gates and three Gate Waves in Korea.”
“Holy shit. So he’s a war veteran. Welcome, undead warrior.”
Black cat or white cat.
People said it didn’t matter whether a cat was black or white as long as it caught mice. Even so, Chuck Hagel’s way of thinking was truly extraordinary.

My grandfather was a goddamn Indian-killer who even received medals. But I don’t give a fuck about that. If someone can deal with fucking terrorists and Gates and has the heart to devote themselves to helping people, what does skin color matter?
“Chuck. He doesn’t have skin.”
“Don’t care what color his bones are, either.”

Chuck Hagel’s willingness to look past not just race but species was enough to make my heart swell. He even showed an ambition I could hardly believe coming from the Secretary of Defense of the United States.
“I won’t tell the President.”
“I was hoping you’d say that, Chuck, but... can you really do that?”
“He didn’t ask.”
“Oh.”
“That’s how the military works. If you don’t get caught, it’s fine. Write ‘military,’ read it as ‘sham.’”
Of course, that was complete nonsense. How could a country’s Secretary of Defense know something like this and keep quiet just because the President hadn’t asked?

But it was also the sort of crazy thing Chuck Hagel could get away with. Uncle Chuck was, along with Magic Johnson, a symbol of the United States. The legendary war heroes born from the Great Cataclysm had been granted tremendous love and affection—along with an unspoken free pass.
Even with that free pass, it’s still crazy. Hm.
Fortunately, Chuck Hagel had done crazy things often enough.
I looked at him warmly.
“What’s with that look?”
“I just really like you, Chuck.”
“Was that why you were so close to Johnson?”
“...That’s how you took it? Come to think of it, where are the other two?”
I hadn’t seen Team Leader Choi or Magic Johnson anywhere nearby. Chuck Hagel chewed on his cigar as he answered.
“They’re investigating the Gate. These bastards even had a secret Magic Gem laboratory.”
A secret laboratory. I’d half expected it.

A middling terrorist group might not have had the resources, but Al-Qaeda carried out attacks around the world. It had people and supplies to spare. A Magic Gem laboratory cost an astronomical amount to run, but finding one here wasn’t much of a surprise.
“How big?”
“Bigger than we expected. Choi and Johnson think it was built at least ten years ago.”
“Ten years?”

“Yes. I don’t know whether they conducted other experiments here before this, or whether they were planning terrorist attacks using Magic Gems, as we feared... But it’s clear that they’ve been plotting something for quite a long time.”
“Hmm.”
Apparently Go Jun hadn’t been the first to think of using Magic Gems to kill people. Given that Al-Qaeda was a terrorist organization, that wasn’t exactly surprising.
“Did they get anywhere? Have they found something?”
“Who knows? We’ll have to squeeze the terrorist researchers for answers. But if they’d achieved anything, I imagine an even bigger incident would already have happened.”
“That’s true.”

“At the very least, the terrorist attacks that took place in Texas and elsewhere this time have little to do with Al-Qaeda. If it had been them, they would have already obtained data through human experimentation. They would have had no reason to put on such a stupid show of suicide.”

He had a point. If the attacks had succeeded, that might have been different. But Al-Qaeda had no reason to throw away valuable Hunters and Magic Gems on a suicide show that only advertised their stupidity. It wasn’t a banzai charge or a kamikaze attack.
They would just attract a whole lot of attention and get beaten to a pulp.
As I thought that, Chuck Hagel spoke again.
“Lately, I’ve found myself thinking about something. Maybe it’s impossible to completely eradicate these bastards. Maybe that’s something we’ll never be able to do.”
He looked unusually drained today. The cigar he had been holding in his mouth was extended toward me.
“I don’t smoke.”
“I know. The point is, this goddamn American military cigar was in their possession.”
I muttered quietly.
“They have someone on the inside?”

“If it had only been the cigar, I wouldn’t have said anything. But... there was enough to fill a mountain. Food, experimental equipment, medical equipment, advanced missiles, even artifacts. Most of it was the kind of material that couldn’t be taken overseas without approval from the Ministry of National Defense.”
I firmly patted his shoulder as he muttered bitterly.
“Cheer up, Chuck. It’s not the first time, is it? And it’s not as if you didn’t know.”
“Hah. That’s comforting.”
As we had destroyed more than a few dozen terrorist organizations, the only things we had seen weren’t corpses and pools of blood. What we had seen most nakedly was the shameful face of the world.
How did they get all that stuff? Who gave it to them?
Military officials? Senior politicians? Black-market dealers who’d do anything for money? Maybe all of them.
I didn’t know. But one thing was certain: someone was watering the weeds we needed to pull out by the roots.
“Bastards.”
Chuck Hagel hurled his cigar into the distance. Its faint ember vanished in the cold darkness of the desert. He watched it disappear, then spoke on a sigh.
“Crazy Korean. What are you going to do now?”
The sudden question pulled me from my thoughts, but I answered calmly. I had already made up my mind several days ago.
“I’m going back.”
“To South Korea? Well, it couldn’t be North Korea, so I suppose that’s right.”
“Hard to say.”
Half right, half wrong. I neither confirmed nor denied it, only shrugged.
Chuck Hagel smiled ruefully.
“Right. You can’t keep playing masked vigilante in that ridiculous getup forever.”
“Hmm. I wouldn’t call it particularly ridiculous.”
“You serious? Is it a South Korean fashion thing?”
I let out a quiet laugh.
“I didn’t mean to us.”
“Hm?”
“The rebels and terrorists. How do you think it looks to them?”
Chuck Hagel’s mouth closed tightly.
I looked up at the night sky, crowded with constellations I couldn’t name.
“The Mujahideen. Al-Qaeda. ISIS’s Syrian branch...”
I recited the names of the major terrorist groups whose leaders and headquarters we’d destroyed over the past week, then the names of the smaller groups we’d uprooted entirely.
“We haven’t dealt with all of them, but we’ve sent a clear warning.”
They didn’t know our names or ages, let alone our nationalities or what we looked like.
We wore masks, avoided surveillance with Magic Johnson’s Magic, and fought while changing our weapons and combat methods.
And...
“Nothing’s scarier than an enemy you can’t identify.”

In just one week, we’d become something terrorist organizations feared. They couldn’t catch us, even with enormous bounties on our heads. Without knowing who we were, they couldn’t use their favorite tactic against us: retaliatory attacks.
On top of that, several leaders of some of the world’s most notorious international terrorist organizations had already died at our hands or been controlled into starting internal conflicts.
“If they don’t want the same thing to happen to them, they’ll keep their heads down.”
A weak deterrent invited defiance. Overwhelming force inspired fear.

The prisoners we’d freed had already stood before microphones and cameras to tell the world what they’d seen and suffered. Once again, the international community was burning like a furnace—over the horrors unfolding around the world, and over us.
“Given time, things will get a little better.”
The weed called malice sprouts first in a person’s heart. People who harbor it go on to do evil.
But what could you do? You couldn’t pull every weed out of every heart. You could pull out the weeds you could see.
“It’s not about how many weeds you pull. It’s about how many people pull them together. You and me, Chuck. Like we did.”
One person could pull one. Someone else, two. Or three.
If everyone paid attention and did their part, wouldn’t the weeds eventually disappear? I’d only recently come to that small but profound realization.
“Well, that’s what I think, anyway.”
Had I been talking too much? I let the silence settle. Chuck Hagel studied me with an odd expression, then spoke.
“Hey. Can I ask you something?”
“Anything.”
“I didn’t get an answer earlier... Where exactly are you going back to? Judging by what you just said, it sounds like you should at least be going to the Vatican.”
I laughed quietly.
“It’s hard to explain. Somewhere like this.”
“Where, Afghanistan?”
“Farther than that. Much farther.”
“...Much farther?”
Chuck Hagel looked bewildered, and my smile deepened despite myself.
Yes. It was time to go back.
After I took care of the one thing I’d put off until the very end.

chapters.title: Chapter 612
paragraphs: “Come out.”
His voice was low and steady, his eyes glinting sharply in the dark.
I watched him without answering. After a brief silence, a click sounded and the living room lit up.
The man took a cautious step forward and spoke again, putting more force into his voice.
“I know you’re hiding. Come out. Do you know who I am?”
Of course I did. I knew his name and face, even his age and hometown. I just hadn’t expected him to pull this the moment I came home.
“All right, last chance. If you don’t come out by the time I count to three, I’m calling a younger buddy of mine. He’s a really strong, successful Hunter. One. Two...”
I was curious about what would happen after he counted to three, but after seeing everything there was to see, continuing to watch felt embarrassing.
I spoke with a sigh.
“Don’t tell me that close younger friend is me?”
“Well, would you look at that. Guess I was right.”
Jinho stood frozen like a statue, staring at me with his eyes wide.
“Wh-What? Why are you coming out of there?”
“I knew you were going to call me anyway, so I came early. Happy?”
Jinho fell silent for a moment, then asked with a grave expression, “How much did you see?”
“From ‘Come out.’”
“Ah, fuck...”
“You looked cool. Your presence was so overwhelming I almost came out without being asked.”
“Are you making fun of me?”
“Yeah.”
Jinho stared at me after that shameless answer, then let out a quiet laugh.
“You bastard. You haven’t changed at all.”
Why did those few words make me so glad to see him? So grateful?
I smiled back. “I’m hungry. Make me some ramyeon.”
Sitting across from each other with a steaming pot between us felt like going back a year.
Of course, we’d both changed a lot since then.
“First time I’ve seen you in a suit, hyung. You used to wear nothing but those ragged tracksuits.”
“Hey, they weren’t ragged. That’s a pretty expensive brand.”
“When did you buy them?”
“Hmm. High school?”
How old had Jinho hyung been then? After thinking for a moment, I nodded.
“So they weren’t like rags. They were rags. Get me some water. No, wait. Got any soju?”
“You might as well walk into a barbecue restaurant and ask if they have meat.”
“...At this rate, you’re going to die young.”

“I would’ve quit ages ago if it weren’t for that asshole Section Chief Kim. That fucking bastard isn’t even that far from me in age, but he picks fights over every little thing and acts like a complete jackass.”
Jinho yanked his tie loose and downed three shots of soju in a row.
Late last year, he’d finally passed the civil service exam he’d spent so long preparing for.
“So you really did become a civil servant. The world’s coming to an end.”
“Listen to this bastard. You thought I wouldn’t?”
“No. Becoming one is beside the point. I thought you’d drop dead in the act while watching porn before you ever got there.”
“...Hmm. That’s actually a fair point.”
The fact that he didn’t deny it meant he still had a shred of conscience.
If the government had a Ministry of Porn, he could have risen all the way to minister. With Sora Aoi as deputy minister and Asuka Kirara as spokesperson, he’d have ruled Pornhub.
Unfortunately, no such deranged ministry existed. Instead, Jinho had passed a special recruitment exam and been assigned to the Hunter and Gate Management Department, known as a plum posting.
I suspected our friendship had earned him a few invisible bonus points.
Glug, glug, glug.
Jinho filled his glass to the brim, then asked, “What brings you here?”
“In case you’ve forgotten, this is my place. Though lately I can’t tell if it’s an officetel or a garbage dump.”
“I’m asking because the owner hasn’t shown his face in over two or three months, you punk.”
“Well, I came to see you. And there’s something I need to pick up.”
“Pick up? If it’s clothes, just buy some. You’ve got money coming out of your ears.”
“Money won’t help. Nobody sells it.”
“What is it?”
Jinho looked puzzled, then gave a short exclamation.
“Oh. That old capsule?”
“Yeah. Good thing you didn’t throw it away.”
“You said you’d kill me if I did.”
“That’s why it’s a good thing. I really would’ve had to kill you. Phew.”
“...You’re joking, right? Please tell me you’re joking.”
The game capsule that had first led me to the Murim had sat here unused ever since the System allowed me to Login and Logout freely without it.
But that didn’t make it a piece of junk I could toss aside. That old capsule had done more than anything else to make me who I was. It was priceless.
“I don’t wipe the dining table, but I wipe that capsule down once a week,” Jinho said. “It still doesn’t work, though. Why take it?”
“Just because. For decoration, I guess.”
“Isn’t that thing haunted? Remember when you lived at Hope Goshiwon? You slept in it and had some weird nightmare...”
Oh. That had happened, hadn’t it?
Jinho was bringing up my first Logout. I hurried to change the subject.
“Did you see the news? Things got pretty crazy in the Middle East and Afghanistan.”
“Huh? Where did that come from?”
“I’m asking if you saw it.”

“Of course I did. Yesterday the Middle Eastern terrorist groups and the Afghan rebels even issued a joint statement. Said they’d refrain from terrorism and keep their men in line from now on. Basically surrendered because they got scared.”
“Don’t let your guard down. It’ll only last a little while.”
“Still, those five weirdos in masks are incredible, aren’t they?”
The change of subject seemed to have worked. I breathed an inward sigh of relief and nodded.
“They are.”
“Well, anyway.”
Jinho slurped up his noodles, washed them down with soju, and went on.
“You’ve had it rough. A Monster Wave right after the new year, humans worse than monsters, and now trips to the desert and Africa.”
“What do you mean, rough? It was just something I had to do...”
I suddenly faltered and let the end of the sentence trail off.
Wait. What the hell had he just said?
“Sorry, what?”
“What you heard. I took a shot in the dark, and it looks like I was more or less right.”

“Come on. How many people in the world could do something like that? Everyone says they wish the terrorists would die and they never want to see those rebel bastards again. But who’d actually put on a mask and do something about it? More to the point, who could?”
Jinho gave a quiet laugh at my wide-eyed stare.

“Some people have probably guessed, too, but they’re keeping quiet. There’s no evidence, and it’s not as if they have any reason to blame you. But one low-ranking civil servant happens to know what kind of person the masked man is—and even shares ramyeon with him—so he can casually sound him out like this.”
I rubbed the back of my head, which somehow felt numb.
I had suspected I would be named as a prime suspect, but I hadn’t expected to get caught this absurdly easily.
“I-I’m really not him.”
“Sure. Let’s say you aren’t. When did you get back?”
Damn it. There was no saving this.
I sighed, filled my soju glass, and answered. “Three days ago. No, four.”
“Good. Now you’re cooperating.”
“Don’t tell anyone. Never mind that it’s classified—you’d be in danger.”
Team Leader Choi, my family, and I were always surrounded by protection no one could see. Jinho wasn’t.
He understood what I meant immediately and smacked his lips.
“Hmm. I feel like a big shot.”
“You might get a bomb delivered before you become one.”
“Maybe. But even if they all know, they won’t be able to touch me, will they? They won’t know what Jin Taekyung might do if he completely loses it. Hah, isn’t this what you call Untouchable?”
Jinho laughed without a care, then asked, “Anyway, how busy have you been? You can’t even remember when you got back.”
“Hmm.”
How busy?
I scratched at the beard that had grown thick before I knew it.
“I train day and night. Eat with my family, then train some more.”
“Train? Why does someone at your level need to train?”
“You graduated from a prestigious university and still spent nearly ten more years studying. Same thing.”
“You bastard, going straight for the sore spot. Besides, how are we the same? It’s not just a different field—we’re on completely different levels.”
He had a point. His prestigious university admitted hundreds of students every year, and about as many graduated.
But I still needed training.
There was no end to learning, and gongbu—study—wasn’t limited to academics.
To be precise, I’m not learning something new. I’m slowly going back over what I already know.
In that sense, my training was a kind of review. Study for my own sake, and for the sake of this world.
Unfortunately, I still hadn’t managed to bring it all together.
“Ugh, look at that serious expression. It makes me want to slap you in the cheek.”
“...I’m in the middle of being serious, so could you shut that mouth of yours?”
“Put yourself in my shoes. What would you do?”
“Hmm. Fair enough. Have a drink.”
We clinked glasses. Jinho knocked back his soju, poked at the noodles that had gone cold, and asked, “So? Is the training going well?”
“More or less. I started preparing about a month ago, so I’m nearly done, but... it’s not easy.”
I wasn’t exaggerating.

I was like a child trying to assemble a ten-thousand-piece puzzle. As I checked each piece and fit them together, I felt my own shortcomings and regretted what I lacked. Now, unable to find the final piece, I was groping around in the dark.
And I already knew the name of the darkness obscuring my sight.
The heart demon.
The dark cloud over my heart refused to clear. My worries about the Murim and the modern world... and, more than anything, the last sight of Kim Hwajong kept returning to me.
His voice, which seemed as though it could fade away at any moment.
His eyes slowly closing in the red snowfield covered with blood.
Maybe I hadn’t come here for the capsule after all. Maybe I’d come to find some comfort.
Not with the family I loved or the companions at my side, but with a friend living his own life in a completely different world. Maybe I’d just wanted to clink glasses with him like we used to.
Yeah. That was it.
All at once, I felt more at ease.
I hadn’t shaken off the heart demon entirely, but acknowledging everything that had happened—and everything that troubled me—lifted some of the weight from my heart.
I also realized that I wasn’t where I needed to be.
“I’m leaving.”
“The ramyeon’s cold. I was going to make tofu kimchi to go with the drinks... Wait, now?”
“Yeah. I remembered something I have to do. Drink by yourself.”
“Are you crazy?”
“No. I’m your landlord. Want to start paying rent this month?”
Jinho hyung, who had been glaring at me fiercely, immediately bent deeply at the waist.
“Get home safely, Boss.”
“Will do.”
I laughed quietly and headed for the front door. Behind me, Jinho called out in a rush.
“Hey! What about the capsule?”
“Next time. I’ll take it next time.”
Even as I said it, I knew that next time, I might give him the same answer and leave the capsule where it was. I might come only to clink glasses with him, just as I had today.
“All right. Hang in there, you bastard.”
Someone’s quiet murmur reached my ears as I walked on.

I watched him without answering.
After a brief silence, a click sounded and the living room lit up.
The man took a cautious step forward and spoke again, putting more force into his voice.
“I know you’re hiding.
Come out.
Do you know who I am?”
Of course I did.
I knew his name and face, even his age and hometown.
I just hadn’t expected him to pull this the moment I came home.
“All right, last chance.
If you don’t come out by the time I count to three, I’m calling a younger buddy of mine.
He’s a really strong, successful Hunter.
One.
Two...”
I was curious about what would happen after he counted to three, but after seeing everything there was to see, continuing to watch felt embarrassing.
I spoke with a sigh.
“Don’t tell me that close younger friend is me?”
“Well, would you look at that.
Guess I was right.”
Jinho stood frozen like a statue, staring at me with his eyes wide.
“Wh-What?
Why are you coming out of there?”
“I knew you were going to call me anyway, so I came early.
Happy?”
Jinho fell silent for a moment, then asked with a grave expression, “How much did you see?”
“From ‘Come out.’”
“Ah, fuck...”
“You looked cool.
Your presence was so overwhelming I almost came out without being asked.”
“Are you making fun of me?”
“Yeah.”
Jinho stared at me after that shameless answer, then let out a quiet laugh.
“You bastard.
You haven’t changed at all.”
Why did those few words make me so glad to see him?
So grateful?
I smiled back.
“I’m hungry.
Make me some ramyeon.”
Sitting across from each other with a steaming pot between us felt like going back a year.
Of course, we’d both changed a lot since then.
“First time I’ve seen you in a suit, hyung.
You used to wear nothing but those ragged tracksuits.”
“Hey, they weren’t ragged.
That’s a pretty expensive brand.”
“When did you buy them?”
“Hmm.
High school?”
How old had Jinho hyung been then?
After thinking for a moment, I nodded.
“So they weren’t like rags.
They were rags.
Get me some water.
No, wait.
Got any soju?”
“You might as well walk into a barbecue restaurant and ask if they have meat.”
“...At this rate, you’re going to die young.”
“I would’ve quit ages ago if it weren’t for that asshole Section Chief Kim.
That fucking bastard isn’t even that far from me in age, but he picks fights over every little thing and acts like a complete jackass.”
Jinho yanked his tie loose and downed three shots of soju in a row.
Late last year, he’d finally passed the civil service exam he’d spent so long preparing for.
“So you really did become a civil servant.
The world’s coming to an end.”
“Listen to this bastard.
You thought I wouldn’t?”
“No.
Becoming one is beside the point.
I thought you’d drop dead in the act while watching porn before you ever got there.”
That’s actually a fair point.”
The fact that he didn’t deny it meant he still had a shred of conscience.
If the government had a Ministry of Porn, he could have risen all the way to minister.
With Sora Aoi as deputy minister and Asuka Kirara as spokesperson, he’d have ruled Pornhub.
Unfortunately, no such deranged ministry existed.
Instead, Jinho had passed a special recruitment exam and been assigned to the Hunter and Gate Management Department, known as a plum posting.
I suspected our friendship had earned him a few invisible bonus points.
Glug, glug, glug.
Jinho filled his glass to the brim, then asked, “What brings you here?”
“In case you’ve forgotten, this is my place.
Though lately I can’t tell if it’s an officetel or a garbage dump.”
“I’m asking because the owner hasn’t shown his face in over two or three months, you punk.”
“Well, I came to see you.
And there’s something I need to pick up.”
“Pick up?
If it’s clothes, just buy some.
You’ve got money coming out of your ears.”
“Money won’t help.
Nobody sells it.”
“What is it?”
Jinho looked puzzled, then gave a short exclamation.
“Oh.
That old capsule?”
“Yeah.
Good thing you didn’t throw it away.”
“You said you’d kill me if I did.”
“That’s why it’s a good thing.
I really would’ve had to kill you.
Phew.”
“...You’re joking, right?
Please tell me you’re joking.”
The game capsule that had first led me to the Murim had sat here unused ever since the System allowed me to Login and Logout freely without it.
But that didn’t make it a piece of junk I could toss aside.
That old capsule had done more than anything else to make me who I was.
It was priceless.
“I don’t wipe the dining table, but I wipe that capsule down once a week,” Jinho said.
“It still doesn’t work, though.
Why take it?”
“Just because.
For decoration, I guess.”
“Isn’t that thing haunted?
Remember when you lived at Hope Goshiwon?
You slept in it and had some weird nightmare...”
Oh.
That had happened, hadn’t it?
Jinho was bringing up my first Logout.
I hurried to change the subject.
“Did you see the news?
Things got pretty crazy in the Middle East and Afghanistan.”
“Huh?
Where did that come from?”
“I’m asking if you saw it.”
“Of course I did.
Yesterday the Middle Eastern terrorist groups and the Afghan rebels even issued a joint statement.
Said they’d refrain from terrorism and keep their men in line from now on.
Basically surrendered because they got scared.”
“Don’t let your guard down.
It’ll only last a little while.”
“Still, those five weirdos in masks are incredible, aren’t they?”
The change of subject seemed to have worked.
I breathed an inward sigh of relief and nodded.
“They are.”
“Well, anyway.”
Jinho slurped up his noodles, washed them down with soju, and went on.
“You’ve had it rough.
A Monster Wave right after the new year, humans worse than monsters, and now trips to the desert and Africa.”
“What do you mean, rough?
It was just something I had to do...”
I suddenly faltered and let the end of the sentence trail off.
Wait.
What the hell had he just said?
“Sorry, what?”
“What you heard.
I took a shot in the dark, and it looks like I was more or less right.”
“Come on.
How many people in the world could do something like that?
Everyone says they wish the terrorists would die and they never want to see those rebel bastards again.
But who’d actually put on a mask and do something about it?
More to the point, who could?”
Jinho gave a quiet laugh at my wide-eyed stare.
“Some people have probably guessed, too, but they’re keeping quiet.
There’s no evidence, and it’s not as if they have any reason to blame you.
But one low-ranking civil servant happens to know what kind of person the masked man is—and even shares ramyeon with him—so he can casually sound him out like this.”
I rubbed the back of my head, which somehow felt numb.
I had suspected I would be named as a prime suspect, but I hadn’t expected to get caught this absurdly easily.
“I-I’m really not him.”
“Sure.
Let’s say you aren’t.
When did you get back?”
Damn it.
There was no saving this.
I sighed, filled my soju glass, and answered.
“Three days ago.
No, four.”
“Good.
Now you’re cooperating.”
“Don’t tell anyone.
Never mind that it’s classified—you’d be in danger.”
Team Leader Choi, my family, and I were always surrounded by protection no one could see.
Jinho wasn’t.
He understood what I meant immediately and smacked his lips.
“Hmm.
I feel like a big shot.”
“You might get a bomb delivered before you become one.”
“Maybe.
But even if they all know, they won’t be able to touch me, will they?
They won’t know what Jin Taekyung might do if he completely loses it.
Hah, isn’t this what you call Untouchable?”
Jinho laughed without a care, then asked, “Anyway, how busy have you been?
You can’t even remember when you got back.”
“Hmm.”
How busy?
I scratched at the beard that had grown thick before I knew it.
“I train day and night.
Eat with my family, then train some more.”
“Train?
Why does someone at your level need to train?”
“You graduated from a prestigious university and still spent nearly ten more years studying.
Same thing.”
“You bastard, going straight for the sore spot.
Besides, how are we the same?
It’s not just a different field—we’re on completely different levels.”
He had a point.
His prestigious university admitted hundreds of students every year, and about as many graduated.
But I still needed training.
There was no end to learning, and gongbu—study—wasn’t limited to academics.
To be precise, I’m not learning something new.
I’m slowly going back over what I already know.
In that sense, my training was a kind of review.
Study for my own sake, and for the sake of this world.
Unfortunately, I still hadn’t managed to bring it all together.
“Ugh, look at that serious expression.
It makes me want to slap you in the cheek.”
“...I’m in the middle of being serious, so could you shut that mouth of yours?”
“Put yourself in my shoes.
What would you do?”
“Hmm.
Fair enough.
Have a drink.”
We clinked glasses.
Jinho knocked back his soju, poked at the noodles that had gone cold, and asked, “So?
Is the training going well?”
“More or less.
I started preparing about a month ago, so I’m nearly done, but... it’s not easy.”
I wasn’t exaggerating.
I was like a child trying to assemble a ten-thousand-piece puzzle.
As I checked each piece and fit them together, I felt my own shortcomings and regretted what I lacked.
Now, unable to find the final piece, I was groping around in the dark.
And I already knew the name of the darkness obscuring my sight.
The heart demon.
The dark cloud over my heart refused to clear.
My worries about the Murim and the modern world... and, more than anything, the last sight of Kim Hwajong kept returning to me.
His voice, which seemed as though it could fade away at any moment.
His eyes slowly closing in the red snowfield covered with blood.
Maybe I hadn’t come here for the capsule after all.
Maybe I’d come to find some comfort.
Not with the family I loved or the companions at my side, but with a friend living his own life in a completely different world.
Maybe I’d just wanted to clink glasses with him like we used to.
Yeah.
That was it.
All at once, I felt more at ease.
I hadn’t shaken off the heart demon entirely, but acknowledging everything that had happened—and everything that troubled me—lifted some of the weight from my heart.
I also realized that I wasn’t where I needed to be.
“I’m leaving.”
“The ramyeon’s cold.
I was going to make tofu kimchi to go with the drinks...
Wait, now?”
“Yeah.
I remembered something I have to do.
Drink by yourself.”
“Are you crazy?”
“No.
I’m your landlord.
Want to start paying rent this month?”
Jinho hyung, who had been glaring at me fiercely, immediately bent deeply at the waist.
“Get home safely, Boss.”
“Will do.”
I laughed quietly and headed for the front door.
Behind me, Jinho called out in a rush.
“Hey!
What about the capsule?”
“Next time.
I’ll take it next time.”
Even as I said it, I knew that next time, I might give him the same answer and leave the capsule where it was.
I might come only to clink glasses with him, just as I had today.
“All right.
Hang in there, you bastard.”
Someone’s quiet murmur reached my ears as I walked on.

chapters.title: Chapter 613
paragraphs: The Training Room was silent again today.
Countless kinds of weapons lay strewn across the floor, and the walls—enchanted with automatic restoration magic—had been reduced to a miserable ruin.
At the center of it all... I sat cross-legged, lost in thought.
More. Just a little more.
I was almost there.
The final piece of this enormous puzzle.
Right after parting ways with Jinho hyung, I had shut myself in the Training Room and begun the last stretch of work to find it.
Even if the stress made all my hair fall out, even if the worst happened and I risked qi deviation, I had to get through it.
No matter what it took, I had to complete this puzzle before I left.
For the future.

I had only started searching for the final piece recently, but I’d decided to put the puzzle together months ago. It was probably after the battle with the Arch Lich—the incident dubbed the Small Cataclysm.
If this keeps up, everyone will be in danger.
The thought had come to me out of nowhere one day. As time passed, my unease turned into certainty.
Magical power levels had risen abnormally. Monsters had grown stronger, and human casualties—which had fallen dramatically after the Great Cataclysm—were once again mounting everywhere.
Humanity needed another kind of power. After a great deal of thought, I made my decision.
I would create martial arts.
I would give them a new sword and shield against the dangers and disasters growing by the day.
Of course, it was anything but easy. What I created had to be safe enough for even the lowest-rank Hunter to learn, yet limited enough in power that evildoers couldn’t exploit it.
But... at last, I found the final piece of the puzzle.
Yes. This is it.
After hundreds of attempts, I had found a single path.
The moment I completed the still-unnamed cultivation technique—
Ding. Ding. Ding.
As if congratulating me, a series of lively alerts rang out.
Team Leader Choi—or rather, Choi Minwoo, now Guild Master of the Peace Guild and Vice Guild Master of Ares Guild—was so busy he barely had time to breathe.
During the week he’d been away, the matters awaiting his attention had multiplied into the hundreds. His temporary personal secretary was sweating bullets as calls from powerful figures poured in.
“G-Guild Master. The Blue House has proposed a luncheon.”
“Political figures and the Federation of Korean Industries would like you to attend a social gathering...”
“The Guild Alliance has proposed a partnership on Gate-related business...”
“Regarding the establishment of overseas branches...”
Some invitations couldn’t be refused. Others easily could. Choi Minwoo’s answer was always the same.
“All right. Schedule it.”
He followed a schedule planned down to the minute, spending each day like a machine and barely sleeping. The people around him watched his punishing routine with concern.
“Okay, pick one. Team Leader Choi, Guild Master Choi, or Vice Guild Master Choi. What should we call you?”
“Please call me Team Leader Choi. That’s what I was when we met.”
“All right, then. Team Leader Choi, I’ll be direct... Get some rest. Cut back your schedule and leave the little things to your secretary.”
“She’s right, Team Leader Choi. You may be young, but you can’t keep this up without wearing yourself out.”
“I’m fine. Please don’t worry, either of you.”
“Team Leader Choi.”
“No, listen...”
As for me, I’m fine.
His voice was calm, and his answer never changed. Song Song and Im Kkeokjeong, who had tried to talk him out of it, could only fall silent.
The answer that reached their ears was the same as before, but the answer that reached their hearts was different.
As for me, I’m fine.
Choi Minwoo left them with that one phrase, the same and yet different, and continued burying himself in work.
He even dismissed the personal secretary who had been helping him a little, then plunged into days busier than ever.
So it was hardly surprising when the subject came up during a private meeting with President Baek Hanseong.
“You seem very busy these days.”
“That’s why I like it.”
“I hear you don’t even have a secretary anymore. Is there a particular reason?”
“Coffee.”
“Pardon?”
“She couldn’t make coffee. That’s all.”
President Baek Hanseong assumed it was a joke and laughed it off, but every answer Choi Minwoo had given him was sincere.
Choi Minwoo liked being buried in work so completely, and the coffee made by his young secretary had been strangely awful.
More than that, he was grateful to forget, if only for a little while, the longing and grief for someone who kept coming to mind.
“Enough idle talk from me. Let’s move on to the next item.”
One day passed. Then another.
While Jin Taekyung trained in an isolated space, Choi Minwoo isolated himself amid countless people.
Perhaps that was why, one day, a name suddenly came to mind. As he drove himself mercilessly hard, just as he always did, the longing he had buried deep inside rose to the surface.
“Driver Jung, turn the car around.”
“Pardon? I’m sorry, but I believe our next appointment is at...”
“Cancel everything today. There’s somewhere I need to go.”
The driver’s startled eyes met his in the rearview mirror. Choi Minwoo sank back into the limousine seat.
Warm spring air and sunlight came through the half-open window as he headed to meet someone.
Step. Step.
The hill he climbed alone was high and steep, and his footsteps were heavy. Or perhaps it was his heart.
Sorrow and guilt over the one person he could never reach, even if he climbed this high, steep path a hundred or a thousand times, weighed on Choi Minwoo’s heart.
Pluck. Pluck.
Along the way, he picked an armful of early spring flowers. The pure white violets didn’t seem like enough, so he added scarlet moss phlox from the clusters growing beside the path.
The man who was no longer by his side had always said he liked red.
And yet he always wore black suits.
It was only recently that Choi Minwoo had learned what color he liked most, and why he had sold all those motorcycles.
Why he had quit drinking despite once keeping alcohol so close, and why he had trimmed the shaggy beard and long hair he had grown out before neatly parting it.
Why did you do all that? You were enough for me.
He knew everything now, but he had learned it all too late.
With an ache in his chest, Choi Minwoo kept walking.
On the warm, breezy hilltop, a large burial mound awaited him, and the three characters carved into the granite gravestone stood out with unusual clarity.
The late Kim Hwajong.
What could he say?
Choi Minwoo stared at the old butler, laid to rest on this warm hill instead of a cold, snow-covered mountain. At last, he opened his mouth.
“I’m here.”
His usually steady eyes trembled. He bit down on his trembling lip and slowly went on.
“...Grandfather.”
The word he had held in his heart, but never once said while the old man was alive, finally escaped him.
Whoosh—
A wind swept over him from somewhere. The grass on the hill bent low, and the branches waved.
Choi Minwoo set his bouquet beside the mound. Then he froze.
What’s that?
His eyes widened. He was looking at the back of the gravestone.
Words he had never noticed before were carved there.
You came. Thank you, and I love you. Be happy.
Who had carved them? He should have wondered, but right now, it didn’t matter.
Choi Minwoo stood frozen like a stone statue, staring endlessly at the short message.
His heart shook like flowers in the wind. Something rose from deep inside him, closing his throat and making his eyes burn.
“Ah.”
Overwhelmed, he let out a choked sigh.
“You came sooner than I expected. I thought I’d have to wait at least a few more days.”
A voice sounded behind him.
Choi Minwoo turned. Someone stood there holding a small box.
It was the Skeleton King.
Why was he here? What did he mean, wait?
The questions vanished as quickly as they came. What Choi Minwoo needed now wasn’t a reason, but warmth. An answer to a question he couldn’t resolve alone.
“May I ask you one thing? Just one?”
Normally, the Skeleton King would have curtly said no. This time, he readily nodded.
“Anything.”
“If it were Mr. Jin Taekyung... what would he do at a time like this?”
The Skeleton King understood the sudden question at once.
“Why do you ask?”
“Because he’s stronger than anyone I know.”
The Skeleton King stared at Choi Minwoo in silence before answering in a low voice.
“He would have cried. Without a doubt.”
“And then he would overcome it and go on living, forever remembering the person who left.”
That was enough.
Choi Minwoo let the tears he had held back fall. With them, he let out his grief and regret, his longing and guilt.
The Skeleton King quietly stepped away. It would be better to give him the contents of the box a little later.
He remembered what Jin Taekyung had said when he entrusted him with it about half a day ago.
“Sorry, but I need a favor.”
“No. I refuse. Go away.”
“Give this to Team Leader Choi. No one else.”
“You damnable human. Now you’re not even pretending to listen. Do I look like an errand boy to you?”
“I’m not asking because you’re an errand boy. I’m asking because I trust you.”
“...What exactly am I supposed to give him?”
“Martial arts.”
“What?”
“He’ll understand when you tell him. There’s a letter in the box, too. Make sure he reads it.”
“No. How am I supposed to find someone I haven’t even seen lately...?”
“Wait at Butler Kim’s grave. Even if you see him before then, don’t say a word. He’ll probably need time to get through this.”
No matter how the Skeleton King looked at it, Jin Taekyung was a strange human.
For one thing, Choi Minwoo had arrived at the grave just as Taekyung had said he would.
And he was even stranger for the fact that once he fell asleep, he would not so much as blink even if someone grabbed him by the collar and shook him awake.
Damn him. He has the nerve to give me a petty errand like this while he sleeps without a care?
Jin Taekyung had repeatedly begged him not to wake him under any circumstances, so he was probably dead asleep by now.
The more the Skeleton King thought about Jin Taekyung, the more infuriating he found him. But honestly, for some strange reason, he did not feel all that bad.
I can entrust it to you because I trust you. Trust, huh? Hmm. Hmmm.
The Skeleton King nodded as he remembered the box in his hands and Jin Taekyung’s words, then muttered quietly.
“...Sweet dreams, you devious human.”
Whoosh—
The wind blew once more. It swallowed one man’s sobs and the voice of a monster who had, before he knew it, grown close to people.
