I thought I’d have to wait at least a few more days.”
A voice sounded behind him.
Choi Minwoo turned.
Someone stood there holding a small box.
It was the Skeleton King.
Why was he here?
What did he mean, wait?
The questions vanished as quickly as they came.
What Choi Minwoo needed now wasn’t a reason, but warmth.
An answer to a question he couldn’t resolve alone.
“May I ask you one thing?
Just one?”
Normally, the Skeleton King would have curtly said no.
This time, he readily nodded.
“Anything.”
“If it were Mr.
Jin Taekyung... what would he do at a time like this?”
The Skeleton King understood the sudden question at once.
“Why do you ask?”
“Because he’s stronger than anyone I know.”
The Skeleton King stared at Choi Minwoo in silence before answering in a low voice.
“He would have cried.
Without a doubt.”
“And then he would overcome it and go on living, forever remembering the person who left.”
That was enough.
Choi Minwoo let the tears he had held back fall.
With them, he let out his grief and regret, his longing and guilt.
The Skeleton King quietly stepped away.
It would be better to give him the contents of the box a little later.
He remembered what Jin Taekyung had said when he entrusted him with it about half a day ago.
“Sorry, but I need a favor.”
“No.
I refuse.
Go away.”
“Give this to Team Leader Choi.
No one else.”
“You damnable human.
Now you’re not even pretending to listen.
Do I look like an errand boy to you?”
“I’m not asking because you’re an errand boy.
I’m asking because I trust you.”
“...What exactly am I supposed to give him?”
“Martial arts.”
“What?”
“He’ll understand when you tell him.
There’s a letter in the box, too.
Make sure he reads it.”
“No.
How am I supposed to find someone I haven’t even seen lately...?”
“Wait at Butler Kim’s grave.
Even if you see him before then, don’t say a word.
He’ll probably need time to get through this.”
No matter how the Skeleton King looked at it, Jin Taekyung was a strange human.
For one thing, Choi Minwoo had arrived at the grave just as Taekyung had said he would.
And he was even stranger for the fact that once he fell asleep, he would not so much as blink even if someone grabbed him by the collar and shook him awake.
Damn him.
He has the nerve to give me a petty errand like this while he sleeps without a care?
Jin Taekyung had repeatedly begged him not to wake him under any circumstances, so he was probably dead asleep by now.
The more the Skeleton King thought about Jin Taekyung, the more infuriating he found him.
But honestly, for some strange reason, he did not feel all that bad.
I can entrust it to you because I trust you.
Trust, huh?
Hmm.
Hmmm.
The Skeleton King nodded as he remembered the box in his hands and Jin Taekyung’s words, then muttered quietly.
“...Sweet dreams, you devious human.”
Whoosh—
The wind blew once more.
It swallowed one man’s sobs and the voice of a monster who had, before he knew it, grown close to people.

paragraphs: System Synchronization begins. 10, 9, 8, 7... 1, 0. Synchronization completed successfully. Updated stats have been applied to the body. The use of certain Titles is restricted. Login complete.
Ding.
Before the familiar System notifications had even finished, I felt rough straw against my skin and smelled wet grass.
I spat out the piece of rice straw stuck to my lips and muttered inwardly.
I’m back.
Back in the Murim.
I’d spent barely over a month in the modern world, yet my time here felt like the distant past. It wasn’t just my imagination.
I’ve had way too much going on.
The Murim. The modern world.
Everything around me in both worlds was changing fast. One thing kept happening after another. Even two bodies wouldn’t have been enough to keep up.
Come to think of it, I did have two bodies. Having to control them one at a time was what made it so damn exhausting.
Anyway...
Ah. I don’t want to get up.
The straw covering me was warmer and softer than I’d expected. I wanted nothing more than to lie there and sleep. I’d barely slept for nearly a week while developing a martial art for widespread use.
I might have drifted off if I hadn’t heard voices nearby.
“Hmm. You’re asking what kind of person Captain is?”
“Yes. I’ve been curious for a while. The other two aren’t here yet, and I’m bored. You’re curious too, aren’t you, Escort Song?”
I knew those voices. After Hyuk Mujin and Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom—the Soul-Chasing Guest—answered gruffly.
“Not particularly.”
“Did you hear that? Escort Song is curious too.”
“I said I’m not.”
“I’ll give you two more silver nyang.”
“...I’m a little curious.”
Money-grubbing bastard.
Once Song Ilseom had been won over by the big spender’s silver donation, Mujin spoke again, sounding hesitant.
“Hmm. This is hard to answer. Captain’s definitely still asleep, right?”
“Yes. Yes.”
“He is. His breathing is steady.”
“Well, once he falls asleep, he wouldn’t notice if a ghost carried him away.”
Steady, my ass.
I was controlling my breathing. I was curious what Mujin would say, too.
And my loyal right pinky toe didn’t let me down.
“Our captain is that famous, really famous... uh, how do I put it...?”
“A handsome, impressive young prodigy?”
At Ju Hwaran’s question, delivered in a voice as clear and lovely as a Young Chang piano, Hyuk Mujin answered without a trace of hesitation.
“He was a fucking bastard.”

“These days, people call him the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon and all that. But a year or two ago, you’d have had a hard time finding a bigger fucking bastard. He went to pleasure houses and got shit-faced every day, stole public funds, and blew them at gambling dens. He was so bad that his sobriquet back then was...”
“Hey.”

“That’s right. The Night King. In that field, even all Ten Kings together wouldn’t have been a match for him. Every night, he’d strap a money pouch to his side and stride off to a pleasure house like he owned the place. My fellow gate guards and I used to say, ‘That fucking bastard’s using the Heavenly Demon Reign Step again.’ I see you’ve heard of him, Great Hero Song. You really do know a lot.”
“What are you talking about?” Song Ilseom asked, sounding uneasy. “I didn’t say anything.”
“What?”
“I didn’t say anything.”
“Come on. You said ‘hey’ just now.”
“No, I didn’t.”
“It was definitely a man’s voice. Don’t joke around. Then who...?”
His voice cut off.
After a short, heavy silence, someone carefully lifted the straw from my face.
Rustle. Ssshh.
The straw blocking my view fell away. In the faint moonlight, my eyes met Mujin’s.
I gave him a warm, friendly smile. It had been a while.
“Hey.”
Mujin stared down at me in silence, his gaze growing somber. Then he laid the straw back over my face.
Very carefully, as though nothing had happened.
“Move it.”
“The moon must be bright tonight. I’m hearing things...”
“If you don’t move it, your life’s going to get dark. Move it.”
“Yes, sir.”
The straw had stopped feeling warm and cozy.
Like a vampire waking after centuries sealed away by an exorcist, I rose from the wagon’s cargo bed.
Whoooosh.
A chilly wind blew the bits of straw from my clothes.
Ju Hwaran met my eyes and hastily looked away. By the campfire—when had he even lit that?—Song Ilseom got to his feet, muttering that he needed to feed the horse some hay.
My shadow swelled in the flickering firelight and fell across Mujin.
“Any last words?”
“Captain, please. Hear me out.”
“That’s why I asked.”
“You said they were my last words. It sounds like a will.”
“It probably is.”
“You were having a great time. As your captain, I can’t tell you how happy it makes me to see my subordinate enjoying himself.”
That was half true. I really couldn’t contain myself.
I’d busted my ass in the Murim, busted my ass in the modern world, and come back without getting any sleep—only to find my own subordinate talking shit about me behind my back.
And the name of the emotion that followed this situation straight out of a light novel was rage.
“Face, arms, legs, abdomen, back. Pick one.”
“Are those my possible causes of death?”
“I’m not going to kill you. I’m just going to beat you within an inch of your life.”
Mujin thought for a moment.
“The abdomen.”
“Why?”
“Wounds on the back are... a martial artist’s shame.”
I let out an exclamation at his spirit.
“What a load of bullshit.”
“I did wrong, so I’ll take my punishment. Come at me.”
“Since you picked your abdomen, I’ll pick the rest.”
“What?”
“What do you mean, ‘what’? It wouldn’t be fair if only you got to choose. I should get a turn too.”
“No, wait. How is that fair—”
Wham!
The blow cracked through the night.
Above the slowly burning campfire, the shadow of a man soaring upward with blood spraying from his nose loomed large.
I’m already using my fists the moment I get back.
We were on Mount Daebyeol, where Anhui and Hubei bordered Henan.
Two figures approached from the distance, with Mujin’s screams providing the background music. They were the final members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion: a pair of rootless unorthodox faction nobodies.
“...Why are they beating him?”
“Taishan! Is here!”
At last, the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s Nanman expedition party had gathered in one place. I left them with a short but powerful lecture, then turned away.
“All right, let’s finish beating this bastard and get going.”
Nobody objected.

Right now, I wasn’t Jin Taekyung the S-rank Hunter. I was the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, the orthodox Murim’s greatest young prodigy, and Jin Taekyung, Fire Dragon Pavilion Master—their direct superior.
Crack!
“Urgh! Aaaagh!”
I really do love the Murim. Except for that damned Dark Heaven.
Not a single ray of light reached that pitch-black place.
In the darkness, where neither sound nor any sign of life could be felt, figures lay facedown and trembled.
Then—
“Heaven above, earth below!”
“All demons bow in submission!”
The cries erupted as one, thunderous. Crimson-black flames surged up from the darkness.
Fwoosh!
A ring of fire blazed fiercely. Yet despite being unmistakable flames, they gave off a chill that seeped into the bones. Beyond them, someone’s shadow wavered.
“It has been a long time.”
Man or woman, young or old—even the pitch of the voice was impossible to tell.
The strange voice resounded from every direction, pressing down on the figures prostrate on the floor.
“My servants.”
Everyone trembled at the overwhelming power in those two words. Some shook with fear of the absolute being before them; others with joy and rapture at seeing the one they served.
Together, they cried out.
“These foolish, lowly servants humbly pay their respects to the great Lord of Heaven!”
Lord of Heaven. Master of the heavens.
No other words could describe him.
An absolute being of unmatched dignity and greatness. The heavens above the clouds were his palace; every lowly creature on the earth below was his servant and subject.
No. They would make it so.
“How much time has passed?”
Every one of them understood the living god’s question. The figures prostrate before him were servants of the Lord of Heaven, loyal and devoted beyond words.
The young man bowing low against the floor was no different.
“Exactly one hundred and thirty-six days since the great Lord of Heaven last awoke!”
The fierce flames wavered at his answer.
“Yes. I remember. Western Heaven. That was the day the child left.”
“We are deeply ashamed!”
Led by the young man, they cried out again. This time, shame and self-reproach filled their voices.

When the Western Heaven Demon Lord and the Dark Heaven forces under his command had been annihilated at the Sichuan Tang Clan, the unexpected defeat had thrown them into confusion. They had been forced to wake their master from his deep sleep.
“Great Lord of Heaven, never again... will such a thing happen.”
The words came through the young man’s clenched teeth. The flames stirred once more.
“No. The mistake was mine, for trusting you despite your shortcomings.”
“Blood Lord. You have your own shortcomings, do you not?”
At the most painful reprimand of all, the pupils of the young man—Blood Lord—trembled.
Blood Lord knew better than anyone what the master he worshiped meant.
Henan.

The day the orthodox Murim had named the Shaolin Bloodshed was one of the most painful memories of his life. He had accomplished far less than planned, and suffered the humiliation of leaving an arm behind.
If he hadn’t at least brought back Shaolin’s sacred treasure, the Green Jade Buddha Staff... He didn’t want to think about it.
The Sword Saint. And Jin Taekyung.
Thinking of those two bastards made him want to kill. Even tearing them apart alive wouldn’t satisfy him.
But a loyal servant must not show such thoughts before his master. Blood Lord barely suppressed his murderous intent and spoke.
“P-Please forgive me.”
Whoooong.
A chilly wind swept through the darkness in place of an answer. Blood Lord and the others huddled lower.
Then a quiet voice reached their ears.
“What is lacking can be filled.”
The air grew heavy. The wind stopped, and every living thing held its breath.
In the stillness, the Lord of Heaven continued.
“I shall fill what you lack.”
It was a command, backed by a force none of them could resist.
Fwoooooosh.
Darkness and shadow rippled.
An immense surge of qi flowed from somewhere unseen and settled into Blood Lord’s body. His eyes widened with rapture.
“L-Lord of Heaven!”
Blood Lord and the others understood once more: the master they served was a living god, an absolute being who encompassed heaven and earth.
They understood, too, what the power he had bestowed on them meant.
“Tell Southern Heaven and North Heaven.”
Rumble, rumble, rumble!
The earth trembled. The world shook.
Beyond the overwhelming energy that distorted everything, his voice rang out like thunder.
“Now... we begin the Great War.”
Heaven above, earth below. All demons bow in submission.
As his loyal servants cried out in rapture and madness, the unseen shadow waved a hand.
The crimson-black flames that had colored the pitch-black space disappeared, and darkness descended once more.

chapters.title: Chapter 615
paragraphs: The road to Yunnan Province—the region officially known by that name, though people in the Central Plains commonly called it Nanman—was long and arduous.
Prrrff. Prrf.
The horse’s breathing was ragged.

We had ridden without a break for a full four shichen since leaving Mount Daebyeol. Now, having entered Hubei on the fine horses Ju Hwaran had procured, we eased the reins for a moment in an unfamiliar ravine.
“If we keep traveling like this, it’ll take quite a while. You’ve been to Sichuan before, Pavilion Master, so you know that, don’t you?”
“Me?”
Of course I knew. Just thinking about it made my calves cramp even now.
I nodded without thinking as Ju Hwaran looked at me with her clear, sparkling eyes.
“Of course. It was really fucki—”
“Pardon?”
“It was a little... difficult. A little.”
I’d barely stopped myself from saying that something had almost fallen off back then.
I, Jin Taekyung, was merciless toward men, but a warm and considerate gentleman toward women.
Of course, despite having lived this long, I had never once been in a relationship.
“Even using a movement technique, it took me nearly half a month.”
“Sichuan alone is well over three thousand li away. And if you traveled without any shortcuts, that’s remarkable.”
The praise felt good, but she probably hadn’t brought this up just to compliment me.
I gave her a questioning look. Ju Hwaran smiled and pulled an old leather scroll from inside her robes.
What’s that?
Just as I began to wonder, Song Ilseom, who was sitting in the saddle and inspecting the edge of his willow-leaf saber, spoke with an unexpected look on his face.
“It’s made of horsehide. Is that from the horse caravans?”
Ju Hwaran nodded.
“You recognize it. Yes—more precisely, it’s a map they used.”
“I heard you couldn’t buy one of their maps for ten thousand gold pieces.”

“As Young Bureau Head of the Yongbong Escort Bureau, I can tell you there’s nothing in this world money can’t buy. But my grandfather gained a friendship worth more than gold. He was given this map as a token of it.”
Hmm. I see.
...Actually, I didn’t understand a damn thing.
Except that Ju Hwaran’s grandfather, Escort King Ju Gongsan, had received an amazing map from someone in these horse caravans.
After patiently listening to them, I spoke up.
“Um, Young Lady Ju. Sorry, but what exactly are the horse caravans?”
“They’re descendants of the northern mounted tribes.”
“For hundreds of years, they traveled the ancient trade routes, carrying goods between the Outer Lands and the Central Plains. There aren’t nearly as many of them now.”
Well, all right. Now I knew what the horse caravans were.
But I was pretty sure I had asked Ju Hwaran. Why were the answers coming from two dark-clad men?
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo, who had spoken almost at the same time, turned to look at each other.
“You’re more knowledgeable than you look.”
“Than I look? Have you forgotten where the Black Dragon Demon Gate is located? Horse caravans are still active in Gansu, where our sect is based.”
“Operate? You mean they’re being squeezed dry?”
Song Ilseom gave a short laugh.
“I’ve heard the rumors. The Black Dragon Demon Gate controls the trade routes and collects enormous tolls.”
“I heard you were a wandering martial artist. Do you have some bad blood with our sect?”
“Not particularly. I just want to kill any demonic, heterodox practitioner I see.”
“We agree on that point. I can’t stand meeting people who draw their weapons before anything else. So, are you finished tending to your weapon?”
“Not yet. But it’ll have blood on it soon enough, so I can finish later.”
“Then let’s move somewhere else for a while.”
How the hell had the conversation gotten here?
I stared blankly at the two men as they amicably turned their horses around, then opened my mouth.
“Move where, you lunatics?”
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo answered at the same time.
“It’s personal. Stay out of it.”
“The horses need a rest anyway. Have some tea. We’ll be back shortly.”
One was an individualist. The other was Guan Yu.
The Nanman expedition had barely set out, and already it was showing signs of falling apart. As Fire Dragon Pavilion Master, I had to step in.
Whish!
Two sharp blasts cut through the air.
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo landed on the ground after avoiding the Finger Qi I had fired at them. Just as they reflexively began to draw their weapons, I warned them in a calm voice.
“You’ll regret drawing those.”
It wasn’t just a warning. They felt the immense qi pressing in from every direction and froze.
Unmistakable astonishment appeared in their trembling eyes.
He’s strong.
That was what their gazes said.
And it was an undeniable fact.

Sama Pyo, the Black Dragon Saber, was Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, the dominant power in Gansu, and the unorthodox faction’s foremost young prodigy. Song Ilseom, the Soul-Chasing Guest, had become a legend by cutting down countless enemies on battlefields and in life-and-death duels. Both of them understood exactly what they were facing.
No—because they were anything but mediocre Peak masters, they understood it all the better.
A person standing at a higher place could see farther and grasp the whole picture.
I was already two moves above them before, but the pressure they’re feeling now must be much greater.
As always, I had woken up stronger than I’d been when I fell asleep.

While developing a martial art that could be widely taught to modern Hunters, I’d gained a small insight. I hadn’t created anything extraordinary, so I couldn’t call it a full step forward...but even a quarter of a step was a significant gain.
It was a shame my allies were the first to feel the results instead of Dark Heaven.
“We have thousands of li left to go. If you still want to fight, do it now and keep going until one of you dies. Otherwise—”
“Pavilion Master.”
I was fond of Ju Hwaran, but now wasn’t the time to listen to her. I gave her a slight shake of my head at her tense expression and continued.
“Otherwise, team up and come at me. This is your only chance. You won’t get another.”
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo stared at each other, lips pressed tight. It didn’t take them long to decide.
Shrrrk. Click.
With a cold scraping sound, the two blades that had been faintly exposed disappeared from view.
They climbed back into their saddles as though nothing had happened. Ju Hwaran watched them and let out a quiet sigh.
“Whew... I’d hoped this wouldn’t happen.”
So had I. But I’d thought long and hard about the possibility before accepting those two into the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Their feelings toward each other probably aren’t very good. Especially from Song Ilseom’s perspective.
It went back decades, to when the orthodox and demonic factions had divided the world between them and fought their decisive battle.
A bold young escort named Zhu had accepted a woman’s commission and made the Ten-Thousand-Mile Escorts a legend. The child that woman bore grew up, had a son, and passed away.
That son was Song Ilseom—the last descendant of the Guangdong Chen Family, which had been wiped out by demonic, heterodox arts.
Unless he was Buddha or Jesus, it was only natural that he would harbor hatred toward the unorthodox faction.
I just didn’t think it would come to a head this fast.
Shit, how many shichen had we even been on the road? Was the whole expedition already about to fall apart? I was starting to understand why college students hated group projects.
And that was true even if I excluded the two men who had become archenemies faster than anyone in Murim history.
“Captain, maybe it’s because I got hit in the stomach earlier, but I keep needing to take a shit.”
“My lord. Don’t fight. Taishan worries when my lord is in danger. And gets hungry.”
Look at this lineup. For fuck’s sake.
Watching Hyuk Mujin, whose stomach was more active than his body, and Taishan, the Tiger Giant Child, who seemed to have an inventory instead of a stomach, made my vision go dark.
But even here, I had one ray of light.
“Young Lady Ju.”
“Yes?”
“Thank you. I’m really glad you’re here.”
I meant it. Beautiful or not, she was the most normal person in the group.
It was true that her martial arts were slightly weaker than those of the other members, but she had extensive knowledge of Murim and was excellent at finding her way.
The fact that she had found a shortcut known only among the horse caravans proved it.
So why wasn’t she answering?
“Young Lady Ju?”
“Um, Young Lady Ju?”
I called again, but she said nothing. Still gripping the reins, she turned her head away and stammered.
“I-I think we should go this way.”
“What? No, you’ve done a great job. I meant—”
“I’ll ride ahead and look for the horse caravans’ markers. Hyah!”
“Uh. Wait—what?”
I didn’t get another word out. Ju Hwaran hurried away as though she and her horse were one, leaving me staring blankly after her. Then I felt eyes prickling the back of my head and turned.
...What’s with these guys now?
Song Ilseom. Sama Pyo. Hyuk Mujin. Even Taishan.
Exactly four pairs of eyes were fixed in place, staring holes through me.
Their mysterious gazes were impossible to interpret. I flinched instinctively and asked,
“What? Why are you all looking at me like that?”
“Hmm. It’s nothing.”
“I’ll go on ahead, Pavilion Master.”
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo slowly rode forward, both wearing complicated expressions. Hyuk Mujin and Taishan answered reluctantly.
“Uh, I was just looking. Because I need to take a dump.”
“If you need to take a dump, why look at me?”
“When I look at you, whatever was about to come out goes right back in.”
“Taishan. Just looking because hungry. Nothing else.”
“What the hell does being hungry have to do with me?”
“Nothing. Just... just... Hmm. Taishan gets it now. Taishan understands a little.”
What kind of bullshit was that?
I could understand Hyuk Mujin, but having that giant glutton look at me with such pity was deeply unsettling.
Before I could press him, Taishan smacked his half-dead horse on the rump and charged off.
“Taishan! Go! Horse go too!”
The horse, already looking half-dead, staggered into a run. Hyuk Mujin hurried after him.
“Hey, wait! Let’s go together!”
“No! Don’t follow! Taishan only runs forward!”
“I have jerky.”
“Taishan! Found friend! Together forever!”
Lunatics...
But why did I feel like I was the one being ignored by those lunatics?
I grabbed my reins, my face twisting as though I’d bitten into something foul.
“Hey. Let’s go too.”
Prrrff.
Now even the damn horse was giving me a look.
I smacked its head as it snorted, then squeezed its sides hard. With a small whinny, it raced through the ravine.

chapters.title: Chapter 616
paragraphs: Becoming a successful merchant in Murim meant surviving fierce competition.
The map the horse caravans had reportedly made while traveling between the Outer Lands and the Central Plains was proof enough of how they had amassed such wealth.
“This is the place. The marker’s faint, but it’s definitely one of the horse caravans’.”
“Huh. Who would’ve thought there was a road through here?”
Secret shortcuts hidden throughout the Central Plains, swift and accurate despite their concealment.
Some had vanished over the years, and those that remained could be treacherous precisely because they were hidden. But that wasn’t much of a problem for us.
“Captain, isn’t this slope too steep?”
“It is. The road’s narrow, too. But we have to go.”
“Then I’m afraid we’ll have to leave the horses behind.”
“Why would we do that? We can carry them.”
“Pardon?”
Correction. It wasn’t much of a problem for me.
Everyone who heard me stared wide-eyed.
“What did you say?”
“They’re not big warhorses. They came from the grasslands, so they’re fairly light, aren’t they?”
“...Light or not, they’re horses. Can you really carry them?”
As it turned out, I could. More easily than I’d expected, in fact.

My strength had long since surpassed human limits. I slung two horses over my shoulders and strode uphill, while Taishan—who wasn’t as strong as me but was a natural strongman with the build to match—could manage three.
“Pavilion Master. Taishan. Heavy. No choice. Eat one horse here. No, leave one here.”
“...Swallow your spit and try saying that again.”
His appetite was a bigger problem than the weight.
And as the shortcuts cut down our travel time and distance, greater obstacles waited for us.
“According to the map, there should be a road ahead. But...”
“It’s gone. Or rather, blocked.”
“Escort Song is right. I heard there was a landslide nearby a month or two ago. That must have blocked it.”

“Then we’ll have to go around. The map says this road runs for at least ten li. If only a few dozen jang were buried, perhaps, but clearing a road like this is out of the question... Pavilion Master, what are you doing?”
“Getting ready to clear the road.”
“What?”

“It’s not like we have to tunnel through the mountain. Clear some dirt, move a few rocks and boulders, and we should be able to get through. You said the landslide was only a month or two ago, right?”
“Well, yes, but...”
“As they say, when the body is weak, the head has to work harder.”
“...That sounds wrong. Isn’t it usually the other way around?”
“Usually.”
For days, we carried horses up mountains, dug through buried roads, and walked and ran until we crossed Hubei and reached Sichuan at a ridiculous pace.
We owed it all to Ju Hwaran. She knew the shortcuts once shared by only a handful of horse caravans, and she remembered everything her maternal grandfather—the Escort King—had left behind.
I can’t believe we got here so quickly.
We’d made this kind of time without even taking the waterways.

Granted, I’d played no small part in making the impossible possible. But Hwaran had more than fulfilled the role she’d promised to take on before joining the Fire Dragon Pavilion. She’d exceeded my expectations.
Martial arts really aren’t everything.
No matter how much of a Supreme Peak master I became, I couldn’t do anything like this. I gave Ju Hwaran a heartfelt exclamation of admiration.
“You’re incredible. There’s no one like you, Young Lady Ju.”
“I-I’ll go feed the horses some hay.”
“What? Why? They aren’t Taishan. How long has it even been since they ate hay... Young Lady Ju? Young Lady Ju?”
What the hell was going on?
At this point, I couldn’t tell whether she couldn’t hear me or had decided not to listen.
As I watched Ju Hwaran hurry away using a movement technique, I turned my head at the gaze I felt from beside me.
Swish!
The movement was quick as lightning, but not quick enough to escape my notice. I eyed the culprit.
“Hey.”
He flinched.
“I saw you. Don’t pretend you weren’t looking.”
Song Ilseom, seated by the water, glanced around awkwardly.
“Hmm. Are you speaking to me?”
“You’re the only one here. And you know you look awkward as hell, right?”
“...I have no idea what you mean.”
“If you were watching, you were watching. Why hide it? And do you sharpen that willow-leaf saber every chance you get? It’ll be a needle by the time we reach Nanman.”
Splash.
Song Ilseom poured water over the blade, polished so carefully it gleamed like a mirror. His face hardened.
“Watch what you say. This weapon means something to me.”
He wasn’t particularly expressive to begin with, but he’d gone so serious that there had to be a story behind it.
Then again, he’s been through a lot.
There was no excuse for reopening someone else’s wounds. Thinking I’d made a careless mistake, I spoke cautiously.
“Is it a treasured blade passed down through your family?”
“Hardly. I was told they couldn’t bring out so much as a single martial arts manual. My grandmother never learned martial arts in her life. The fact that she survived that war was a miracle.”
“Right. It did look pretty worn for a treasured blade. Something your father left you, then?”
“No.”
A wistful smile touched Song Ilseom’s lips, as if he were remembering better days. He ran a hand along the blade.

“I received this willow-leaf saber when I was young, while serving as a sword boy for a Third Rate wandering martial artist. I cut a person with it for the first time in my life. I was probably twelve.”
“...Oh. Right.”
Wounds, my ass.
My budding guilt melted away like spring snow.
He’d been a martial artist from the start. Watching Song Ilseom fondly recall his first killing, I could only think he was... out of his mind.
Yeah. He’s not right in the head either.
Murim had all kinds of people, but lunatics made up a good share of them. Maybe you had to be one to survive here.

You could die over a meal. You could die in a fight. You could survive the fight, only to die when your wounds got worse. You could endure enough hardship to become a master, then die from qi deviation during training.
What was that novel called? I read one where a martial artist retired peacefully with golden-basin handwashing.
It took coming to Murim to realize that a novel was just a novel.
I’d once asked Jeok Cheongang about golden-basin handwashing. His answer had gone like this:
“Golden-basin handwashing? Easy.”
“Oh. It is?”
“Of course. First, buy a basin made of gold and invite plenty of close acquaintances.”
“It already reeks of social butterflies and capitalism, but all right. What next?”
“Wash your hands without a care. Of course, the moment you take your hand off your weapon, an assassin hidden among your acquaintances will throw a hidden weapon at you.”
“And one more thing. The person you thought was an acquaintance might be an assassin, too. What do you think? Isn’t it easy?”
As my dear Fire-Rice Grandpa had so wisely put it, that was fucking Murim for you.
Golden-basin handwashing, my ass. Most martial artists should be grateful just to wake up in the morning and wash their faces with ice water.
After all, the next day they might have to bathe and purify themselves in the waters of the Sanzu River instead of ice water.
I supposed that counted as retirement, too. The only difference was whether you were still breathing.
What is this, Murim Escape Number One?

The old show had been canceled, but a Murim edition would be a smash hit. Assuming television caught on here, it might pull a 107 percent viewership rating, like turnout in a Russian presidential election.
They could hire a master of demonic, heterodox arts as their experiment expert. He’d smile warmly and run the demonstration himself.
“All right, fellow martial artists. What happens if you dodge this form like so?”
Stab.
“See? Dead. Heh heh.”
They’d run out of experimenters in no time...
It was only my imagination, but Murim was the kind of place where it could become reality as soon as someone brought in a TV.
And in this insane world, I had to travel with lunatics and fight more lunatics.
“...Whew.”
I was staring silently at the river, feeling sorry for myself, when Song Ilseom spoke.
“I was watching.”
“Hm? Watching what?”
“What happened earlier. I never answered you.”
So that was what he meant. I shrugged.
“I knew you were watching. Why were you staring?”
“I heard something, so I looked.”
“Try being honest.”
“Your words and actions looked so stupid that I couldn’t help staring.”
“...Wow. That’s a little too honest.”
“But it’s true. Isn’t that why Young Lady Ju keeps leaving whenever you say things like that?”
For some reason, I felt wronged.
“What did I do? I was impressed, so I gave her an honest compliment.”
“Even a passing dog wouldn’t believe that.”
“It’s true.”
“Enough. It isn’t funny.”
“I haven’t found any of this funny.”
“Fine. Let’s say it’s true.”
Song Ilseom let out a quiet laugh, as though I’d made a joke. Then he saw my expression, and his own turned uncertain.
“Is it true?”
“I keep telling you it is.”
“You’re saying that, in all honesty, you have no idea what your words and actions mean? No idea why Young Lady Ju leaves every time?”
“I swear to heaven. I’ll stake my balls on it.”
“Huh. You’re staking your own balls instead of Hyuk Mujin’s... Then it must be true.”
The verification process seemed odd, but he believed me now, so I let it pass.
Song Ilseom stared at me as if he’d seen a unicorn.
“How can anyone be this clueless?”
“What?”
“Wasn’t your old sobriquet the Night King? You’d think you would at least know the basics.”
How long would I have to clean up the shit that promiscuous predecessor had left behind? If they’d called him the Porn King, I could have admitted there was some truth to it. But the Night King?
“...It’s a long story.”
Song Ilseom nodded at my weary reply.
“Of course. You must have spent many long nights.”
“You son of a bitch. Draw your sword. You’re fucking dead today.”
“Unfortunately, we’ll have to put that off until later. Thanks to you, I have to find an employer who still hasn’t appeared even after fifteen minutes.”
“You seem to have forgotten I’m the Fire Dragon Pavilion Master. Your direct superior.”
“But my employer is the one who pays me silver nyang. Protecting her is my job.”
Song Ilseom sheathed his freshly polished willow-leaf saber and rose from the water’s edge.
Crunch. Crunch.
He turned away without another word, his feet pressing into sand and gravel. Then he stopped.
“If you don’t know why Young Lady Ju acts that way, think about it carefully with that nonexistent sense of tact you have. You have to find the answer yourself.”
“What?”
“She may look strong, but she’s suffered a great deal. I hope she doesn’t get hurt—or die for nothing.”
That was all.
I watched him walk on as though nothing had happened, and a thought came to me.
Is silver nyang really why he’s stayed by Ju Hwaran’s side all this time?
Before I could find an answer, a sound rang across the surging waters of the Yangtze in Sichuan.
Boom. Ba-boom. Boom!
Drums beat hard. Ship prows cut swiftly and forcefully through the current.
A dozen or so swift ships emerged from the fog, flags of the Water Dragon Stronghold fluttering above them.
“Our taxi’s here,” I muttered.

The map the horse caravans had reportedly made while traveling between the Outer Lands and the Central Plains was proof enough of how they had amassed such wealth.
“This is the place.
The marker’s faint, but it’s definitely one of the horse caravans’.”
“Huh.
Who would’ve thought there was a road through here?”
Secret shortcuts hidden throughout the Central Plains, swift and accurate despite their concealment.
Some had vanished over the years, and those that remained could be treacherous precisely because they were hidden.
But that wasn’t much of a problem for us.
“Captain, isn’t this slope too steep?”
“It is.
The road’s narrow, too.
But we have to go.”
“Then I’m afraid we’ll have to leave the horses behind.”
“Why would we do that?
We can carry them.”
“Pardon?”
Correction.
It wasn’t much of a problem for me.
Everyone who heard me stared wide-eyed.
“What did you say?”
“They’re not big warhorses.
They came from the grasslands, so they’re fairly light, aren’t they?”
“...Light or not, they’re horses.
Can you really carry them?”
As it turned out, I could.
More easily than I’d expected, in fact.
My strength had long since surpassed human limits.
I slung two horses over my shoulders and strode uphill, while Taishan—who wasn’t as strong as me but was a natural strongman with the build to match—could manage three.
“Pavilion Master.
Taishan.
Heavy.
No choice.
Eat one horse here.
No, leave one here.”
“...Swallow your spit and try saying that again.”
His appetite was a bigger problem than the weight.
And as the shortcuts cut down our travel time and distance, greater obstacles waited for us.
“According to the map, there should be a road ahead.
But...”
“It’s gone.
Or rather, blocked.”
“Escort Song is right.
I heard there was a landslide nearby a month or two ago.
That must have blocked it.”
“Then we’ll have to go around.
The map says this road runs for at least ten li.
If only a few dozen jang were buried, perhaps, but clearing a road like this is out of the question...
Pavilion Master, what are you doing?”
“Getting ready to clear the road.”
“What?”
“It’s not like we have to tunnel through the mountain.
Clear some dirt, move a few rocks and boulders, and we should be able to get through.
You said the landslide was only a month or two ago, right?”
“Well, yes, but...”
“As they say, when the body is weak, the head has to work harder.”
“...That sounds wrong.
Isn’t it usually the other way around?”
“Usually.”
For days, we carried horses up mountains, dug through buried roads, and walked and ran until we crossed Hubei and reached Sichuan at a ridiculous pace.
We owed it all to Ju Hwaran.
She knew the shortcuts once shared by only a handful of horse caravans, and she remembered everything her maternal grandfather—the Escort King—had left behind.
I can’t believe we got here so quickly.
We’d made this kind of time without even taking the waterways.
Granted, I’d played no small part in making the impossible possible.
But Hwaran had more than fulfilled the role she’d promised to take on before joining the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
She’d exceeded my expectations.
Martial arts really aren’t everything.
No matter how much of a Supreme Peak master I became, I couldn’t do anything like this.
I gave Ju Hwaran a heartfelt exclamation of admiration.
“You’re incredible.
There’s no one like you, Young Lady Ju.”
“I-I’ll go feed the horses some hay.”
“What?
Why?
They aren’t Taishan.
How long has it even been since they ate hay...
Young Lady Ju?
Young Lady Ju?”
What the hell was going on?
At this point, I couldn’t tell whether she couldn’t hear me or had decided not to listen.
As I watched Ju Hwaran hurry away using a movement technique, I turned my head at the gaze I felt from beside me.
Swish!
The movement was quick as lightning, but not quick enough to escape my notice.
I eyed the culprit.
“Hey.”
He flinched.
“I saw you.
Don’t pretend you weren’t looking.”
Song Ilseom, seated by the water, glanced around awkwardly.
“Hmm.
Are you speaking to me?”
“You’re the only one here.
And you know you look awkward as hell, right?”
“...I have no idea what you mean.”
“If you were watching, you were watching.
Why hide it?
And do you sharpen that willow-leaf saber every chance you get?
It’ll be a needle by the time we reach Nanman.”
Splash.
Song Ilseom poured water over the blade, polished so carefully it gleamed like a mirror.
His face hardened.
“Watch what you say.
This weapon means something to me.”
He wasn’t particularly expressive to begin with, but he’d gone so serious that there had to be a story behind it.
Then again, he’s been through a lot.
There was no excuse for reopening someone else’s wounds.
Thinking I’d made a careless mistake, I spoke cautiously.
“Is it a treasured blade passed down through your family?”
“Hardly.
I was told they couldn’t bring out so much as a single martial arts manual.
My grandmother never learned martial arts in her life.
The fact that she survived that war was a miracle.”
“Right.
It did look pretty worn for a treasured blade.
Something your father left you, then?”
“No.”
A wistful smile touched Song Ilseom’s lips, as if he were remembering better days.
He ran a hand along the blade.
“I received this willow-leaf saber when I was young, while serving as a sword boy for a Third Rate wandering martial artist.
I cut a person with it for the first time in my life.
I was probably twelve.”
Right.”
Wounds, my ass.
My budding guilt melted away like spring snow.
He’d been a martial artist from the start.
Watching Song Ilseom fondly recall his first killing, I could only think he was... out of his mind.
Yeah.
He’s not right in the head either.
Murim had all kinds of people, but lunatics made up a good share of them.
Maybe you had to be one to survive here.
You could die over a meal.
You could die in a fight.
You could survive the fight, only to die when your wounds got worse.
You could endure enough hardship to become a master, then die from qi deviation during training.
What was that novel called?
I read one where a martial artist retired peacefully with golden-basin handwashing.
It took coming to Murim to realize that a novel was just a novel.
I’d once asked Jeok Cheongang about golden-basin handwashing.
His answer had gone like this:
“Golden-basin handwashing?
Easy.”
“Oh.
It is?”
“Of course.
First, buy a basin made of gold and invite plenty of close acquaintances.”
“It already reeks of social butterflies and capitalism, but all right.
What next?”
“Wash your hands without a care.
Of course, the moment you take your hand off your weapon, an assassin hidden among your acquaintances will throw a hidden weapon at you.”
“And one more thing.
The person you thought was an acquaintance might be an assassin, too.
What do you think?
Isn’t it easy?”
As my dear Fire-Rice Grandpa had so wisely put it, that was fucking Murim for you.
Golden-basin handwashing, my ass.
Most martial artists should be grateful just to wake up in the morning and wash their faces with ice water.
After all, the next day they might have to bathe and purify themselves in the waters of the Sanzu River instead of ice water.
I supposed that counted as retirement, too.
The only difference was whether you were still breathing.
What is this, Murim Escape Number One?
The old show had been canceled, but a Murim edition would be a smash hit.
Assuming television caught on here, it might pull a 107 percent viewership rating, like turnout in a Russian presidential election.
They could hire a master of demonic, heterodox arts as their experiment expert.
He’d smile warmly and run the demonstration himself.
“All right, fellow martial artists.
What happens if you dodge this form like so?”
Stab.
“See?
Dead.
Heh heh.”
They’d run out of experimenters in no time...
It was only my imagination, but Murim was the kind of place where it could become reality as soon as someone brought in a TV.
And in this insane world, I had to travel with lunatics and fight more lunatics.
“...Whew.”
I was staring silently at the river, feeling sorry for myself, when Song Ilseom spoke.
“I was watching.”
“Hm?
Watching what?”
“What happened earlier.
I never answered you.”
So that was what he meant.
I shrugged.
“I knew you were watching.
Why were you staring?”
“I heard something, so I looked.”
“Try being honest.”
“Your words and actions looked so stupid that I couldn’t help staring.”
That’s a little too honest.”
“But it’s true.
Isn’t that why Young Lady Ju keeps leaving whenever you say things like that?”
For some reason, I felt wronged.
“What did I do?
I was impressed, so I gave her an honest compliment.”
“Even a passing dog wouldn’t believe that.”
“It’s true.”
“Enough.
It isn’t funny.”
“I haven’t found any of this funny.”
“Fine.
Let’s say it’s true.”
Song Ilseom let out a quiet laugh, as though I’d made a joke.
Then he saw my expression, and his own turned uncertain.
“Is it true?”
“I keep telling you it is.”
“You’re saying that, in all honesty, you have no idea what your words and actions mean?
No idea why Young Lady Ju leaves every time?”
“I swear to heaven.
I’ll stake my balls on it.”
“Huh.
You’re staking your own balls instead of Hyuk Mujin’s...
Then it must be true.”
The verification process seemed odd, but he believed me now, so I let it pass.
Song Ilseom stared at me as if he’d seen a unicorn.
“How can anyone be this clueless?”
“What?”
“Wasn’t your old sobriquet the Night King?
You’d think you would at least know the basics.”
How long would I have to clean up the shit that promiscuous predecessor had left behind?
If they’d called him the Porn King, I could have admitted there was some truth to it.
But the Night King?
“...It’s a long story.”
Song Ilseom nodded at my weary reply.
“Of course.
You must have spent many long nights.”
“You son of a bitch.
Draw your sword.
You’re fucking dead today.”
“Unfortunately, we’ll have to put that off until later.
Thanks to you, I have to find an employer who still hasn’t appeared even after fifteen minutes.”
“You seem to have forgotten I’m the Fire Dragon Pavilion Master.
Your direct superior.”
“But my employer is the one who pays me silver nyang.
Protecting her is my job.”
Song Ilseom sheathed his freshly polished willow-leaf saber and rose from the water’s edge.
Crunch.
Crunch.
He turned away without another word, his feet pressing into sand and gravel.
Then he stopped.
“If you don’t know why Young Lady Ju acts that way, think about it carefully with that nonexistent sense of tact you have.
You have to find the answer yourself.”
“What?”
“She may look strong, but she’s suffered a great deal.
I hope she doesn’t get hurt—or die for nothing.”
That was all.
I watched him walk on as though nothing had happened, and a thought came to me.
Is silver nyang really why he’s stayed by Ju Hwaran’s side all this time?
Before I could find an answer, a sound rang across the surging waters of the Yangtze in Sichuan.
Boom.
Ba-boom.
Boom!
Drums beat hard.
Ship prows cut swiftly and forcefully through the current.
A dozen or so swift ships emerged from the fog, flags of the Water Dragon Stronghold fluttering above them.
“Our taxi’s here,” I muttered.

chapters.title: Chapter 617
paragraphs: Splash!
A dozen or so swift ships were approaching the riverbank. Anyone who wasn’t blind could see them.
For a martial artist who had reached a realm stage, spotting them was even easier.
“Water Dragon Stronghold...”
Sama Pyo rushed over using his movement technique. He narrowed his eyes at the ships’ flags, then turned to me.
“You told me to wait. Was this why?”
“Yep.”

“Sichuan is a land filled with treacherous terrain, so if we travel down the Yangtze, we can certainly move faster than we are now. Still, I’m somewhat concerned that our counterparts are the Yangtze River Channel League.”

He had reason to distrust them. The Yangtze River Channel League was, at its core, a band of water bandits who made their living by plunder. And the prevailing opinion was that its leader, the Seafaring King Pa Ryun, was a devious man, regardless of his martial prowess.
He didn’t attend the formation of the Murim Alliance, either, for some reason.
I didn’t know whether illness or distance had kept him away. He had sent an envoy to announce his intention to join, then made it official. The Green Forest Alliance had done the same.
Both groups were closer to the unorthodox faction than the orthodox one. More accurately, they were plunderers who had carved out powerful domains of their own.
“I hear Pa Ryun is impossible to read,” Sama Pyo said. “Rumors about him have been circulating quietly even in Henan.”
“That he’ll side with Dark Heaven when the time comes? That kind of rumor?”
“So you’ve heard.”
“Are my ears just decoration? And since you brought up what people say...”
I looked at him and lowered my voice.
“By that standard, the Yangtze River Channel League and the Black Dragon Demon Gate are two of a kind.”
“Am I wrong?”
After a brief silence, Sama Pyo answered with a sour look.
“Now that I think about it, you may be right.”
“Not may be. I am, you bastard. Look closely and the Black Dragon Demon Gate might be worse. At least those guys rob orthodox and unorthodox factions alike. There’s no denying which side you’re on.”
“...I understand. You can stop. Listening to this is making my head spin.”
Taishan, who had been prowling around Sama Pyo like an enormous dog, joined in.
“Lord. Taishan hungry too. Head spinning.”
Watching you two is making my head spin.
I rubbed my throbbing temple and opened my mouth.
“And one more thing. You can trust those water bandits, so stop worrying.”
“Trustworthy water bandits? You might as well tell me there’s a martial artist who’s never learned martial arts.”
“It’s a long story, but we’ve got a pretty strong bond.”
I didn’t know what kind of man the Seafaring King Pa Ryun was. Even if everything people said about him was true, though, it wouldn’t change my opinion of Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song.
The Mu Song I knew kept his word and held to his principles. A disciple didn’t necessarily take after his master.
The fact that they came as soon as I sent word from Sichuan says enough.
While I was thinking that, the swift ships reached the bank and a dozen or so men poured ashore.
Splash!

They moved with the rough energy of bandits who knew the Yangtze inside and out, sending river water spraying in every direction. Bronze-colored muscles showed through their loose robes as they raced over and clasped their hands in salute.
“Great Hero Jin!”
“We came as fast as we could when we got your message.”
These were Mu Song’s trusted men, all squad leaders or higher in the Water Dragon Stronghold. I’d seen them several times a day on my last visit to Sichuan, but the face I knew best was missing.
“All familiar faces. But I don’t see Senior Mu Song.”
The Deputy Stronghold Lord answered at once.
“I’m sorry to say he left for headquarters two days ago.”
“Headquarters... The Yangtze River Channel League’s?”
“Yes, sir. It was on the League Leader’s orders, so he couldn’t delay even a moment.”
“I see.”
Within the Yangtze River Channel League, the Seafaring King’s orders were absolute. His direct Disciple, Ship-Fire Boy Mu Song, had no choice but to answer a summons.
I looked over the bandits, disappointed that I’d missed him but grateful they had come.
“You still got here quickly, even with Senior Mu Song away.”
The Deputy Stronghold Lord waved his hands in alarm.
“Oh, please don’t say that. The Stronghold Lord must have seen this coming. Before he left, he gave us strict instructions about you.”
“About me?”

“Yes, sir. He said a person ought to repay a favor. And considering what happened with the late Yangtze One Saber, Great Hero Hwang, he told us to do everything we could if the Jin Family of Taiyuan or Great Hero Jin ever needed help.”
“Oh. Senior Mu Song understands loyalty. A true hero.”
See that, you bastard?
I smiled at Sama Pyo. Just then, a burly bandit beside the deputy leaned in and whispered, looking puzzled.
“Deputy Stronghold Lord.”
“Hm?”
“Didn’t the Stronghold Lord also say Great Hero Jin would raise hell if we didn’t help? That we should give him whatever he wanted instead of letting him wreck perfectly good swift ships?”
“Ah. Uh. Jang Pil, you little—!”
Silence fell.
Never mind the water bandits. The gazes of the proud members of our Fire Dragon Pavilion were painfully sharp.
In the hush, Ju Hwaran murmured so quietly I could barely hear her.
“What on earth have you been doing to make even water bandits...”
That went straight through me. I looked out over the endless Yangtze, my chest tightening.
I wanted to make an excuse, but I had thrown tantrums and treated their ships like taxis. I couldn’t say a thing.
“In some ways, you’re worse than the unorthodox faction,” Sama Pyo muttered.
I did my best to ignore his final blow and turned mournful eyes on the deputy.
“Let’s just get going.”
“Y-yes, sir.”
“And come see me later. Bring Jang Pil, too.”
The Deputy Stronghold Lord stared at me in terror for a moment before shouting in a choked voice,
“Raise the anchor! Raise the anchor!”
I must have imagined the tears in his voice.
Whoosh!
The ship’s bow cut swiftly and powerfully through the water.
Spring had arrived, and the wind was at our backs. Years of plunder had made the bandits peerless rowers.
Of course, even though these were fairly decent water bandits who had been reformed by Mu Song, their innate instincts remained.
“Five ships to the southeast!”
“Deputy Stronghold Lord, they’re sizable merchant ships!”
“Merchant ships? Let’s rob them!”
Rob them? Now? You lunatics.
Everyone watched in disbelief, myself included. The Deputy Stronghold Lord’s face twisted.
“You idiots! We have honored guests aboard! What do you think you’re doing? Do you people have no basic manners?”
“S-sorry.”
For a water bandit, he sounded exactly like Judge Bao.
After sternly rebuking his subordinates, the Deputy Stronghold Lord approached us and bowed politely.
“I apologize for letting you see us behave that way.”
“Heh heh. Think nothing of it.”
I gave him an amiable smile.
“I understand. Robbing ships is your line of work. I can see how it happened.”
“Thank you for understanding. We’ll rob them quickly and get back on our way.”
“Huh?”
“Half a shichen at most. We’ll take a little off them and let them go...”
“Get down.”
There had been a slight incident, but after I made the Deputy Stronghold Lord drop and hold the push-up position a few times, even that impulse disappeared.
All the while, the swift ship kept moving with the wind at its back.
One day passed. Then two. Then three...
Aboard the ship, the Fire Dragon Pavilion members each settled into their own preparations.
Swish! Whoosh!
After that first day, Sama Pyo and Song Ilseom trained in their respective martial arts without clashing again.
“Taishan likes sashimi. But no fish caught. Give Taishan one.”
“You’ve got some nerve. I worked hard to catch these few fish, and you want me to hand one over? Captain, he won’t leave me alone. Can you get him off my back?”
“Give me all the fish you’ve caught so far. Slice them into sashimi first, obviously.”
“Taishan impressed. Is Pavilion Master a genius?”
Hyuk Mujin and Taishan spent most of their time fishing at the bow.
They often caught nothing. When Mujin did catch fish, someone else usually took them. He hardly complained, but I knew it wasn’t because he’d given up.
He wasn’t fishing to catch fish in the first place.
That’s why he doesn’t say anything.
Hyuk Mujin fished to clear his mind, even if only for a while.

Even when the bobber trembled right in front of him, he didn’t bother yanking on the fishing rod. Every night, he locked himself in the cabin to practice martial arts or devote himself to circulating his qi.
Day by day, hour by hour, we drew closer to Yunnan. Everyone was preparing in their own way for a fight that might come.
I was no different.
Open the Quest window.
Ding.

System Quest Journey to Nanman Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak has assigned the Fire Dragon Pavilion its first mission. You must now head to Nanman and actively respond to any situation that may arise. There is no way to know what lies ahead for you and the Fire Dragon Pavilion. Always remain vigilant and act with a flexible mindset. Grade: Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung and Fire Dragon Pavilion members Mission: Enter Nanman (Incomplete) Reward: Chain Quest ??? Failure: Obtain Title: Can’t Go to Nanman Fame and trust greatly reduced
In Murim time, I’d received that Quest about half a month ago. Counting my time in the modern world, it had been over a month.
I was studying the Quest Window again for anything I might have missed when a faint floral scent drifted in on the breeze.
“Why are you staring so hard at empty space?”
It was Ju Hwaran.
I closed the holographic window and gazed solemnly at the star-filled sky.
“I was reading the heavenly patterns.”
“Oh. Really?”
“Yes, really.”
“That’s impressive.”
She gave a quiet laugh.
“So what did the heavens tell you?”
“They said the weather would be nice today.”
“Really?”
“Yes. Young Lady Ju, see the Big Dipper over there?”
Ju Hwaran looked up at the sky along my pointing finger and blinked.
“Uh. Um.”
“What?”
“Pavilion Master, I’m sorry, but that isn’t the Big Dipper.”
“...That can’t be right. Did it change shape while I wasn’t looking?”
“What?”
What the hell kind of answer was that?
I realized how ridiculous it sounded as soon as I said it. I scratched my chin, flustered, and Ju Hwaran burst out laughing.
“That’s an interesting way to read the heavenly patterns.”
“Honestly, I don’t know how to read them. I just deal with whatever comes up as best I can.”
“I know. But now I want to hear more. There’s something I’ve been wondering about. May I ask?”
I smacked my lips.
“I already told you I can’t read the heavenly patterns.”
“And I already told you I know. I don’t want to ask the heavens. I want to ask you.”
“In that case, go ahead. I’ll answer if I can.”
Tap.
Ju Hwaran lightly jumped onto the bow and looked out at the pitch-black river before opening her mouth.
“What do you think will happen from here on? To us?”
Nanman was close now. She had to be anxious.
I thought for a moment about how to reassure her.
“I don’t know. There’s a strong possibility that Dark Heaven is plotting something, but it’s also possible that nothing will happen.”

Nanman was remote enough to be counted among the Outer Lands. It was also a vast territory home to the Nanman Beast Palace, the dominant power in Nanman, as well as numerous ethnic groups, including the Miao people.
If my forebodings were right and Dark Heaven was plotting something there, countless dangers awaited the Fire Dragon Pavilion and me.
But...
“Nothing will happen to us. Whatever we face, we’ll make it home safely. I can promise you that.”
Ju Hwaran didn’t answer. Instead, she watched me with an unreadable look for a moment—no, for a long time.
“Young Lady Ju?”
“...I see.”
At last she spoke. A faint smile touched her lips, and she shook her head gently. Her glossy hair, which even the human-skin mask couldn’t hide, rippled like the river.
“I’ll trust you, Pavilion Master.”
Something felt off. I was wondering whether I’d said the wrong thing when the Deputy Stronghold Lord appeared carrying a torch, his face flushed.
“Great Hero Jin. We’ve arrived.”

“In some ways, you’re worse than the unorthodox faction,” Sama Pyo muttered.
I did my best to ignore his final blow and turned mournful eyes on the deputy.
“Let’s just get going.”
“Y-yes, sir.”
“And come see me later.
Bring Jang Pil, too.”
The Deputy Stronghold Lord stared at me in terror for a moment before shouting in a choked voice,
“Raise the anchor!
Raise the anchor!”
I must have imagined the tears in his voice.
Whoosh!
The ship’s bow cut swiftly and powerfully through the water.
Spring had arrived, and the wind was at our backs.
Years of plunder had made the bandits peerless rowers.
Of course, even though these were fairly decent water bandits who had been reformed by Mu Song, their innate instincts remained.
“Five ships to the southeast!”
“Deputy Stronghold Lord, they’re sizable merchant ships!”
“Merchant ships?
Let’s rob them!”
Rob them?
Now?
You lunatics.
Everyone watched in disbelief, myself included.
The Deputy Stronghold Lord’s face twisted.
“You idiots!
We have honored guests aboard!
What do you think you’re doing?
Do you people have no basic manners?”
“S-sorry.”
For a water bandit, he sounded exactly like Judge Bao.
After sternly rebuking his subordinates, the Deputy Stronghold Lord approached us and bowed politely.
“I apologize for letting you see us behave that way.”
“Heh heh.
Think nothing of it.”
I gave him an amiable smile.
“I understand.
Robbing ships is your line of work.
I can see how it happened.”
“Thank you for understanding.
We’ll rob them quickly and get back on our way.”
“Huh?”
“Half a shichen at most.
We’ll take a little off them and let them go...”
“Get down.”
There had been a slight incident, but after I made the Deputy Stronghold Lord drop and hold the push-up position a few times, even that impulse disappeared.
All the while, the swift ship kept moving with the wind at its back.
One day passed.
Then two.
Then three...
Aboard the ship, the Fire Dragon Pavilion members each settled into their own preparations.
Swish!
Whoosh!
After that first day, Sama Pyo and Song Ilseom trained in their respective martial arts without clashing again.
“Taishan likes sashimi.
But no fish caught.
Give Taishan one.”
“You’ve got some nerve.
I worked hard to catch these few fish, and you want me to hand one over?
Captain, he won’t leave me alone.
Can you get him off my back?”
“Give me all the fish you’ve caught so far.
Slice them into sashimi first, obviously.”
“Taishan impressed.
Is Pavilion Master a genius?”
Hyuk Mujin and Taishan spent most of their time fishing at the bow.
They often caught nothing.
When Mujin did catch fish, someone else usually took them.
He hardly complained, but I knew it wasn’t because he’d given up.
He wasn’t fishing to catch fish in the first place.
That’s why he doesn’t say anything.
Hyuk Mujin fished to clear his mind, even if only for a while.
Even when the bobber trembled right in front of him, he didn’t bother yanking on the fishing rod.
Every night, he locked himself in the cabin to practice martial arts or devote himself to circulating his qi.
Day by day, hour by hour, we drew closer to Yunnan.
Everyone was preparing in their own way for a fight that might come.
I was no different.
Open the Quest window.
Ding.
System Quest Journey to Nanman Murim Alliance Leader Mae Jonghak has assigned the Fire Dragon Pavilion its first mission.
You must now head to Nanman and actively respond to any situation that may arise.
There is no way to know what lies ahead for you and the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Always remain vigilant and act with a flexible mindset.
Grade: Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung and Fire Dragon Pavilion members Mission: Enter Nanman (Incomplete) Reward: Chain Quest ???
Failure: Obtain Title: Can’t Go to Nanman Fame and trust greatly reduced
In Murim time, I’d received that Quest about half a month ago.
Counting my time in the modern world, it had been over a month.
I was studying the Quest Window again for anything I might have missed when a faint floral scent drifted in on the breeze.
“Why are you staring so hard at empty space?”
It was Ju Hwaran.
I closed the holographic window and gazed solemnly at the star-filled sky.
“I was reading the heavenly patterns.”
“Oh.
Really?”
“Yes, really.”
“That’s impressive.”
She gave a quiet laugh.
“So what did the heavens tell you?”
“They said the weather would be nice today.”
“Really?”
“Yes.
Young Lady Ju, see the Big Dipper over there?”
Ju Hwaran looked up at the sky along my pointing finger and blinked.
“Uh.
Um.”
“What?”
“Pavilion Master, I’m sorry, but that isn’t the Big Dipper.”
“...That can’t be right.
Did it change shape while I wasn’t looking?”
“What?”
What the hell kind of answer was that?
I realized how ridiculous it sounded as soon as I said it.
I scratched my chin, flustered, and Ju Hwaran burst out laughing.
“That’s an interesting way to read the heavenly patterns.”
“Honestly, I don’t know how to read them.
I just deal with whatever comes up as best I can.”
“I know.
But now I want to hear more.
There’s something I’ve been wondering about.
May I ask?”
I smacked my lips.
“I already told you I can’t read the heavenly patterns.”
“And I already told you I know.
I don’t want to ask the heavens.
I want to ask you.”
“In that case, go ahead.
I’ll answer if I can.”
Tap.
Ju Hwaran lightly jumped onto the bow and looked out at the pitch-black river before opening her mouth.
“What do you think will happen from here on?
To us?”
Nanman was close now.
She had to be anxious.
I thought for a moment about how to reassure her.
“I don’t know.
There’s a strong possibility that Dark Heaven is plotting something, but it’s also possible that nothing will happen.”
Nanman was remote enough to be counted among the Outer Lands.
It was also a vast territory home to the Nanman Beast Palace, the dominant power in Nanman, as well as numerous ethnic groups, including the Miao people.
If my forebodings were right and Dark Heaven was plotting something there, countless dangers awaited the Fire Dragon Pavilion and me.
But...
“Nothing will happen to us.
Whatever we face, we’ll make it home safely.
I can promise you that.”
Ju Hwaran didn’t answer.
Instead, she watched me with an unreadable look for a moment—no, for a long time.
“Young Lady Ju?”
“...I see.”
At last she spoke.
A faint smile touched her lips, and she shook her head gently.
Her glossy hair, which even the human-skin mask couldn’t hide, rippled like the river.
“I’ll trust you, Pavilion Master.”
Something felt off.
I was wondering whether I’d said the wrong thing when the Deputy Stronghold Lord appeared carrying a torch, his face flushed.
“Great Hero Jin.
We’ve arrived.”

chapters.title: Chapter 618
paragraphs: The air had grown hot and muggy. In the distance, high mountains and deep valleys came into view.
The Deputy Stronghold Lord of the Water Dragon Stronghold pointed toward the rapidly approaching shore.
“This is as far as we can take you, Great Hero Jin. Once you disembark, head straight on for ten li and you’ll be in Yunnan. It won’t take long.”
The Yangtze’s tributaries stretched across a vast part of the continent, but they didn’t reach the interior of Yunnan Province.
No, that wasn’t strictly true. The waterways didn’t simply end there.
The problem was that continuing by water to the plateau in northern Yunnan would take us much longer to reach our destination.
Our highest priority is the Nanman Beast Palace, after all.
The Quest I had received required me to reach Nanman, but the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s mission required us to head for the Nanman Beast Palace.
I gave the Deputy Stronghold Lord a small bow.
“Thank you. You must be busy raiding merchant ships, yet you brought us all the way here.”
“Oh, please, don’t say that. You’re no ordinary person. If Great Hero Jin calls for us, we should drop everything and come running at any time. I’m almost sorry to part ways with you, heh heh heh.”
He looked far too happy for someone who was supposedly sorry.
Then again, I’d made him bang his head against the ground and hold a push-up position in front of his men whenever the mood struck me. He probably was happy to say goodbye.
I laughed along with him. “Ha ha. Really?”
“Of course. Heh heh.”
“Then it would be perfect if you stayed nearby, wouldn’t it?”
“Heh heh heh. What?”
“I was worried about how we’d get back after we finished here. But if you’re sorry to part ways, that solves it.”
“So wait nearby.”
The smile vanished from the Deputy Stronghold Lord’s face. He stammered, “Ah, no. That might be a little difficult. We have things to do as well...”
“I know. You can send the rest of the ships back and leave just one or two here.”
“G-Great Hero Jin, please. Wouldn’t it be better if you sent word once you’d finished your business in Yunnan?”
“Hmm. But then I’d have to wait too long.”
There was no trace of happiness left on his face. As he hung his head, I gently rubbed his shoulder.
“I know it’s an unreasonable request, but let’s impose on you a little.”
“No, even so...”
“Come on. Let’s impose on you a little.”
“Ah, fuck. Answer me already. You’ve got to know how to conduct yourself if you want to survive in Murim.”
“Gasp.”
The Deputy Stronghold Lord’s face went dark. His answer was all but decided.
A short while later, I finally extracted a promise that they would remain anchored nearby until we returned. After I disembarked, the gazes directed at me were far from ordinary.
“I thought I was watching a Third Rate wandering martial artist.”
“I mean no offense by this, but does the Jin Family of Taiyuan have roots in the unorthodox faction?”
“That’s our Captain. You never disappoint.”
“Taishan thought Pavilion Master was a water bandit.”
“I think the Pavilion Master made the right decision. If something happens in Nanman, we can ask them for help. Don’t you agree?”
That last answer was the only correct one.
As expected, Ju Hwaran is the only person who understands me.
I turned to her, moved. “Exactly. You said what I was thinking, down to the last word.”
“Oh! Is that really what you were thinking?”
“Huh?”
“I only took your side because everyone else was criticizing you. I thought someone should support the Pavilion Master...”
Is my image really okay as it is?
I was still pondering that as we walked along a crude road nothing like those in the Central Plains. Then a familiar sound rang in my ears.
Ding.

System Entered Nanman. Mission, Enter Nanman, completed. Quest, Journey to Nanman, successfully completed! Quest completion rewards acquired! A small amount of EXP acquired! A small amount of Fame acquired! Achievement, Thousands of Li in Search of Nanman, achieved! Nanman is a perilous land with erratic weather, filled with all manner of wild beasts and venomous creatures. Outsiders must always beware of endemic diseases and poison. Acquired: High-Grade Antidote ×10, Intermediate Antidote ×20, Basic Antidote ×30! A new Chain Quest has been created. Would you like to check the Quest window? Y / N
System notifications sounded one after another as holographic windows filled the air.
The Deputy Stronghold Lord had been telling the truth. We hadn’t seen a single person nearby, but after walking for a short while, we had apparently stepped into Nanman territory.
Pretending nothing had happened, I answered in my head.
Confirm.
Ding.

System Quest Seeds Planted in Nanman You have arrived in Nanman after traveling thousands of li, but Nanman is sparsely populated and outsiders are not welcome. With your limited knowledge and information, you cannot afford to act rashly. Make contact with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent the Murim Alliance planted in Nanman long ago and obtain detailed information. Grade: Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung and Fire Dragon Pavilion members Mission: Make contact with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent (Incomplete) Reward: Chain Quest ??? Failure: Stats decreased
Hmm.
Make contact with a Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent.
I read the new Chain Quest several times, then recalled a conversation I’d had with Song Ho, the Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, before leaving Henan.

“After the Great Faction War ended and the first Alliance Leader, the Martial God, disappeared, the Hidden Shadow Pavilion was disbanded. But even now, decades later, enough people remain to keep its intelligence network alive.”
“You mean...”
“Didn’t I tell you? The Hidden Shadow Pavilion has eyes and ears everywhere.”
After the Great War that had shaken the world ended, people had gradually settled into peace. But not everyone had.
The Thousand-Faced Fox Song Ho and the Hidden Shadow Pavilion certainly hadn’t.

“They’ve stayed at their posts all these years with nothing but a sense of duty to a greater cause and the courage to see it through. Find our man as soon as you reach Nanman. He’ll be able to give you information and plenty of help besides.”
“How am I supposed to find him? You’re not just going to give me his name and address, are you?”
“There’s a secret code known only to Hidden Shadow Pavilion agents. I’ll tell you where to go to verify it. You should be able to meet him there.”
It struck me again how remarkable that was. Nearly fifty years had passed since the Great Faction War, yet the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s intelligence network was still alive.
Especially in a backwater like Nanman. They must have wanted to leave.
Thanks to their sacrifice, though, the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s mission could become much easier.
After sorting out my thoughts, I spoke to the Fire Dragon Pavilion members as they moved forward while keeping watch over their surroundings.
“We’re going to Yeongin.”
“Yeongin?”
Hyuk Mujin tilted his head. “Never heard of it. Where is it?”
“It’s a county seat about two hundred li from here. Much less developed than any county seat in the Central Plains, of course.”
Ju Hwaran had answered for me. She went on, “Several different ethnic groups live there together. That doesn’t mean they never clash, though.”
Something about how readily she answered caught my attention. “Have you been there before?”
Ju Hwaran smiled and nodded.
“Didn’t I tell you? Three years ago, I finally pestered my father into letting me join an escort journey to Nanman.”
“Oh. So that was Yeongin.”
“Yes. I wasn’t there long, but I still remember it vividly. Captain Song came along too.”
Everyone turned to Song Ilseom. He raised an eyebrow.
“I never want to come to Nanman again. It was a horrible place. But Yeongin was relatively tolerable. The ethnic groups there were comparatively mild-tempered.”
From Song Ilseom, that was high praise.
Then again, that must have been why he had been able to escort a shipment across this rough and dangerous land of Nanman.
“But why are we going to Yeongin?” Ju Hwaran asked.
Now everyone looked at me. They’d probably wanted to ask from the start and had held back.
There was no reason to hide it. “I’m planning to meet a Murim Alliance informant there.”
“Then we certainly need to go. News from Nanman rarely reaches the outside world.”
Nanman was about as remote as a place could get.
Dozens of ethnic groups lived deep in its jungles. They were deeply wary of the Han Chinese from the Central Plains, and they had fought countless wars among themselves to defend their territories.

That was why even major Escort Bureaus and merchant companies were reluctant to make the journey. A successful trip could bring back spices, medicinal herbs, and rare gems—but the dangers lurking in the jungle could cost them their lives.
Even without an ethnic group suffering from anger-management issues, countless poisonous creatures, wild beasts, and highly lethal endemic diseases were serious obstacles.

“But Yeongin should be fine,” Ju Hwaran said with a bright smile. “Our Yongbong Escort Bureau has had ties with the people there since the time of its former leaders, and the ethnic groups living there are relatively friendly toward the Han Chinese.”
“Oh. Is that so?”
“Yes. You’ll see when you meet them. They’re good people.”
Hk, ptui.
A glob of sticky phlegm landed by our feet.
Living up to the name Bai, or “White,” a tribesman dressed in white glared menacingly at us before disappearing from sight.
I watched him go, then turned cautiously to Ju Hwaran.
“Um, I’m asking just in case, but does someone like that count as one of the nicer ones among the ethnic groups?”
“Young Lady Ju?”
After a pause, she said, “Hmm. That man seems a bit rough. Most people aren’t like that.”
“Right?”
“Yes, yes. Of course. I know because I’ve been here myself.”
The moment Ju Hwaran finished speaking, a middle-aged ethnic woman dressed in clothes as colorful as a peacock covered a child’s eyes and muttered,
“My word. Those Han bastards had the nerve to come all the way here. Let’s go inside before the sight of them ruins your eyes.”
“Mom. Mom. I can’t see.”
“It’s okay, sweetheart. Let’s hurry away from those vicious men. Honey! Come out quickly! Han bastards have entered the village!”
“What? Wait there. I’ll get my plow and smash those Han sons of bitches’ heads in!”
For an instant, Ju Hwaran’s pupils shook violently.
Clinging to one last shred of hope, I asked, “They’re just a little rougher than average too, right?”
“...Probably. I think.”
But Ju Hwaran’s hopes were brutally ignored.
Before long, the ethnic tribesmen filling the roadside began openly displaying their hostility toward us.
“So they really are Han Chinese.”
“They’ve got some nerve. Send word to the chief at once.”
“I already sent someone.”
“Get the women and children indoors. Gather the men and keep an eye on those Han bastards.”
I felt like a criminal.
No. To them, we were already criminals who deserved to be torn apart and killed.
The others could feel it too, even though they couldn’t rely on the System to translate for them as I could, or speak the local language as Ju Hwaran did.
“Captain.”
“What?”
“I think we’re fucked.”
Hyuk Mujin swallowed hard and went on in a whisper. “I don’t know what they’re saying, but the atmosphere is extremely hostile. Wouldn’t it be better to get out of here?”
Hmm.
A leader’s job included calming his subordinates. I answered sternly.
“It’s not like that.”
“It isn’t?”
“No. They’re staring because they’re curious about Han Chinese.”
“Then why do they have axes?”
“They probably came over after chopping firewood.”
“And the swords?”
“They probably came over after slaughtering something.”
Don’t look at me like that. I feel guilty enough.
I did my best to ignore Hyuk Mujin’s distrustful gaze and crossed through the ethnic tribesmen radiating a menacing aura. I stopped in front of a wooden building.
Poison Flower Pavilion
The sign was so old it looked ready to crumble. This was the meeting place the Thousand-Faced Fox had told me about.
