No.
To them, we were already criminals who deserved to be torn apart and killed.
The others could feel it too, even though they couldn’t rely on the System to translate for them as I could, or speak the local language as Ju Hwaran did.
“Captain.”
“What?”
“I think we’re fucked.”
Hyuk Mujin swallowed hard and went on in a whisper.
“I don’t know what they’re saying, but the atmosphere is extremely hostile.
Wouldn’t it be better to get out of here?”
Hmm.
A leader’s job included calming his subordinates.
I answered sternly.
“It’s not like that.”
“It isn’t?”
“No.
They’re staring because they’re curious about Han Chinese.”
“Then why do they have axes?”
“They probably came over after chopping firewood.”
“And the swords?”
“They probably came over after slaughtering something.”
Don’t look at me like that.
I feel guilty enough.
I did my best to ignore Hyuk Mujin’s distrustful gaze and crossed through the ethnic tribesmen radiating a menacing aura.
I stopped in front of a wooden building.
Poison Flower Pavilion
The sign was so old it looked ready to crumble.
This was the meeting place the Thousand-Faced Fox had told me about.

chapters.title: Chapter 619
paragraphs: Poison Flower Pavilion...
A fitting name for a place in Nanman, where venomous beasts were everywhere. The catch was that it looked less like an inn or pleasure house than a mansion ready to collapse.
If the Thousand-Faced Fox’s directions were right, this should be the place.
I eyed the decrepit wooden building with suspicion. Around us, the mood grew more hostile by the second.
“You fucking Han bastards!”
“Go back to your own land!”
Whoosh! Crack!
Sama Pyo dodged a rock flying at the back of his head and muttered with a sigh, “Pavilion Master, we’d better go inside. Unless you intend to fight them right now.”
“That’s out of the question.”
For once, he was absolutely right. We couldn’t make enemies of every local in Nanman the moment we arrived.
I glanced at the crowd radiating a menacing aura, then opened the door to the Poison Flower Pavilion.
Creeeak.
The old wooden door gave a feeble scrape.
Dim light and a gloomy air filled the inn. A few crude tables stood far apart, like weeds growing here and there. The patrons seated at them turned toward us.
“Never seen those faces before... Han Chinese?”
Hk, ptui.
Were they Hydras?
People around here used phlegm like a passive Skill.
The ethnic patrons spat onto the dusty floor and rose from their seats, their faces flushed red.
“Han bastards dare come here? Do they want to die?”
“They’ve ruined the taste of my liquor. Let’s go. Nothing good will come of staying here with them.”
Bang!
Once the door slammed shut behind them, Ju Hwaran spoke with a troubled expression. “Something must have gone badly wrong. It wasn’t like this the last time I came.”
Song Ilseom nodded. “I agree. The ethnic groups of Nanman are wary of outsiders, but Yeongin was different. It’s the place closest to the Central Plains.”
“Exactly. Merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains used to pass through here. It wasn’t common, but it happened. So why...”
As Hwaran trailed off, an elderly voice cut in.
“Why? Because of an Escort Bureau. Han bastards just like you.”
We weren’t the only ones left in the Poison Flower Pavilion.

An old man who had been sleeping off his liquor until a moment ago thumped his bent back and went on. “Bad luck all around. For you lot, crawling into Nanman without knowing what’s happened. And for a certain old man whose business is about to dry up because of those fearless Han bastards.”
I realized who he was. “Are you the owner?”
The old man looked at me in surprise when I spoke the local language fluently.
“You can speak our language. Are you perhaps one of the Miao people?”
“No.”
“Then you don’t look like the Bai or Man people either. Judging by your face, you’re definitely Han Chinese... but you speak remarkably well. I’d believe you were born and raised here.”
As expected of the Integrated Language Pack. It certainly did its job.
Even Ju Hwaran looked surprised by my pronunciation. “When did you learn their language?”
“Well...”
I couldn’t exactly explain it, so I let the answer trail off before saying casually, “I picked it up somewhere along the way. Just a little trick.”
Beside me, Hyuk Mujin muttered under his breath, “I thought drinking, women, and gambling were the only tricks our Captain knew...”
“You little shit.”
Bam!
“Urgh!”
Mujin collapsed clutching his solar plexus. The old man clicked his tongue.
“That one sure knows how to get himself hit.”
“He’s always like that, so don’t mind him... Wait. You speak Chinese?”
“To a degree. I served as an interpreter for Han Chinese several times when I was young.”
As though it were nothing, the old man pointed a bony finger at Song Ilseom.
“That dark-looking fellow seems familiar. Were you here about three years ago?”
Ju Hwaran should have stood out most, but perhaps her human-skin mask was why he recognized Song Ilseom first.
Song Ilseom nodded silently. The old man slapped his knee.
“I knew it. Your name was something like Dragon King...”
“Yongbong Escort Bureau. Not Dragon King.”
“Right, Yongbong Escort Bureau. Unlike the other merchant groups and Escort Bureaus from the Central Plains, you Han Chinese came by two or three times a year. I remember you clearly.”
For someone who remembers so clearly, you got the name wrong.
I held my tongue and asked what I’d been wanting to ask since he spoke up. “What did you mean earlier?”
“Hm? What about?”
“You said an Escort Bureau was why things had gotten like this. In your words, Han bastards like us.”
The old man gave me a blank look. “I said that? When?”
“What? You definitely—”
“Don’t remember a thing.”
Like hell you don’t.
I caught on and sighed. “Food. Can you make us something now?”
“Of course. Pay me, and I’ll make you anything.”
At the word food, Taishan sprang up from where he’d been lying facedown on the table, looking close to death.
“Taishan wants five-spice pork!”
“So there’s one fellow with more energy than he knows what to do with. I’ll make chicken.”
“Why chicken? Taishan doesn’t want chicken! Five-spice pork!”
I had no idea how his request for five-spice pork had turned into chicken, but we needed to keep the old man happy. I called to the one person who could stop Taishan’s fit.
“Ma Pyo. What are you doing?”
“It’s Sama Pyo.”
“Right, Sa-pyo.”
“...Taishan. Enough. Sit down.”
Sama Pyo glared at me before settling Taishan down. Meanwhile, the old man held out his hand as if it were the most natural thing in the world.
“What?”
“Payment up front.”
“Ah.”
“Let’s see. One chicken per person is the minimum, so that’s five chickens. At one silver nyang each... ten silver nyang altogether.”
“...Ten silver nyang? Even if it’s one nyang per chicken, that should be five silver nyang.”
“Is that so? Then make it two nyang each.”
“What?”
“I said two nyang per chicken.”
“If you don’t like it, spit on the floor and leave. There isn’t another village within a hundred li, mind you.”
What a shameless racket. If this man had been born in Yongsan fifty years ago, he’d have ended up a landlord.
I wondered why we hadn’t met any bandits on the road. Turns out they were in the inn, not the mountains.
It was highway robbery, but now wasn’t the time to save money. I took ten silver nyang from the hefty expense pouch the Murim Alliance had given me and handed them over.
“Here. Ten silver nyang.”
“For a Han, you catch on quickly.”
Rustle.
The old man swept up the gleaming silver with a grin. “Now, what about liquor?”
“No, thank you.”
“Drink.”
“I said drink.”
I didn’t have the energy to argue. Looking glum, I opened my pouch again.
Our first meal in Nanman was remarkable for all the wrong reasons.
The chicken was so scrawny it looked malnourished. The strong liquor had clearly been opened and partly drunk by someone else.
It was astonishing that the old man charged us dozens of silver nyang for all this. More astonishing still was how much of the food and liquor he consumed himself.
“Burp. That was good.”
Why are you the one who had a good meal?
The question rose to my throat, but I swallowed it. We had bought information with our money and our meal.
“The Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau?”
“That’s right. As I recall, they definitely said they came from Sichuan. There was one woman, and with the other men, there were nearly thirty of them.”
The old man nodded, his face flushed with drink. “At first, nobody thought much of it. Han Chinese had come to Yeongin before, and their group wasn’t particularly large.”
But they had been wrong. His eyes reddened by drink, the old man slowly recalled what had happened.
“People from a nearby village held a feast to welcome them. By the next morning, every last one of the villagers had been slaughtered.”

“Our village was spared, thank goodness. But when we checked later, we found that some two hundred people had died that night. Men, women, children, even the elderly. Not one survived. It was those Han bastards’ doing, of course.”
“Good grief.”
It was a shocking and horrific story. Only now did I fully understand the hostile looks and oppressive atmosphere that had been directed at us.
Two words came to mind.
Dark Heaven. And the Southern Heaven Demon Empress.
It was hardly an overreaction to be troubled by one woman who had been part of the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau.
I exchanged glances with the Fire Dragon Pavilion members, who had been listening with grim expressions, then took a sheet of paper from my Inventory.
“Sorry to interrupt, but could you look at this?”
“What is it?”

The paper I had taken out was a drawing. More precisely, it was a likeness of Honglan—or rather, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress—created from the testimony and memories of several people, including me.
I showed it to him on the off chance he’d recognize her. His reaction was lukewarm.
“That artist is quite skilled. Who is she?”
“Hmm, no. I was just wondering if you recognized her.”
“Never seen the woman in that drawing. I’d remember a beauty like that. Old as I am, I’m still a man.”

It wasn’t the answer I’d hoped for, but I wasn’t too disappointed. Whatever sort of person the Southern Heaven Demon Empress was, she had a striking appearance. Ju Hwaran had hidden her face with the human-skin mask Song Ilseom made for her. The Demon Empress could have done the same in any number of ways.
It wouldn’t be strange at all for the Southern Heaven Demon Empress to have mastered an extraordinary disguise technique.
I turned back to the old man. “Where are those Central Plains people from the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau now?”
The Quest required us to meet an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion, but if those people were still nearby, that changed things.
As if reading my thoughts, the old man asked, “Why? Thinking of going after them?”
“If we can.”
“Well, it’s an admirable thought, but it’ll be difficult. More than fifteen days have already passed.”
“If you know which way they went, or have some idea where they were headed, it’s worth a try.”
Every Fire Dragon Pavilion member here was formidable. Even Hyuk Mujin, the least skilled among us, was a Supreme First Rate master who had survived countless battles and brushes with death.
Yet despite my attitude, the old man merely let out a short laugh.
“It’s impossible.”
“Sir, I don’t think you understand—”
“I’m not the one who fails to understand. You are. Every one of those Central Plains people is dead.”
I froze. “What?”

“I mean exactly what I said. There were countless tribal warriors among those who suffered that calamity. Do you think people like that would have stood by and let themselves be slaughtered? The Central Plains people all died too. We found their bodies after they were poisoned with deadly venom and collapsed before they could get very far.”
“No matter how skilled you are, you can’t chase them into the afterlife. And that goes for...”
His voice trailed off. A moment later, he sighed.
“...an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion who’s already old as dirt.”
Gulp. Gulp.
The old man drained the last of the strong liquor and smiled at me.
“Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”

chapters.title: Chapter 620
paragraphs: “Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”
A low voice burrowed into my ears, and a ripple of agitation spread through the room. But instead of being startled, I stared quietly at the old man.
As we talked, I’d begun to suspect he might be an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
He certainly fit the bill.
The old man before me was the owner of the meeting place Thousand-Faced Fox had told us about. And unlike the other non-Han locals, he hadn’t shown us any particular hostility.
Still, if you didn’t want to misstep, you had to knock on even a stone bridge before crossing it.
The System had warned me through the Journey to Nanman Quest, too. To stay alert at all times and act flexibly.
At least this time, I intended to follow that advice faithfully.
Shhhh.
Invisible internal energy spread through the inn, sealing it off from outside sound. Only then did I speak.
“Are you with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
That was probably the question everyone wanted to ask.
With every eye on him, the old man rubbed a thumb over his filthy liquor cup.
“It’s been so long now since I was given my second name: Namho.”
Namho. Literally, “amber from the south.”

The Hidden Shadow Pavilion was an intelligence organization, so it gave its agents codenames to conceal their identities. The name Namho matched the information Thousand-Faced Fox had given us exactly.
“A certain fox said a fierce wind was blowing in Nanman.”
“Even if a typhoon rages, the Poison Flower rooted deep in the ground will not be shaken.”
That was the secret countersign too. Now I was sure.
I filled the old man’s cup—Namho’s cup—and said, “I was suspicious right up to the end. But you really are with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.”
Namho drained his cup in one gulp and asked,
“Why? Did you never imagine that an agent of the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion might be one of the non-Han peoples?”
Just as Namho said, he was indeed not Han Chinese. His skin was dark from Nanman’s fierce sun, and his distinctive features were plainly not Han Chinese. Anyone with half an eye could tell.
I gave a small nod and answered,

“To be honest, I can’t say I didn’t think that. It’s just that you’re so far from the Central Plains that it was hard to believe you were with the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion. And from what I could sense, you didn’t seem to have learned martial arts, either.”
“Everyone has their own story. What matters is that most people think the way you do.”
“And because they do, no one suspects you?”
“Who would suspect an old non-Han man who hasn’t learned even a single martial arts move? It would be absurd.”
Namho emptied the last bottle of liquor. Then he looked up as though something had just occurred to him.
“Oh. Are you blocking sound with your internal energy?”
“Of course. We can’t let anyone outside hear us.”
“Then lower it for a moment. There’s something I absolutely must do.”
Something he had to do?
What was it?
I wanted to ask in more detail, but Namho’s expression was utterly serious. The moment I withdrew the internal energy sealing off the inn, Namho turned to Hyuk Mujin.
“You there. Is someone standing behind you?”
“Huh?”
Crash!
“Get the hell out of here, you rude Han bastards!”
It happened in an instant.
A liquor bottle struck Hyuk Mujin squarely in the back of the head, cracking his skull. The cheap bottle shattered, spraying fragments everywhere.
And Namho, the obvious culprit, started yelling at the top of his lungs.
“You bastards! Even tearing you apart wouldn’t satisfy me! How dare you cause trouble here!”
Everyone, myself included, stared with our mouths hanging open at the sudden turn of events.
No one was more stunned than Hyuk Mujin. Clutching the back of his head, he gaped at Namho before bursting out, “Has this old man gone insane?”
“Yeah, I’m insane! You motherless, fatherless Han bastard!”
“Whoa. That’s crossing a line. You’re crossing a line!”
“You Han bastards crossed the line! Murdering people in Nanman wasn’t enough, so now you’re eating without paying?”
“No, fuck! What did you do with the silver coin I gave you earlier? Boil soup with it?”
“You didn’t give me a single penny, so what kind of bullshit are you spouting? I took pity on you and gave you a meal after agonizing over it, and now get the hell out of my sight!”
Whoosh! Crash!
Bottles and bowls flew across the room. Within seconds, the inn was a wreck.
Namho screamed every insult he could think of and threw everything within reach. Then he looked at me, his lips moving just enough for me to read them.
Half a shichen from now. Meet me by the lakeside ten li away.
Only then did I understand the meaning behind his actions. I signaled to the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, and Sama Pyo caught on at once. They sprang up, overturned the table, and started smashing things. Each contributed a word.
“The food!”
“Dog!”
“Tastes like shit!”
Crash-crash-crash!
Crack! Rumble!
An unfortunate pillar broke apart, and the ceiling tilted.
Poison Flower Pavilion had already been on the verge of collapse. At this rate, it might as well change its name to Crumble Mansion.
I grabbed Hyuk Mujin, who was still shouting at Namho at the top of his lungs, and Taishan, who was shoveling the remaining food into his mouth, by the backs of their necks and ran.
“You crazy old man! Did you get this old by shoving years up your ass—urk!”
“No! Taishan’s chicken leg! He was saving it!”
“Quit your bullshit and get out! All of you!”
Crunch!
Screams mingled with clouds of dust. I led the Fire Dragon Pavilion out through the chaos—and found a crowd of a hundred people waiting for us.
“The Han bastards are coming out!”
“They dared attack Elder Chao!”
“Kill them!”
“No, throw them into the snake pit alive!”
Of course, there wasn’t a single sane person among us who wanted to be thrown alive into a snake pit.
Swish! Thud!
I sighed and dodged a pickaxe. A belated System notification sounded in my ear.
Ding.

System Mission Contact with a Hidden Shadow Pavilion Agent completed! - Quest Seeds Planted in Nanman completed successfully! - Quest completion Reward acquired! - A small amount of EXP acquired! - A small amount of Fame acquired! - A new linked Quest has been generated!
Okay, but where’s the lakeside?
Namho appeared exactly half a shichen later, as promised. He carried a bundle in one hand. The other was wrapped in bandages.
“The pillar. Who broke it?”
“The inn I ran for forty years collapsed. I nearly died without leaving a will.”
I tried to console him. “We didn’t know that would happen. It’ll be all right.”
“You call that consolation? Does saying it’s all right make it all right?”
“We’ll compensate you properly later.”
“That helps a little.”
There was nothing like financial therapy. Namho’s condition improved at once, and he turned to the rest of us.
“Try to understand what happened at the inn. I had to keep the villagers from getting suspicious. Things have been tense lately. If I’d defended you, they’d have started watching me too.”
Hyuk Mujin replied sourly, “So you had to kill off my parents when they’re both alive and well?”
“I apologize for saying you had no mother or father. I had no choice.”
“How would you feel if someone said that to you?”
“I grew up alone. My parents died when I was little. I don’t even remember their faces.”
“Oh.”
You didn’t spend years as a Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent without learning a thing or two. Namho had silenced Hyuk Mujin in a handful of words.
He took something from his bundle and held it out.
“What’s this?”
“A wooden map. For the past fifty-odd years, whenever I had time, I traveled around Nanman recording its terrain and the locations of its tribes in detail.”
Many years had passed since the Great Faction War, but not everyone had settled into peace. Namho had kept working, never forgetting his duty.
“Nanman is full of treacherous terrain, predators, and venomous beasts,” Ju Hwaran said. “That couldn’t have been easy. You must have worked terribly hard.”
Namho looked bitter.
“I only did what needed doing. Truthfully, even as I made this map, I hoped no one would ever need it.”
But peace had ended, despite his hopes.

Dark Heaven had shed the shell of the Demonic Cult and run rampant. Blood had stained every corner of the Central Plains, and that dark shadow was now stretching beyond the Central Plains into Nanman.
“I’ve already heard what’s happened,” Namho said. “The Pavilion Master is deeply concerned. Do you share those concerns?”
“Yes.”
I nodded without hesitation.

After everything that had happened around the Water God Dragon in Hubei, Nanman looked like a powder keg about to explode. It teemed with spiritual creatures, venomous beasts, and predators on a scale the Central Plains couldn’t begin to match.
“I assume you’ve heard about the rift.”
“Nanman is remote. Word hasn’t reached the people here, but I received a missive by messenger eagle. If the Pavilion Master hadn’t sent it, I wouldn’t have believed it.”
Anyone would have felt the same. Even people in the Central Plains who’d heard about the Water God Dragon dismissed it as a ridiculous rumor.
But it wouldn’t be long before these impossible things became reality—just as they had during the time people in the modern world called the Great Cataclysm.
“Dark Heaven is definitely targeting Nanman. Even if nothing has surfaced yet, something will happen before long.”
Namho stared at me with sunken eyes as I spoke with complete certainty.

“Long ago, I left Nanman of my own accord, traveling with a merchant caravan from the Central Plains. For the past fifty-odd years, though, I haven’t left this land once. And except for that recent incident, nothing has happened.”
“Do you mean the incident where the Central Plains people claiming to have come from the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau attacked a nearby village?”
“Yes. The non-Han locals grew furious, and the atmosphere became dangerous, but that was all. It wasn’t common, but it wasn’t something that had never happened before, either.”
“I don’t know whether that incident had anything to do with Dark Heaven, but...”
I lowered my voice.
“What’s coming will be a tragedy far worse than that.”
Namho’s eyes trembled.
This was his homeland, the place where he’d spent his life. After a brief silence, he spoke in a tired, elderly voice.
“Even as I packed my things and left my home, I didn’t want to believe it. But there’s no avoiding it now.”
He slung the bundle over his shoulder and started walking.
“Come. Wherever you’re headed, I’ll guide you.”

sentences.text: “Good to meet you, Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”
A low voice burrowed into my ears, and a ripple of agitation spread through the room.
But instead of being startled, I stared quietly at the old man.
As we talked, I’d begun to suspect he might be an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
He certainly fit the bill.
The old man before me was the owner of the meeting place Thousand-Faced Fox had told us about.
And unlike the other non-Han locals, he hadn’t shown us any particular hostility.
Still, if you didn’t want to misstep, you had to knock on even a stone bridge before crossing it.
The System had warned me through the Journey to Nanman Quest, too.
To stay alert at all times and act flexibly.
At least this time, I intended to follow that advice faithfully.
Shhhh.
Invisible internal energy spread through the inn, sealing it off from outside sound.
Only then did I speak.
“Are you with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
That was probably the question everyone wanted to ask.
With every eye on him, the old man rubbed a thumb over his filthy liquor cup.
“It’s been so long now since I was given my second name: Namho.”
Namho.
Literally, “amber from the south.”
The Hidden Shadow Pavilion was an intelligence organization, so it gave its agents codenames to conceal their identities.
The name Namho matched the information Thousand-Faced Fox had given us exactly.
“A certain fox said a fierce wind was blowing in Nanman.”
“Even if a typhoon rages, the Poison Flower rooted deep in the ground will not be shaken.”
That was the secret countersign too.
Now I was sure.
I filled the old man’s cup—Namho’s cup—and said, “I was suspicious right up to the end.
But you really are with the Hidden Shadow Pavilion.”
Namho drained his cup in one gulp and asked,
“Why?
Did you never imagine that an agent of the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion might be one of the non-Han peoples?”
Just as Namho said, he was indeed not Han Chinese.
His skin was dark from Nanman’s fierce sun, and his distinctive features were plainly not Han Chinese.
Anyone with half an eye could tell.
I gave a small nod and answered,
“To be honest, I can’t say I didn’t think that.
It’s just that you’re so far from the Central Plains that it was hard to believe you were with the Murim Alliance’s Hidden Shadow Pavilion.
And from what I could sense, you didn’t seem to have learned martial arts, either.”
“Everyone has their own story.
What matters is that most people think the way you do.”
“And because they do, no one suspects you?”
“Who would suspect an old non-Han man who hasn’t learned even a single martial arts move?
It would be absurd.”
Namho emptied the last bottle of liquor.
Then he looked up as though something had just occurred to him.
“Oh.
Are you blocking sound with your internal energy?”
“Of course.
We can’t let anyone outside hear us.”
“Then lower it for a moment.
There’s something I absolutely must do.”
Something he had to do?
What was it?
I wanted to ask in more detail, but Namho’s expression was utterly serious.
The moment I withdrew the internal energy sealing off the inn, Namho turned to Hyuk Mujin.
“You there.
Is someone standing behind you?”
“Huh?”
Crash!
“Get the hell out of here, you rude Han bastards!”
It happened in an instant.
A liquor bottle struck Hyuk Mujin squarely in the back of the head, cracking his skull.
The cheap bottle shattered, spraying fragments everywhere.
And Namho, the obvious culprit, started yelling at the top of his lungs.
“You bastards!
Even tearing you apart wouldn’t satisfy me!
How dare you cause trouble here!”
Everyone, myself included, stared with our mouths hanging open at the sudden turn of events.
No one was more stunned than Hyuk Mujin.
Clutching the back of his head, he gaped at Namho before bursting out, “Has this old man gone insane?”
“Yeah, I’m insane!
You motherless, fatherless Han bastard!”
“Whoa.
That’s crossing a line.
You’re crossing a line!”
“You Han bastards crossed the line!
Murdering people in Nanman wasn’t enough, so now you’re eating without paying?”
“No, fuck!
What did you do with the silver coin I gave you earlier?
Boil soup with it?”
“You didn’t give me a single penny, so what kind of bullshit are you spouting?
I took pity on you and gave you a meal after agonizing over it, and now get the hell out of my sight!”
Whoosh!
Crash!
Bottles and bowls flew across the room.
Within seconds, the inn was a wreck.
Namho screamed every insult he could think of and threw everything within reach.
Then he looked at me, his lips moving just enough for me to read them.
Half a shichen from now.
Meet me by the lakeside ten li away.
Only then did I understand the meaning behind his actions.
I signaled to the members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion.
Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, and Sama Pyo caught on at once.
They sprang up, overturned the table, and started smashing things.
Each contributed a word.
“The food!”
“Dog!”
“Tastes like shit!”
Crash-crash-crash!
Crack!
Rumble!
An unfortunate pillar broke apart, and the ceiling tilted.
Poison Flower Pavilion had already been on the verge of collapse.
At this rate, it might as well change its name to Crumble Mansion.
I grabbed Hyuk Mujin, who was still shouting at Namho at the top of his lungs, and Taishan, who was shoveling the remaining food into his mouth, by the backs of their necks and ran.
“You crazy old man!
Did you get this old by shoving years up your ass—urk!”
“No!
Taishan’s chicken leg!
He was saving it!”
“Quit your bullshit and get out!
All of you!”
Crunch!
Screams mingled with clouds of dust.
I led the Fire Dragon Pavilion out through the chaos—and found a crowd of a hundred people waiting for us.
“The Han bastards are coming out!”
“They dared attack Elder Chao!”
“Kill them!”
“No, throw them into the snake pit alive!”
Of course, there wasn’t a single sane person among us who wanted to be thrown alive into a snake pit.
Swish!
Thud!
I sighed and dodged a pickaxe.
A belated System notification sounded in my ear.
Ding.

chapters.title: Chapter 621
paragraphs: “Come. Wherever you’re headed, I’ll lead the way.”
I looked at Namho, the elderly Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent, with admiration. Even at his age, his resolve was firm.
“You’d lead us even down the road to the afterlife. I don’t know how to thank you for such devotion, Elder Namho.”
“I didn’t say I’d go as far as the afterlife...”
“Your joints must ache these days, and I’m sure your memory isn’t what it used to be. Thank you for stepping forward anyway. You’ll be a great help to us.”
“...How very kind of you. Listening to you, I can feel strength and enthusiasm welling up through this old body of mine.”
“You’re welcome. No need to thank me.”
Namho stared at me sourly, then spoke.
“Where do you intend to go? I may have other ideas, but first I’d like to hear your destination.”
Our destination. Instead of answering, I glanced into the empty air.
There was nothing there, of course. But as had happened countless times before, I could read information in that empty space that no one else here could see.

System Quest Nanman Beast Palace The Nanman Beast Palace is one of the great powers of the Outer Lands. It lies in the deepest, most secluded part of Nanman, a land that is itself fiercely closed off. The Murim of the Central Plains needs its help for the Great War to come. The time has come to awaken the beast that has long slept in the jungle. Or perhaps... to save it from a danger that has yet to reveal itself. Grade: Supreme Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung and Fire Dragon Pavilion members Mission: Arrive at the Nanman Beast Palace (Incomplete) Reward: Chain Quest ??? Failure: ???
The Chain Quest had updated right after we met Namho. It pointed in the same direction as my own thoughts.
“The Nanman Beast Palace. That’s where we’re going.”
At my belated answer, Namho nodded, his gaze deep and somber.
Nanman was vast and rugged beyond belief.
It covered less ground than Sichuan, but traveling through it took far more effort than traveling through the Central Plains.
“The Pavilion Master once told me that ten li in Nanman is like a hundred li in the Central Plains.”
Anyone who didn’t understand Namho’s words had never set foot in Nanman. In just half a day, the Fire Dragon Pavilion and I had learned exactly how shitty this place was.
Bzzzz. Smack!
“Mujin, what was that?”
“Nothing. Just a mosquito. Something stung the back of my neck, that’s all.”
“Oh, really? Be careful anyway. You never know. Want me to ask Elder Namho about it?”
“Come on, Captain. I’m not a child. Hyuk Mujin, a battle-hardened warrior who has fought countless fierce battles at the right hand of the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon! That’s me.”
Exactly one shichen later, the battle-hardened warrior Hyuk Mujin collapsed, vomiting.
“Bleeaagh!”
“Gasp, Mujin!”
“What happened?”
“Elder Namho! Mujin’s collapsed!”
“I may be old, but I can see that. Was he bitten by a mosquito?”
“Cough. Yes. About one shichen ago. It had blue stripes...”
“Blue stripes? And that was a shichen ago? An antidote! Bring an antidote, quickly!”

Fortunately, getting the battle-hardened warrior back on his feet wasn’t too difficult. I had the Myriad-Poison Ring, a divine artifact of the Sichuan Tang Clan, and fifty antidotes I’d received as Quest rewards.
But that was no reason to relax.
“They usually travel in swarms of dozens and even hunt predators. Another shichen, and he’d be dead.”
We set off again with Namho’s stern warning in mind, heading deeper into secluded country to avoid the non-Han peoples who would charge at Han Chinese on sight.
Which meant heading somewhere even more dangerous.
“Taishan! Taishan’s stomach hurts! Feels like it’s tearing apart!”
“Elder Namho!”
“What did you eat this time?”
“Taishan was hungry. Picked red mushrooms off a tree and ate them.”

“What kind of dog and pig bastard are you? After all the warnings I gave you, you ate blood-feeding fungus that even a tiger couldn’t withstand just because you were hungry? Antidotes won’t work on this!”

Namho flew into a rage, but his anger soon gave way to bewilderment. Taishan went into the brush to do his business and came back looking perfectly fine, despite eating a fungus that could kill a tiger.
“Taishan. Feels better after taking a dump. Fine now.”
“...Is he even human?”
Sama Pyo considered Namho’s earnest question for a moment before answering without much confidence.
“Probably.”
“Taishan’s stomach is empty again. Taishan is hungry.”
“I swear by heaven and earth, if you ever eat another mushroom, you’ll never have to worry about being hungry again.”
“Oh. Taishan. Tempting.”
“...I regret not learning martial arts. If I had, I’d have killed him with a single palm strike by now.”
We left the old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent to his lament and kept walking.
At every turn, dense jungle and humid, sweltering heat awaited us. In the thick brush and swamps, the eyes of lurking predators glowed bright yellow.
Did we come to Nanman, or did we end up in the Amazon?
What a dogshit place.
There were more tigers than stray cats around a university neighborhood full of studio apartments, and crocodiles swarmed like tadpoles in Cheonggyecheon.

Even those were nothing compared to the strange poisonous flowers and plants that could do you in with their scent alone, or the bees with stingers bigger than their own bodies. At least the predators were large enough to spot.
There was a reason Hyuk Mujin had started complaining within a day or two of leaving Yeongin.
“To hell with the Nanman Beast Palace. I think I’ll be dead by the day after tomorrow.”
Maybe not the day after tomorrow, but in four days his life might well be in danger. He’d been poisoned about four times on the first day alone, and over the past two days he’d become skin and bones.
Shanxi Province counted as a borderland by Central Plains standards, but Nanman was far beyond anything we’d expected.
“Can’t we take another route? The roads might be run-down and rough, but compared to this, they’d be a walk down a flower-lined path.”
It wasn’t as if Nanman had no roads at all.

It was badly underdeveloped compared to the Central Plains, but I’d heard that the dozens, perhaps hundreds, of non-Han peoples settled here each had their own territory. Travel between them wasn’t particularly rare, so long as it didn’t cause disputes.
Despite Mujin’s desperate plea, Namho was firm.
“Impossible. You know why.”
“If it’s because the locals are dying to kill us, I’d rather face them head-on. And if we can talk things out, all the better.”
“Talk?”
Namho blinked at Mujin’s hopeful answer.
“Are you serious?”
“Of course.”
“An entire village vanished. Some two hundred people welcomed Han Chinese in good faith and were slaughtered, young and old alike. Do you think they’ll want to talk?”
“...No. I wasn’t actually serious.”
“Now you’re being honest. Good. Then shut up and walk.”
“Yes, sir.”
Look at him change his tune faster than light.
But this time, Namho was right about everything.

Fighting the non-Han peoples who attacked us would amount to declaring war on all of Nanman. They might snarl at one another ordinarily, but when an outsider appeared, they united as if their quarrels had never existed.
No wonder even the Demonic Cult failed to conquer all of Nanman during the Great Faction War.
The Cult’s hundred thousand demonic soldiers had once swallowed half the world, yet all they managed here was to plant their flags on Nanman’s outskirts before withdrawing.
They knew that going any deeper into a jungle rife with brutal endemic diseases, treacherous terrain, predators, and venomous beasts would cost more than it gained them.
And we can’t exactly go around announcing who we are.
I doubted the non-Han peoples’ hatred of Han Chinese would ease just because we told them our names. More importantly, Dark Heaven was lurking somewhere in Nanman.
They’re definitely targeting Nanman. It’s only a matter of time before something happens.
I was almost certain. We hadn’t traveled like thieves in the night all the way from Henan, where the Murim Alliance headquarters stood, for nothing.

We’d had to reveal our identities to the bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold on our way here, but we’d made sure they kept quiet. It was also why we hadn’t contacted the Emei Sect, the Qingcheng Sect, or the Sichuan Tang Clan, despite the ties we’d made on our last trip to Sichuan.
If we revealed ourselves to the non-Han peoples now, all that effort would go to waste.
Dark Heaven would realize an unseen dagger had come right up to its nose and rush its plans forward. Then the rift would open, and with it the door to disaster.
We can’t reveal who we are until we reach the Nanman Beast Palace at the very least.
The Beast Miao King, lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, had fought in the Great Faction War. I’d also heard he was well disposed toward Jeok Cheongang and the Fire Gate Clan.
Given the importance of our business and his standing in Nanman, he was far more likely to listen than the other non-Han peoples, who were beside themselves with anger.
And thanks to those Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau bastards, we’re getting shit splashed on us too.
One squid makes the whole fish market look bad, as they say. We’d been bundled together with them in the same Han Chinese package, and the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s reputation—mine included—was shot.
I wasn’t even Han Chinese.
...Does this make me a fake Han Chinese or what?
It was unfair as hell, but there was nothing I could do. I could tell the locals, “Actually, I’m not Han Chinese. I’m Korean. South, not North,” and they wouldn’t understand a word.
Besides, when I’d gotten homesick during training at Mount Jiuhua and drawn the Korean flag, Jeok Cheongang had said just one thing.
“Wudang?”
“No.”
“It’s obviously taiji. What kind of bullshit are you talking? Taiji means Wudang.”
“Taiji means Korea.”
“What’s Korea?”
“That’s... Never mind. You don’t need to know, Old Master.”
“Add two hundred geun of iron balls.”
“...Two hundred geun? Why?”
“You don’t need to know.”
Just remembering it brought tears to my eyes.
It felt like only yesterday I’d been suffering in this distant land of another dimension. The miserable part was that the suffering never stopped.
“Whew.”
At the sight of me sighing, Namho glared fiercely.
“What? Do you also want to go down there and settle things through conversation right now? Or would you rather throw down with the non-Han peoples?”
“...Where did that come from? I don’t want to do either.”
“That’s a relief.”
There had already been plenty of chances to throw down with someone, and there would be plenty more in the future. Even now, several predators were wandering around us, letting out their cries.
I scanned the dense jungle and swampland, then asked Namho, “How much farther?”
“Three days if we’re quick. Six if we’re not.”
“That’s a lot farther than I expected.”
“Given that we have to stay out of sight, even that’s quick.”
Namho, whose face had aged noticeably, patted his lower back before starting to walk again.
“Don’t slow down for a moment from here on. If we cross Ailao Mountain today, we can reach the Nanman Beast Palace in four days at the latest.”
He was right.
Exactly four days later, as we crossed a high mountain peak, we spotted a massive structure in the distance, shrouded in thick clouds and mist.
“The Nanman Beast Palace...”
The voice that slipped from someone’s lips spread on a wind that had blown in from somewhere.

An antidote!
Bring an antidote, quickly!”
Fortunately, getting the battle-hardened warrior back on his feet wasn’t too difficult.
I had the Myriad-Poison Ring, a divine artifact of the Sichuan Tang Clan, and fifty antidotes I’d received as Quest rewards.
But that was no reason to relax.
“They usually travel in swarms of dozens and even hunt predators.
Another shichen, and he’d be dead.”
We set off again with Namho’s stern warning in mind, heading deeper into secluded country to avoid the non-Han peoples who would charge at Han Chinese on sight.
Which meant heading somewhere even more dangerous.
“Taishan!
Taishan’s stomach hurts!
Feels like it’s tearing apart!”
“Elder Namho!”
“What did you eat this time?”
“Taishan was hungry.
Picked red mushrooms off a tree and ate them.”
“What kind of dog and pig bastard are you?
After all the warnings I gave you, you ate blood-feeding fungus that even a tiger couldn’t withstand just because you were hungry?
Antidotes won’t work on this!”
Namho flew into a rage, but his anger soon gave way to bewilderment.
Taishan went into the brush to do his business and came back looking perfectly fine, despite eating a fungus that could kill a tiger.
“Taishan.
Feels better after taking a dump.
Fine now.”
“...Is he even human?”
Sama Pyo considered Namho’s earnest question for a moment before answering without much confidence.
“Probably.”
“Taishan’s stomach is empty again.
Taishan is hungry.”
“I swear by heaven and earth, if you ever eat another mushroom, you’ll never have to worry about being hungry again.”
“Oh.
Taishan.
Tempting.”
“...I regret not learning martial arts.
If I had, I’d have killed him with a single palm strike by now.”
We left the old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent to his lament and kept walking.
At every turn, dense jungle and humid, sweltering heat awaited us.
In the thick brush and swamps, the eyes of lurking predators glowed bright yellow.
Did we come to Nanman, or did we end up in the Amazon?
What a dogshit place.
There were more tigers than stray cats around a university neighborhood full of studio apartments, and crocodiles swarmed like tadpoles in Cheonggyecheon.
Even those were nothing compared to the strange poisonous flowers and plants that could do you in with their scent alone, or the bees with stingers bigger than their own bodies.
At least the predators were large enough to spot.
There was a reason Hyuk Mujin had started complaining within a day or two of leaving Yeongin.
“To hell with the Nanman Beast Palace.
I think I’ll be dead by the day after tomorrow.”
Maybe not the day after tomorrow, but in four days his life might well be in danger.
He’d been poisoned about four times on the first day alone, and over the past two days he’d become skin and bones.
Shanxi Province counted as a borderland by Central Plains standards, but Nanman was far beyond anything we’d expected.
“Can’t we take another route?
The roads might be run-down and rough, but compared to this, they’d be a walk down a flower-lined path.”
It wasn’t as if Nanman had no roads at all.
It was badly underdeveloped compared to the Central Plains, but I’d heard that the dozens, perhaps hundreds, of non-Han peoples settled here each had their own territory.
Travel between them wasn’t particularly rare, so long as it didn’t cause disputes.
Despite Mujin’s desperate plea, Namho was firm.
“Impossible.
You know why.”
“If it’s because the locals are dying to kill us, I’d rather face them head-on.
And if we can talk things out, all the better.”
“Talk?”
Namho blinked at Mujin’s hopeful answer.
“Are you serious?”
“Of course.”
“An entire village vanished.
Some two hundred people welcomed Han Chinese in good faith and were slaughtered, young and old alike.
Do you think they’ll want to talk?”
I wasn’t actually serious.”
“Now you’re being honest.
Good.
Then shut up and walk.”
“Yes, sir.”
Look at him change his tune faster than light.
But this time, Namho was right about everything.
Fighting the non-Han peoples who attacked us would amount to declaring war on all of Nanman.
They might snarl at one another ordinarily, but when an outsider appeared, they united as if their quarrels had never existed.
No wonder even the Demonic Cult failed to conquer all of Nanman during the Great Faction War.
The Cult’s hundred thousand demonic soldiers had once swallowed half the world, yet all they managed here was to plant their flags on Nanman’s outskirts before withdrawing.
They knew that going any deeper into a jungle rife with brutal endemic diseases, treacherous terrain, predators, and venomous beasts would cost more than it gained them.
And we can’t exactly go around announcing who we are.
I doubted the non-Han peoples’ hatred of Han Chinese would ease just because we told them our names.
More importantly, Dark Heaven was lurking somewhere in Nanman.
They’re definitely targeting Nanman.
It’s only a matter of time before something happens.
I was almost certain.
We hadn’t traveled like thieves in the night all the way from Henan, where the Murim Alliance headquarters stood, for nothing.
We’d had to reveal our identities to the bandits of Water Dragon Stronghold on our way here, but we’d made sure they kept quiet.
It was also why we hadn’t contacted the Emei Sect, the Qingcheng Sect, or the Sichuan Tang Clan, despite the ties we’d made on our last trip to Sichuan.
If we revealed ourselves to the non-Han peoples now, all that effort would go to waste.
Dark Heaven would realize an unseen dagger had come right up to its nose and rush its plans forward.
Then the rift would open, and with it the door to disaster.
We can’t reveal who we are until we reach the Nanman Beast Palace at the very least.
The Beast Miao King, lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, had fought in the Great Faction War.
I’d also heard he was well disposed toward Jeok Cheongang and the Fire Gate Clan.
Given the importance of our business and his standing in Nanman, he was far more likely to listen than the other non-Han peoples, who were beside themselves with anger.
And thanks to those Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau bastards, we’re getting shit splashed on us too.
One squid makes the whole fish market look bad, as they say.
We’d been bundled together with them in the same Han Chinese package, and the Fire Dragon Pavilion’s reputation—mine included—was shot.
I wasn’t even Han Chinese.
...Does this make me a fake Han Chinese or what?
It was unfair as hell, but there was nothing I could do.
I could tell the locals, “Actually, I’m not Han Chinese.
I’m Korean.
South, not North,” and they wouldn’t understand a word.
Besides, when I’d gotten homesick during training at Mount Jiuhua and drawn the Korean flag, Jeok Cheongang had said just one thing.
“Wudang?”
“No.”
“It’s obviously taiji.
What kind of bullshit are you talking?
Taiji means Wudang.”
“Taiji means Korea.”
“What’s Korea?”
“That’s...
Never mind.
You don’t need to know, Old Master.”
“Add two hundred geun of iron balls.”
“...Two hundred geun?
Why?”
“You don’t need to know.”
Just remembering it brought tears to my eyes.
It felt like only yesterday I’d been suffering in this distant land of another dimension.
The miserable part was that the suffering never stopped.
“Whew.”
At the sight of me sighing, Namho glared fiercely.
“What?
Do you also want to go down there and settle things through conversation right now?
Or would you rather throw down with the non-Han peoples?”
“...Where did that come from?
I don’t want to do either.”
“That’s a relief.”
There had already been plenty of chances to throw down with someone, and there would be plenty more in the future.
Even now, several predators were wandering around us, letting out their cries.
I scanned the dense jungle and swampland, then asked Namho, “How much farther?”
“Three days if we’re quick.
Six if we’re not.”
“That’s a lot farther than I expected.”
“Given that we have to stay out of sight, even that’s quick.”
Namho, whose face had aged noticeably, patted his lower back before starting to walk again.
“Don’t slow down for a moment from here on.
If we cross Ailao Mountain today, we can reach the Nanman Beast Palace in four days at the latest.”
He was right.
Exactly four days later, as we crossed a high mountain peak, we spotted a massive structure in the distance, shrouded in thick clouds and mist.
“The Nanman Beast Palace...”
The voice that slipped from someone’s lips spread on a wind that had blown in from somewhere.

chapters.title: Chapter 622
paragraphs: Even counting only the time I had spent in Murim, well over a year had passed.

One unexpected incident after another had taken me out of Shanxi Province and sent me wandering from place to place. Along the way, I had met all kinds of people and visited the sects they belonged to.
But I could say this much for certain: none of those sects, however large or powerful, could compare to the sight before me.
“Huh.”
“Holy...”
Exclamations broke out all around me.
I’d known the place covered an enormous area when I saw it from the mountain peak. I hadn’t expected this.
As the clouds and mist cleared and we drew closer, my jaw dropped farther and farther.
Wait. This is a sect?
It was astonishing for two reasons. The first was its sheer size. The second was...
Nanman Beast Palace
A fence around the vast grounds, and a wooden sign someone had scrawled on in a clumsy hand.
Not a high, sturdy wall or an iron gate. A fence. Just a fence.
...Wait. This is a sect?
The thought was the same. The meaning was different.
The fence wasn’t even intact.
I studied a half-collapsed stretch for a moment, then turned to Namho.
“Elder Namho, surely this isn’t really...”
“You’re asking if it’s the Nanman Beast Palace?”
“Ah, yes.”
I nodded, and Namho answered calmly.
“Can you read?”
“Of course.”
“Then read that sign. No, perhaps I’d better read it for you.”
He pointed at the clumsily lettered board.
“Nan. Man. Beast. Palace.”
“That’s what it says. The Nanman Beast Palace begins here.”
I knew what the sign said. The problem was how far the place was from anything I’d imagined.
From above, I’d thought there must be an enormous building here. But up close, out of the mist, it was practically an empty field.
“Captain, shouldn’t we call this the Nanman Ranch instead of the Nanman Beast Palace? All I see are fences.”
Ju Hwaran looked around and nodded at Hyuk Mujin’s dubious assessment.
“This is my first time here, so I can’t say I know much about the Nanman Beast Palace, but... it does seem a little lacking for a palace.”
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo, who had been watching in silence, each weighed in.
“There’s certainly something strange about it.”
“As Hyuk Mujin said, the lack of people bothers me. I don’t see any other pavilions or buildings, either. What do you think, Taishan?”
“My lord. Taishan is hungry. Can Taishan eat that mushroom?”
Sama Pyo shook his head at once.
“No.”
“Then the cow? That cow walking over there looks tasty.”
“You’re the Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate, aren’t you? Do me a favor and shut that brute’s mouth. If I hear one more word, I think I’ll burst a blood vessel and die.”
“...I understand.”
“One more thing. Every blade of grass and every animal you can see belongs to the Nanman Beast Palace. Please remember that. And remember I’m about to burst a blood vessel.”
Looking considerably older than he had a moment ago, Namho gave Sama Pyo that stern warning, then pointed across the vast grounds.
“I understand why you’re confused, but I never said this place was the Nanman Beast Palace.”
“What? You said exactly that a moment ago.”
“No, I didn’t.”
“Ah. Have you gone senile?”
His expression darkened so quickly that it seemed certain. I gave him a sympathetic look.
“Oh dear. Still, I’m sure you’ll be fine. Someone close to me also suffered from infirmities of old age, but they’ve almost completely recovered now.”
“Three things. First, I do not suffer from the infirmities of old age. Second—and I ask only because you’ve made me curious—how did this acquaintance of yours recover?”
“Returned to Youth.”
“...An excellent method. Apart from the fact that I’m an eighty-year-old man who’s never learned martial arts.”
“Isn’t eighty when life begins?”
“I’d like to end your life here, but I lack the strength.”
Namho swallowed his anger and went on.
“Third, what I said before still stands. I never said this place was the Nanman Beast Palace. I said the Nanman Beast Palace begins here.”
“Oh.”
Similar words, very different meanings. Now that I understood, I asked, “So what is this place?”

“That’s right. This is one of the lands under the rule of the Nanman Beast Palace. Unlike the other regions of Nanman, it is directly administered by the Palace Lord. That may make it easier to understand.”
“So it’s similar to how the Emperor appoints vassal kings or City Lords throughout the realm. This place is like the capital of a country.”
“Exactly. Of course, the Palace Lord doesn’t have the authority of the Son of Heaven, and Nanman’s tribal chiefs have more authority than City Lords.”
Ju Hwaran, who had been listening, gave a quiet exclamation.

“Now that you mention it, I remember reading something like that in my grandfather’s records. He wrote that Nanman was a single kingdom, and the Nanman Beast Palace was like an enormous ranch spanning five counties.”
“As expected of the Escort King’s granddaughter. But even Great Hero Ju Gongsan never crossed this fence. People who aren’t of Nanman’s ethnic groups aren’t allowed inside.”
“It’s that strict?”
“It is.”
If Namho was telling the truth, then even the Sichuan Tang Clan, a sect whose isolation was second to none in the world, would have to yield to the Nanman Beast Palace.
I clicked my tongue and stared beyond the endless line of fences and grasslands.
“But we need to get in.”
“Yes.”
“Is there another way? Since you’re one of the local ethnic groups, perhaps you can enter...”
“I said outsiders aren’t allowed in. I don’t recall saying it was easy for the local peoples, either.”
“Oh.”

“Here, I’m nothing more than a powerless, ordinary old man of the Miao people. If Dark Heaven hadn’t extended its claws into the world, and if you people hadn’t come looking for me, I would have quietly ended my life... you bastard!”
I flinched at his sudden shout.
“Elder Namho, why are you calling yourself that? What’s wrong with quietly living out your days?”
“Not me! That bastard! Catch that fucking son of a bitch!”
At Namho’s frantic yell, we turned.
A huge backside was crawling over the fence. Beyond it, a yellow calf grazed peacefully.
“Oh. Oh, no.”
“Surely he isn’t...”
“When did that bastard get over there?”
“Young Hero Tae!”
“Taishan!”
Sama Pyo’s cry came last. Taishan flinched.
Moo?

The calf sensed something was wrong and jerked its head up. Taishan had somehow already drawn close. An exclamation mark seemed to pop into the calf’s large, clear eyes, and at the same time, its still-growing hooves struck the grass.
Pat-pat-pat!
A quick decision and an attempt to flee—but Taishan was a step faster.
“Beef! Stop right there!”
With that determined shout, his enormous body flew through the air.
The calf was no tiger or leopard. How was it supposed to evade a Peak master who’d decided to catch it?
Taishan landed with a heavy thud, and the calf pinned beneath him screamed.
Moooooo!
It was a plaintive cry, enough to bring tears to your eyes just hearing it. But after days of forced marches and meager rations, all it did was make Taishan’s mouth water.
“Taishan! Beef!”
“Get that bastard off it!”
Before Namho finished shouting, I’d vaulted the fence and reached Taishan.
Grab.
“Let go! Beef tartare!”
“Stop it, you heartless lunatic. Haven’t you seen The Sound of the Bell?”
“No!”
Well, of course he hadn’t.
That made sense, but it changed nothing. I seized him by the back of the neck and hauled him away.
His mountain-sized body toppled backward. The beef—no, the calf—scrambled to its feet and ran.
Thud-thud-thud-thud!
Grass flew up beneath its hooves, dust rising in its wake. Taishan watched its rump disappear beyond the pasture and muttered mournfully.
“No. Taishan’s rump meat...”
Was this guy born in Majang-dong or something?
While I questioned his origins, Namho erupted.
“You brute!”
“Elder Namho, calm down. Please.”

“How am I supposed to calm down right now? I repeatedly warned you not to touch anything in the Nanman Beast Palace’s territory! And this hulking glutton of a bastard ignored every word an elder said and went and caused trouble?”
Sama Pyo hurried between Namho and Taishan.
“I’m sorry, Elder Namho. I looked away for just a moment, and... Taishan, apologize to him at once.”
Taishan looked Namho straight in the eye.
“Taishan is hungry.”
“That fucking bastard. Let go of my hand. Let go! Are you going to let go or not? Did you think I spent over fifty years getting bitten by mosquitoes in Nanman just to see this?”

Life really did begin at eighty. I only had to look at Namho, who had never learned martial arts yet was giving off an aura fierce enough to make even Jeok Cheongang yield to him for once, to know it.
The old Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent, who had been raging like a live volcano, finally calmed down after fifteen minutes.
“Whew. I’m fine now. Let go of my hand.”
“Are you sure?”
“My insides have turned a full circle, but I’m not about to die.”
A 180-degree turn would have been a problem. A full 360? That was fine.
I nodded to Hyuk Mujin, and he released Namho’s hand. Namho sighed, looking as though he were on his deathbed.
“At least nothing happened in the end. If someone from the Nanman Beast Palace had seen that, we’d have been in trouble before we even began.”

At another sect in the Central Plains, someone might have thought, It’s only one cow. But cultures and people differed. Just as nomads treasured their horses like their own lives, livestock was a valuable asset here, where the boundaries between tribes were sharply drawn and relations between them often strained.
It’s called the Nanman Beast Palace, after all.
Even the name sounded animal-friendly. Namho had warned us from the start not to touch anything for a reason.
“So what do we do now?” Hyuk Mujin asked. “We can’t wait here forever for someone to show up.”
“Entering the Nanman Beast Palace’s territory without permission would cause trouble. We’ll have to find another way.”
Namho reached into his bundle and took something out.
“What’s that?”
“An emergency signal firework. If it goes off, someone should at least come out to investigate.”
He smiled confidently and lit the fuse with his fire striker.
Crackle.
The fuse burned rapidly toward the end. Then, with a tremendous noise, the firework shot upward.
Fwoooosh—boom!
The problem was that the firework’s burst came down on the pasture instead of exploding in the air.
Whoooosh—roar!
The pasture was engulfed in flames alongside the stunned voices of the others.
I watched the livestock flee in every direction and muttered, “...Someone will definitely come out now.”
“...That wasn’t supposed to happen.”
Wasn’t supposed to happen, my ass. We were fucked.
It was then, as I stared miserably at the burning pasture, that it happened.
Roooar!
A savage roar rang out, and a figure appeared beyond the hill on the far side of the flames.

It’s called the Nanman Beast Palace, after all.
Even the name sounded animal-friendly.
Namho had warned us from the start not to touch anything for a reason.
“So what do we do now?” Hyuk Mujin asked.
“We can’t wait here forever for someone to show up.”
“Entering the Nanman Beast Palace’s territory without permission would cause trouble.
We’ll have to find another way.”
Namho reached into his bundle and took something out.
“What’s that?”
“An emergency signal firework.
If it goes off, someone should at least come out to investigate.”
He smiled confidently and lit the fuse with his fire striker.
Crackle.
The fuse burned rapidly toward the end.
Then, with a tremendous noise, the firework shot upward.
Fwoooosh—boom!
The problem was that the firework’s burst came down on the pasture instead of exploding in the air.
Whoooosh—roar!
The pasture was engulfed in flames alongside the stunned voices of the others.
I watched the livestock flee in every direction and muttered, “...Someone will definitely come out now.”
“...That wasn’t supposed to happen.”
Wasn’t supposed to happen, my ass.
We were fucked.
It was then, as I stared miserably at the burning pasture, that it happened.
Roooar!
A savage roar rang out, and a figure appeared beyond the hill on the far side of the flames.

chapters.title: Chapter 623
paragraphs: The young man’s brown skin was handsomely tanned, and fine muscles stood out across his lean frame. At a glance, his features marked him as different from the Han Chinese of the Central Plains.
He looked down the hill and wondered,
...What happened here?
It was a reasonable question. A vast pasture was burning before his eyes.
Even now, the rapidly spreading flames were belching endless clouds of black smoke, while cows, sheep, horses, and other livestock fled frantically through the chaos.
Grrrr.
A low growl and tremor suddenly reached him from below. The young man gently stroked the snow-white mane of the white tiger beneath him.
“It’s all right. It’s okay.”
Grrk.
“You’re really angry, aren’t you?”
Feelings were not conveyed through words alone.
Though one was human and the other a beast, they had spent enough years together to understand each other from the slightest gesture or change in a growl.
The young man met the white tiger’s blue gaze and nodded.
“That’s right. We’ll put out the fire first. We can punish the intruders afterward.”
Left alone, the flames would spread beyond control and reduce the entire pasture to ash.
The land could be restored, of course, but they still had to save the livestock that would otherwise be swallowed by the flames and die.
After that...
How dare they?
It was bad enough that the intruders had entered the Nanman Beast Palace’s territory without permission. They had set it on fire, too. They would answer for that.
The young man glared at the indistinct figures beyond the distant, acrid smoke and stroked the white tiger’s mane.
The white beast understood and shot forward like the wind.
Kraaaar!
Its thunderous roar carried through the flames.
It happened in the blink of an eye.
A white tiger and a non-Han young man had suddenly appeared on the hill, then began rushing about in every direction as though they had become one body.
Whoosh—roar!
I think I saw this in an educational comic when I was little.
Was this what they called a backfire?
Fire met fire. They devoured each other until one went out. The backfire the young man had skillfully set worked remarkably well.
As the flames quickly died down as if nothing had happened, I stepped forward to lend a hand out of sheer conscience.
Boom!
I threw a short, sharp punch. The flames wavered like a candle in the wind...
...and then grew even larger.
ROOOOAR!
“Good grief.”
What the hell?
Namho shouted at me, his voice rising almost to a scream.
“You lunatic! What did you do?”
“...Are you really one to talk, Old Man Nam? The man who farted is getting angry. You set the fire, and now you’re complaining to me?”
“I didn’t know that would happen!”
“Neither did I.”
“Is that what matters? Put the fire out first... Oh! Oh, oh! Behind you! Behind you!”
ROOOOAR!
“Don’t be so dramatic. It’s still fine.”
The flames had not grown that much stronger, but we did need to put them out quickly.
In my haste, I struck again and again with my palms at the swelling fire, without stopping to think.
A moment later, it came to me.
Oh, right.
The palm technique I had just used was called the Flame Divine Palm.
Fwoooooosh!
A moment ago, I could not have said the flames had grown that much stronger. Now I could say it with confidence.
They had grown a hell of a lot stronger.
In a way, it was almost miraculous. Flames that had been on the verge of dying were now roaring several times larger than before.
To the livestock fleeing in every direction, of course, it must have looked like hell.
I stared from the near-inferno around me to my palms and back. Then I looked up and met two pairs of eyes glaring at me through the flames.
They belonged to the white tiger from the hill and the young man riding it. Their eyes were different colors, and they were different species, but they had one thing in common.
They were both pissed as hell.
“You bastard! What do you think you’re doing?”
Kraaaar!
The kid looked young, yet he was speaking casually to me on our first meeting.
He had crossed a line, certainly. Then again, I had burned the line down. As a civilized man of the twenty-first century, I calmly and politely reassured them.
“I don’t know who you are, but don’t worry. I’ll take care of it.”
Of course, there was no guarantee they would feel reassured just because I said so. As demonstrated by the immediate response.
“No! Don’t!”
Kraaaar!
I gently reasoned with the man and tiger shouting in unison.
“It’s okay. I can do this. More importantly, could you quiet the tiger down a little?”
“No, you bastard!”
Kraaaar!
“Don’t do it?”
“Don’t do it!”
KRAAAAR!
Hmm. Opposition as fierce as the fire itself. But I shook my head.
“No. I’m doing it. I believe in myself.”
“You crazy Han Chinese bas—!”
Kraaaar...!
Before either of them could finish, I struck with both palms at lightning speed.
Whoooosh—boom!
Two streams of mighty palm force shot through the air, splitting apart and bursting through the rolling waves of fire.
But if I stopped there, the flames would only surge higher. I would be repeating the same mistake.
Without hesitation, I fired off one palm force after another.
Boom! Boom!
The reason people had trouble putting out fires was simple.
They either lacked enough water, or they lacked wind strong enough to snuff the flames out like candles.
So all you needed was more water or stronger wind. In this case, I went with the latter.
Boom!
The final palm force I sent out was especially powerful.
A typhoon-like wind swept across the pasture. The fleeing livestock lifted briefly off the ground, and grass and trees alike were flattened.
And then...
Whoosh.
The flames spreading in every direction died down in an instant.
All that remained were small embers burning like a campfire and patches of pasture reduced to black ash.
A young man and a snow-white tiger stared at it all in a daze.
“What... What is this?”
Grrrr?
Two pairs of eyes turned to me in disbelief.
I walked over to the last ember nearby, ground it out beneath my foot, and shrugged.
“I told you. I can do it.”
The young man stared at me in pure astonishment. Then he aimed the spear in his hand at me.
“I am Yayul Mok of the Nanman Beast Palace. Who are you?”
So he was from the Nanman Beast Palace. No surprise there.
I nodded and was just about to answer when an elderly voice suddenly rang out from behind me.
“He is Jin Taekyung of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.”
I turned. The members of the Fire Dragon Pavilion had come up behind me, with Namho at their head.

“In the Central Plains, they call him the Blazing Flame Divine Dragon, the foremost young prodigy of his generation. He is also the Pavilion Master of the Fire Dragon Pavilion, which belongs to the Murim Alliance.”
I did not know whether my name and sobriquet had reached Nanman.
But at the very least, the non-Han young man in front of me—Yayul Mok—seemed to understand the words Namho had added perfectly.
“The Murim Alliance...”
He murmured the words and stroked the white tiger’s mane. After watching its growls subside, he lowered his spear and turned away.
“Follow me. Since the Murim Alliance has been mentioned, I will let this go for now. But don’t do anything as foolish as that again.”
Namho shrugged.
“It was an accident. But I’ll keep it in mind.”
“You had better, unless you want to die a sudden death.”
I watched Yayul Mok ride ahead on the white tiger, then gave Namho a sour look.
“That kid’s rude. I know setting the fire was wrong, but still.”
“Hey, Han Chinese. I can hear you.”
Grrrr.
“I meant for you to hear me, punk.”
“What?”
“Is that any way to speak to an elder? Don’t you have a grandfather?”
For a moment, anger flashed across his face. He glared at me, then turned away again. Walking behind me, Namho gave me a flat, unimpressed look and said,
“Watch your tongue.”
“I was taking your side, Old Man Nam. Telling someone who could drop dead any day that he might ‘die a sudden death’? Who says that?”

“Since when could I drop dead any day...? Forget it. I should never have expected anything from you. Do you have some illness that’ll kill you on the spot if you go even one day without stirring up trouble?”
“Do you have a disease that’ll make you senile if you don’t set fire to a pasture owned by the Nanman Beast Palace?”
“Take a good look at yourself before I confiscate your walking stick for three months.”
Namho sighed, having come off much worse in that exchange.
“All right. I admit it. This was clearly my mistake. It was something I had kept for more than fifty years, so I should have been more careful handling it.”
“Nice to see you admit it so readily. The pasture’s still nice and hot, though.”
“...My bones ache every time you speak. Still, be a little more careful with that young man.”
“Why?”
“Why else? You heard his name. Yayul Mok.”
“Yayul Mok, Yayul Mosquito—what am I supposed to...?”
I trailed off. Something I had forgotten was hovering just out of reach.
Yayul Mok. Yayul Mok...
After thinking it over carefully, I turned to Ju Hwaran and asked,
“Excuse me, Young Lady Ju.”
“Yes?”
“What was the name of the lord of the Nanman Beast Palace again?”
“You mean the Beast Miao King?”
“Yes.”

The Beast Miao King, lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, led the Miao people, one of Nanman’s most powerful tribes. Despite his non-Han origins, he also held a place among the Ten Kings, albeit the lowest.
Hwaran smiled and answered kindly.
“Yayul Cheok.”
“Ah. Right.”
“Yes. Yayul is his family name. It’s a rare surname that you don’t often encounter even in Nanman.”
“Then that rude friend of ours must have the surname Ya. And his given name is Yulmok.”
“Forgive me, but are you hoping that’s true?”
“Hmm. What if I am?”
Hwaran was about to answer when the forest blocking Yayul Mok’s path far ahead began to shake.
Rustle. Crackle!
I swear I had not seen so many different animals gathered in one place since I went to the zoo at seven years old.
Jaguars and tigers covered in black fur, leopards, even elephants.
The non-Han men and women riding the beasts spotted Yayul Mok. They hurriedly dismounted and prostrated themselves.
“Young Palace Lord!”
“Are you unharmed?”
“We received an urgent report that a fire had broken out. If Young Palace Lord continues acting so recklessly, the Palace Lord will be terribly worried... But who are these people?”
Dozens of pairs of eyes, human and beast alike, turned toward us.
I quietly considered what they had called him. Then I recalled asking him whether he had a grandfather.
I edged up beside Yayul Mok, draped an arm over his shoulders, and said,
“We’re friends. Right, Mok?”
“Hey. Smile.”

chapters.title: Chapter 624
paragraphs: Ju Hwaran told me that her grandfather, the Escort King Ju Gongsan, had once said this about the Nanman Beast Palace:
“Nanman is practically a kingdom, and the Nanman Beast Palace is a vast ranch encompassing five counties.”
The Escort King had traveled the Four Seas and Five Lakes and the Nine Provinces and Eight Wastes. He had been right.

The territory directly ruled by the Nanman Beast Palace stretched across five counties. In sheer area, even the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families of the Central Plains could not compare.
Direct rule versus indirect rule, I suppose.

The Son of Heaven ruled the Central Plains, but in Nanman, the Nanman Beast Palace held supreme authority. It might not surpass the great orthodox factions in martial power, but its influence here was bound to be far greater.
If there was one thing the Escort King had gotten wrong...
This isn’t a ranch. It’s a safari.
I had never seen such a jumble of animals, plants, temperatures, and terrain in one place.
We followed Yayul Mok and his subordinates across grasslands, through jungles, and over mountains and rivers. I could only shake my head.
“What the hell is wrong with this weather?”
Ju Hwaran, riding to my right, answered my mutter.
“One mountain holds four seasons, and ten li bring a different sky. It’s a saying that describes Nanman’s unpredictable nature quite well.”
“Having seen it for myself, I can’t argue. Young Lady Ju, what made you take an escort job to a place like this?”
“I didn’t know it would be this extreme, either. I’ve accompanied my father on escort journeys before, but this is my first time going so deep into Nanman.”
A thick fur pelt was draped over her shoulders. She smiled, and a cloud of white breath escaped her lips.
Most people associated Nanman with jungles. Like anyone else from the Central Plains, I had thought the same.
But this damned land had somehow packed frigid, temperate, subtropical, and tropical climates together like apartments along a hallway.
“At this point, it’s practically cursed land.”
“...Watch your mouth.”
If Hwaran was on my right, Namho was on my left.
The elderly Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent was riding a black panther with one of Yayul Mok’s subordinates. He hunched low to avoid the branches but still found room to glare at me.
“I’m sure they’d love to hear you say that. Don’t you think?”
“So what? It’s true. Besides, I’m speaking Han Chinese. They can’t understand me.”
A few dozen feet ahead, Yayul Mok spoke without warning.
“I’d prefer it if you kept that mouth of yours shut.”
“...That was Han Chinese.”
“...Han Chinese?”
How the hell did he pull that off?

I felt like a cardsharp caught dealing from the bottom of the deck at a flower-card game. Yayul Mok’s Han Chinese was halting but unmistakable. Namho and I exchanged a look before I asked, “Did you study Han Chinese?”
“A little. I lost interest and quit soon afterward.”
“Oh, really? Only a little? And you quit that quickly?”
Yayul Mok answered my hopeful question with a stony face. “I still understand it well enough. Words like ‘cursed land,’ for example.”
“We’ll arrive soon, and then you can leave this cursed land. Until then, I’d appreciate it if you stayed quiet.”
There was nothing I could say to that. I shut my mouth, and Namho smiled with the wisdom of a sage.
“Well done. Very well done. Thanks to you, the Nanman Beast Palace and the Murim Alliance should be able to join hands with ease.”
“You make that sound like an insult. Still, you heard the good news.”

“It’s good news for Dark Heaven. The Murim Alliance’s foremost young prodigy came to propose an alliance, asked the Young Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace whether he had a grandfather, and called Nanman a cursed land. Come to think of it, are you with Dark Heaven?”
“Do I look like a member of Dark Heaven?”
“No. But I’ll admit I’m starting to wonder. Enough nonsense. What’s this good news I haven’t heard?”
I answered with confidence. “We’ll be at the Nanman Beast Palace soon.”
“God damn it...”
“Hey, don’t swear.”

“Do I look like I can help swearing right now? That A-Gwi bastard they call Taishan—or Geumsugangsan or whatever his name is—is one problem, but in my opinion, you’re no less troublesome, Pavilion Master. You’re already acting like this before we arrive. What are you going to do if your particular brand of insanity flares up when you actually come face-to-face with the Beast Miao King?”

“‘Insanity’ is a bit harsh. I may look reckless, but I know when I can stretch my legs. And Taishan may be lacking in certain areas, but he’s a major asset. When the time comes, he’ll pull his weight. You don’t need to worry so much.”
At that moment, a mournful animal cry rose behind us, followed by a frantic shout.
Gwooooooo!
“Y-Young Palace Lord! This huge Han bastard is biting my bear’s ear off!”
“Taishan! Bear meat!”
“Captain!”
“Taishan! Stop! Stop eating!”
“Seize that Han bastard!”
I glanced back as we rode, then added, “Of course, his appetite is a problem.”
“For fuck’s sake. There’s appetite, and then there’s appetite. Is that thing a beast or a person?”
I couldn’t argue. Lately, I’d begun to suspect Taishan might be some unknown creature occupying the space between human and beast.
Fire Dragon Pavilion. Are we going to be all right like this?

Taishan was chewing on the ear of the bear he’d been riding. Sama Pyo was trying to put a stop to his subordinate’s animal abuse, while the bear howled in pain and made it abundantly clear that it refused to carry passengers any longer.
I was watching them when Yayul Mok spoke with a sigh.
“We’re here. Please stop this and get off already.”
He was right. The chill in the air had vanished. Humid, oppressive heat surrounded us now, and a dense tropical rainforest stood ahead.
Beyond it...
Rumble, rumble.
An iron gate covered in vines and tree trunks swung open, revealing countless pavilions and houses.
This was a glimpse of the Nanman Beast Palace. Tens of thousands of li from the Central Plains, in the deepest and most secluded part of Nanman, its people had built a kingdom of their own.

Any family or sect of a certain size, including the Jin Family of Taiyuan, generally divided itself into an Outer Hall and an Inner Hall. The division gave it an organizational structure and lines of defense in case enemies attacked.
But the Outer Hall of the Nanman Beast Palace was far larger than that of an ordinary sect.
This is practically a city.
