sentences.text: Ju Hwaran told me that her grandfather, the Escort King Ju Gongsan, had once said this about the Nanman Beast Palace:
“Nanman is practically a kingdom, and the Nanman Beast Palace is a vast ranch encompassing five counties.”
The Escort King had traveled the Four Seas and Five Lakes and the Nine Provinces and Eight Wastes.
He had been right.
The territory directly ruled by the Nanman Beast Palace stretched across five counties.
In sheer area, even the Nine Sects and One Gang or the Five Great Families of the Central Plains could not compare.
Direct rule versus indirect rule, I suppose.
The Son of Heaven ruled the Central Plains, but in Nanman, the Nanman Beast Palace held supreme authority.
It might not surpass the great orthodox factions in martial power, but its influence here was bound to be far greater.
If there was one thing the Escort King had gotten wrong...
This isn’t a ranch.
It’s a safari.
I had never seen such a jumble of animals, plants, temperatures, and terrain in one place.
We followed Yayul Mok and his subordinates across grasslands, through jungles, and over mountains and rivers.
I could only shake my head.
“What the hell is wrong with this weather?”
Ju Hwaran, riding to my right, answered my mutter.
“One mountain holds four seasons, and ten li bring a different sky.
It’s a saying that describes Nanman’s unpredictable nature quite well.”
“Having seen it for myself, I can’t argue.
Young Lady Ju, what made you take an escort job to a place like this?”
“I didn’t know it would be this extreme, either.
I’ve accompanied my father on escort journeys before, but this is my first time going so deep into Nanman.”
A thick fur pelt was draped over her shoulders.
She smiled, and a cloud of white breath escaped her lips.
Most people associated Nanman with jungles.
Like anyone else from the Central Plains, I had thought the same.
But this damned land had somehow packed frigid, temperate, subtropical, and tropical climates together like apartments along a hallway.
“At this point, it’s practically cursed land.”
“...Watch your mouth.”
If Hwaran was on my right, Namho was on my left.
The elderly Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent was riding a black panther with one of Yayul Mok’s subordinates.
He hunched low to avoid the branches but still found room to glare at me.
“I’m sure they’d love to hear you say that.
Don’t you think?”
“So what?
It’s true.
Besides, I’m speaking Han Chinese.
They can’t understand me.”
A few dozen feet ahead, Yayul Mok spoke without warning.
“I’d prefer it if you kept that mouth of yours shut.”
“...That was Han Chinese.”
“...Han Chinese?”
How the hell did he pull that off?
I felt like a cardsharp caught dealing from the bottom of the deck at a flower-card game.
Yayul Mok’s Han Chinese was halting but unmistakable.
Namho and I exchanged a look before I asked, “Did you study Han Chinese?”
“A little.
I lost interest and quit soon afterward.”
“Oh, really?
Only a little?
And you quit that quickly?”
Yayul Mok answered my hopeful question with a stony face.
“I still understand it well enough.
Words like ‘cursed land,’ for example.”
“We’ll arrive soon, and then you can leave this cursed land.
Until then, I’d appreciate it if you stayed quiet.”
There was nothing I could say to that.
I shut my mouth, and Namho smiled with the wisdom of a sage.
“Well done.
Very well done.
Thanks to you, the Nanman Beast Palace and the Murim Alliance should be able to join hands with ease.”
“You make that sound like an insult.
Still, you heard the good news.”
“It’s good news for Dark Heaven.
The Murim Alliance’s foremost young prodigy came to propose an alliance, asked the Young Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace whether he had a grandfather, and called Nanman a cursed land.
Come to think of it, are you with Dark Heaven?”
“Do I look like a member of Dark Heaven?”
“No.
But I’ll admit I’m starting to wonder.
Enough nonsense.
What’s this good news I haven’t heard?”
I answered with confidence.
“We’ll be at the Nanman Beast Palace soon.”
“God damn it...”
“Hey, don’t swear.”
“Do I look like I can help swearing right now?
That A-Gwi bastard they call Taishan—or Geumsugangsan or whatever his name is—is one problem, but in my opinion, you’re no less troublesome, Pavilion Master.
You’re already acting like this before we arrive.
What are you going to do if your particular brand of insanity flares up when you actually come face-to-face with the Beast Miao King?”
“‘Insanity’ is a bit harsh.
I may look reckless, but I know when I can stretch my legs.
And Taishan may be lacking in certain areas, but he’s a major asset.
When the time comes, he’ll pull his weight.
You don’t need to worry so much.”
At that moment, a mournful animal cry rose behind us, followed by a frantic shout.
Gwooooooo!
“Y-Young Palace Lord!
This huge Han bastard is biting my bear’s ear off!”
“Taishan!
Bear meat!”
“Captain!”
“Taishan!
Stop!
Stop eating!”
“Seize that Han bastard!”
I glanced back as we rode, then added, “Of course, his appetite is a problem.”
“For fuck’s sake.
There’s appetite, and then there’s appetite.
Is that thing a beast or a person?”
I couldn’t argue.
Lately, I’d begun to suspect Taishan might be some unknown creature occupying the space between human and beast.
Fire Dragon Pavilion.

Taishan was chewing on the ear of the bear he’d been riding.

chapters.title: Chapter 625
paragraphs: People have something called an aura.
Some people’s auras are so faint and hazy they can barely be felt. Others are powerful and rough as waves, overwhelming anyone who faces them.
The Beast Miao King, Yayul Cheok, belonged to the latter sort.
Whoosh.
Yayul Cheok slowly rose to his feet, like a mountain beginning to move.
Though he was well over eighty, the muscles covering his body were as solid as armor. He walked without hesitation, his half-gray beard billowing like a lion’s mane.
Thud. Thud.
Everyone could see him now as he came down the vine-covered steps, trampling them beneath his bare feet.
Yayul Mok and his guards immediately dismounted and dropped to one knee. It was their way of showing respect to the lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.
“Greetings, Palace Lord.”
The Beast Miao King stared intently at Yayul Mok.
“You ran off again without a word.”
“There was a fire in the northeastern pasture. I happened to be nearby...”
“Did you put it out?”
“Yes.”
“And the culprit?”
The question was clearly for Yayul Mok, but the Beast Miao King was looking at me.
I met the fierce light in his tiger-like eyes and stepped forward.
“‘Culprit’ would be putting it a bit strongly. There was a little mistake.”
“It has been a long time since I’ve seen Han Chinese. Are you the culprit who started the fire?”
Before I could answer, he went on in a growling voice.
“Think carefully before you answer. Nanman’s laws are not merciful.”
I thought for a moment. “What’s the punishment for something like this?”
“That depends on the damage. In serious cases, the offender is fed to wild beasts. Or thrown into a pit full of venomous beasts.”
“What about minor cases?”
“Hanged from a vine.”
“That’s minor?”
“Of course. The body remains intact.”
“Ah.”
I nodded, stepped casually aside, and introduced someone.
“Ta-da. He’s the culprit, actually.”
An ordinary person might have panicked, but a Hidden Shadow Pavilion agent with fifty years of experience was made of sterner stuff. Namho spoke calmly.
“Are you fucking insane?”
“I’m not wrong, am I?”
“You fucking bastard...”
Namho was about to launch into a full stream of abuse when the Beast Miao King cut in, his voice rough.
“So you mean to abandon your companion to save your own skin.”
“Hmm. I think you’ve misunderstood. I never said I was abandoning him.”
“A misunderstanding?”
“I’m just getting the facts—no, setting the record straight. We haven’t known each other long, but he’s a good man. And there’s the Murim Alliance’s reputation to consider.”
I had brought up the Murim Alliance deliberately. He could have let the matter drop there, but the fierce light in his eyes did not dim.
“Once you enter Nanman, you follow Nanman’s laws. What if one of you must take responsibility?”
“If you insist...”
I scratched the back of my head.
“Wouldn’t we have to stop that somehow?”
At that moment—
Whoom!
The air around us vanished.
Before the short, heavy sound of air splitting could even be heard, a single punch shot toward me. It carried enough force to resemble a battering ram, and I crossed both arms in front of myself.
Boom!
A deafening roar rang out as though the sky itself had split open, and the shock wave from the collision swept in every direction.
The tremendous force drove me back a full ten feet. I sighed.
“Will that do?”
The Beast Miao King asked, his eyes emitting a glacial light.
“What do you mean?”
“Our first greeting.”
“What?”

“Before coming to Nanman, someone told me something. The Beast Miao King may look ignorant and reckless, but he’s actually warmhearted and loves playing pranks. So take him in stride and get along with him.”
The Fire Dragon Pavilion members’ reaction—standing there with their mouths hanging open—was nothing compared to what came next.
Yayul Mok, the Young Palace Lord, and his guards stared at me in shock before reaching for their weapons at lightning speed.
But before they could act, the Beast Miao King, whose lips had been twitching at my words, burst into laughter.
“Ha ha ha ha! Old Master Jeok hasn’t changed a bit.”
I rubbed my stinging forearms. “He’s as hale as ever.”
“I heard he’d taken a Disciple, but I didn’t expect to meet you so soon.”
He looked me over with fresh interest, then grinned.
“Good to meet you. This old man is Yayul Cheok.”
With anyone else, things might have been different. But before he was lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, he was someone Jeok Cheongang knew.
I clasped my hands respectfully toward the Beast Miao King.
“Jin Taekyung, nineteenth successor of the Fire Gate Clan, pays his respects to Great Hero Yayul Cheok, the Beast Miao King.”
“Good! Ha ha ha!”
He laughed again, rough and hearty, then spoke with unmistakable warmth.
“We have much to discuss. Follow me.”
Everyone stared after him as he strode away, then turned to me. Their faces all asked the same question.
I shrugged. “He’s pretty close with my master.”
As expected, life was all about school ties, regional ties, and blood ties.
The Beast Miao King looked happy. No, he definitely was happy.
Jeok Cheongang had told me he was usually cheerful, but as he sat in the Nanman Beast Palace’s main hall telling old stories, he looked like an oversized child.
“I remember the day I first met Old Master Jeok. He took one look at me and hit me with a Flame Divine Palm.”
“...According to the Old Master—no, according to my master—he didn’t actually let it fly. He said he only almost did.”
“No, he definitely hit me. It knocked the breath out of me and scared the shit out of me.”

The Sect Leaders and Family Heads of the great factions I’d met so far generally maintained some dignity. The Beast Miao King walked around in nothing but tiger-skin pants and didn’t give a damn about dignity.
As proof, he showed me the mark of the Flame Divine Palm stamped into his side and added casually,
“Quite a first meeting. I shit blood twice, went back to see him, and he poured me a drink to disinfect the wound. What a hearty man.”
“...Ah. Right.”
I wondered whether hearty meant what I thought it did. But if the man who’d been hit was fine with it, what could I say?
Besides, criticizing Jeok Cheongang would be like spitting in my own face.
“I regretted not seeing Old Master Jeok after the Great Faction War ended. Meeting his Disciple like this is a pleasure. Do you drink?”
“Of course I do, but I can’t right now.”
“Why not?”
“Something’s more urgent than a drink.”

If the world had been at peace, I would gladly have made a night of it. I would have toasted the Beast Miao King, shouted, “Yayul Cheok’s favorite—random games!” and gotten all the people of other ethnicities completely wasted on drinking games.
But not now.
“This time, I didn’t come as my master’s Disciple. I came as the Pavilion Master of the Murim Alliance.”
The smile on the Beast Miao King’s lips faded a little.
“Because of Dark Heaven?”
“So you know about them.”

“I received a messenger eagle concerning it. Since we’re tens of thousands of li from the Central Plains, the message arrived late. But it’s not as though I know nothing about the situation in the Central Plains.”
“If you don’t mind my asking, when did you receive it?”
“Let me think. More than a month ago now, I believe.”
Considering the distance between Henan and Nanman, as well as the timing, the letter must have been sent before the formation of the Murim Alliance, an event called the Mount Song Resolution.

As many sects as possible had needed to attend the Mount Song Resolution, and Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion Thousand-Faced Fox was not the kind of person who would send a letter without taking even that into account.
Which meant...
“The Nanman Beast Palace refused to join the alliance.”

There had been time to send a reply, or to bring some of the people of Nanman to Mount Song. But the fact that the Nanman Beast Palace had sent no response to the Murim Alliance could only be interpreted as a polite refusal.
The Beast Miao King remained silent for a moment before abruptly opening his mouth.
“It was not an outright refusal. We simply haven’t reached a decision.”
“But surely, Palace Lord, that decision is yours to—”
He raised a hand, cutting me off. Stroking his mane-like beard, he spoke again.
“Old Master Jeok’s Disciple. No, Jin Taekyung, was it?”
“Yes.”
“I have a question for those you brought with you. Do you know who I am?”
The group hesitated. Hyuk Mujin was the first to meet his gaze, and he swallowed hard before answering.
“You’re Great Hero Yayul Cheok, the Beast Miao King. A Supreme Peak master and one of the Ten Kings.”
“Correct. The woman beside you. Yes, you.”
Ju Hwaran answered at once. “As everyone knows, you’re the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.”
“That is also correct. But it is not the answer I want. This time, you beside her—tell me.”
Before anyone could stop him, Taishan blinked his enormous eyes.
“Taishan. Hungry.”
You bastard, Taishan. You answering-machine bastard. You fucking bastard...
The answer was so far from anything I’d expected that even the Beast Miao King looked taken aback.
“Who is he?”
I thought for a moment, then answered honestly. “I’m not really sure anymore.”
“What a strange fellow. Then let the old man beside him answer.”
Namho, who had been firing a rapid stream of profanity at Taishan in a low voice, opened his mouth.
“You are the Great Chieftain who leads the Miao people.”
“Yes.”
The Beast Miao King nodded.

“I am the Great Chieftain who represents countless Miao people. I gathered them under one banner and became the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace with the support of the other tribal chiefs. Mok, do you know how many tribes exist in our land?”
Yayul Mok, who had been standing quietly at attention, answered.
“If we include all of Nanman, there are thirty-two tribes, including four great tribes such as the Miao people.”
“Yes. That is the Nanman Beast Palace.”
I understood what the Beast Miao King was getting at. So did everyone else in the hall.
Except Taishan, of course.
“Are you saying...”
“Before I am Palace Lord, I am the Great Chieftain of the Miao people. And the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace is not a king.”
He couldn’t make every decision alone.
The Nanman Beast Palace was certainly like a separate kingdom, cut off from the Central Plains. But that kingdom was made up of an alliance of large and small tribes.
Why tell us so openly, though?
Are the other tribes opposed, while the Beast Miao King himself is considering agreeing to join the alliance?
I was about to ask when a quiet voice came from beyond the firmly shut doors of the main hall.
“Palace Lord, may I speak with you for a moment?”

But before they could act, the Beast Miao King, whose lips had been twitching at my words, burst into laughter.
“Ha ha ha ha!
Old Master Jeok hasn’t changed a bit.”
I rubbed my stinging forearms.
“He’s as hale as ever.”
“I heard he’d taken a Disciple, but I didn’t expect to meet you so soon.”
He looked me over with fresh interest, then grinned.
“Good to meet you.
This old man is Yayul Cheok.”
With anyone else, things might have been different.
But before he was lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, he was someone Jeok Cheongang knew.
I clasped my hands respectfully toward the Beast Miao King.
“Jin Taekyung, nineteenth successor of the Fire Gate Clan, pays his respects to Great Hero Yayul Cheok, the Beast Miao King.”
“Good!
Ha ha ha!”
He laughed again, rough and hearty, then spoke with unmistakable warmth.
“We have much to discuss.
Follow me.”
Everyone stared after him as he strode away, then turned to me.
Their faces all asked the same question.
I shrugged.
“He’s pretty close with my master.”
As expected, life was all about school ties, regional ties, and blood ties.
The Beast Miao King looked happy.
No, he definitely was happy.
Jeok Cheongang had told me he was usually cheerful, but as he sat in the Nanman Beast Palace’s main hall telling old stories, he looked like an oversized child.
“I remember the day I first met Old Master Jeok.
He took one look at me and hit me with a Flame Divine Palm.”
“...According to the Old Master—no, according to my master—he didn’t actually let it fly.
He said he only almost did.”
“No, he definitely hit me.
It knocked the breath out of me and scared the shit out of me.”
The Sect Leaders and Family Heads of the great factions I’d met so far generally maintained some dignity.
The Beast Miao King walked around in nothing but tiger-skin pants and didn’t give a damn about dignity.
As proof, he showed me the mark of the Flame Divine Palm stamped into his side and added casually,
“Quite a first meeting.
I shit blood twice, went back to see him, and he poured me a drink to disinfect the wound.
What a hearty man.”
Right.”
I wondered whether hearty meant what I thought it did.
But if the man who’d been hit was fine with it, what could I say?
Besides, criticizing Jeok Cheongang would be like spitting in my own face.
“I regretted not seeing Old Master Jeok after the Great Faction War ended.
Meeting his Disciple like this is a pleasure.
Do you drink?”
“Of course I do, but I can’t right now.”
“Why not?”
“Something’s more urgent than a drink.”
If the world had been at peace, I would gladly have made a night of it.
I would have toasted the Beast Miao King, shouted, “Yayul Cheok’s favorite—random games!” and gotten all the people of other ethnicities completely wasted on drinking games.
But not now.
“This time, I didn’t come as my master’s Disciple.
I came as the Pavilion Master of the Murim Alliance.”
The smile on the Beast Miao King’s lips faded a little.
“Because of Dark Heaven?”
“So you know about them.”
“I received a messenger eagle concerning it.
Since we’re tens of thousands of li from the Central Plains, the message arrived late.
But it’s not as though I know nothing about the situation in the Central Plains.”
“If you don’t mind my asking, when did you receive it?”
“Let me think.
More than a month ago now, I believe.”
Considering the distance between Henan and Nanman, as well as the timing, the letter must have been sent before the formation of the Murim Alliance, an event called the Mount Song Resolution.

As many sects as possible had needed to attend the Mount Song Resolution, and Chief of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion Thousand-Faced Fox was not the kind of person who would send a letter without taking even that into account.
Which meant...
“The Nanman Beast Palace refused to join the alliance.”
There had been time to send a reply, or to bring some of the people of Nanman to Mount Song.
But the fact that the Nanman Beast Palace had sent no response to the Murim Alliance could only be interpreted as a polite refusal.
The Beast Miao King remained silent for a moment before abruptly opening his mouth.
“It was not an outright refusal.
We simply haven’t reached a decision.”
“But surely, Palace Lord, that decision is yours to—”
He raised a hand, cutting me off.
Stroking his mane-like beard, he spoke again.
“Old Master Jeok’s Disciple.
No, Jin Taekyung, was it?”
“Yes.”
“I have a question for those you brought with you.
Do you know who I am?”
The group hesitated.
Hyuk Mujin was the first to meet his gaze, and he swallowed hard before answering.
“You’re Great Hero Yayul Cheok, the Beast Miao King.
A Supreme Peak master and one of the Ten Kings.”
“Correct.
The woman beside you.
Yes, you.”
Ju Hwaran answered at once.
“As everyone knows, you’re the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.”
“That is also correct.
But it is not the answer I want.
This time, you beside her—tell me.”
Before anyone could stop him, Taishan blinked his enormous eyes.
“Taishan.
Hungry.”
You bastard, Taishan.
You answering-machine bastard.
You fucking bastard...
The answer was so far from anything I’d expected that even the Beast Miao King looked taken aback.
“Who is he?”
I thought for a moment, then answered honestly.
“I’m not really sure anymore.”
“What a strange fellow.
Then let the old man beside him answer.”
Namho, who had been firing a rapid stream of profanity at Taishan in a low voice, opened his mouth.
“You are the Great Chieftain who leads the Miao people.”
“Yes.”
The Beast Miao King nodded.
“I am the Great Chieftain who represents countless Miao people.
I gathered them under one banner and became the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace with the support of the other tribal chiefs.
Mok, do you know how many tribes exist in our land?”
Yayul Mok, who had been standing quietly at attention, answered.
“If we include all of Nanman, there are thirty-two tribes, including four great tribes such as the Miao people.”
“Yes.
That is the Nanman Beast Palace.”
I understood what the Beast Miao King was getting at.
So did everyone else in the hall.
Except Taishan, of course.
“Are you saying...”
“Before I am Palace Lord, I am the Great Chieftain of the Miao people.
And the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace is not a king.”
He couldn’t make every decision alone.
The Nanman Beast Palace was certainly like a separate kingdom, cut off from the Central Plains.
But that kingdom was made up of an alliance of large and small tribes.
Why tell us so openly, though?
Are the other tribes opposed, while the Beast Miao King himself is considering agreeing to join the alliance?
I was about to ask when a quiet voice came from beyond the firmly shut doors of the main hall.
“Palace Lord, may I speak with you for a moment?”

chapters.title: Chapter 626
paragraphs: “Palace Lord, may I speak with you for a moment?”
A low, rigid voice came through the crack between the closed doors.
Everyone turned toward the doors behind us. But in that brief instant, I caught a change in two faces.
The Beast Miao King. And Yayul Mok.
We outsiders were stones that had happened to roll in from elsewhere. Those two were rooted so deeply in Nanman that they were more like its indispensable core.
I didn’t know who the voice belonged to, but the way their eyes darkened was answer enough.
They’re not exactly on smiling terms.
Just as I reached that conclusion, the Beast Miao King met my gaze and gave a quiet laugh.
“What an interesting fellow.”
“Pardon?”
“It’s nothing. Just something that slipped out.”
As if it were nothing. Anyone could see it was something.
But the Beast Miao King gave a small wave of his thick hand, as if telling me not to ask any further, then addressed everyone—including me.
“I’m sorry, but another guest has arrived. Could you give us some privacy? We still have time. Rest from your journey, and we can talk properly afterward.”
There was a slight contradiction in the Beast Miao King’s words about there still being time. As long as Dark Heaven existed, no one knew what might happen.
Still, I was all for resting a while before we talked.
At least nothing unusual seems to have happened in Nanman yet.
I nodded, and the Beast Miao King looked toward Yayul Mok, standing at attention to his right.
“Mok.”
One word was enough. Yayul Mok bowed respectfully, then gestured for us to follow him.
“We’ll take our leave.”
“Go. I’ll prepare a grand welcome for you.”
Forget the grand welcome. I just hope the talks about joining the alliance and Dark Heaven go well.
We turned away from the Beast Miao King. As we reached the doors, the slabs of carved stone began to move.
Rumble.
Through the slowly widening gap, I could see two muscular men in bear hides pulling chains attached to the doors.
And then...
“It’s been a long time.”
The man with the rigid voice was there too.
At his unexpected greeting, Yayul Mok bowed his head.
“Yayul Mok of the Miao people pays his respects to Uncle Baeksang.”
The middle-aged man of another ethnicity was dressed entirely in white, from head to toe, including his clothing and accessories. The man Yayul Mok had called Uncle Baeksang opened his mouth.
“I heard you’d returned. There was quite a large fire in the northeastern pasture, I hear.”
“It was a minor problem. We put it out quickly.”
“A minor problem.”
The cold gaze that accompanied his rigid voice swept over us. Baeksang examined Yayul Mok and everyone standing behind him.
Me in particular.
“I hope so.”
“And the Palace Lord?”
“He’s waiting inside.”
That was all. Baeksang glanced at Yayul Mok, who still had his head bowed, then passed us without another word.
Rumble.
The stone doors closed with another heavy grinding sound. Only then did Yayul Mok raise his head.
He stared at the shut doors, his lips pressed tight. I asked, “Who was that?”
“None of your business.”
“Don’t want to tell me, huh? Fine. Elder Namho?”
Namho, the Hidden Shadow Pavilion’s walking encyclopedia of Nanman, answered without hesitation.
“He’s the Great Chieftain of the Bai people, one of Nanman’s four most powerful tribes.”
“Oh. No wonder he’s dressed all in white. I saw a few Bai people near the entrance to Nanman. Those whiteys, right?”
Namho sounded taken aback. “Whiteys... Well, you’re not wrong. The tribe reveres the color white.”

More than thirty tribes lived throughout Nanman, each with its own villages and customs. Yeongin was something of a meeting place, where several tribes, including the Bai people, lived together by making compromises.
I didn’t know they were that powerful.
The Great Chieftain of one of the four tribes that divided up this vast land...
I’d suspected he was important when Yayul Mok called him Uncle, but Baeksang was a bigger figure than I’d imagined.
Now that I had the basics, I caught up with Yayul Mok, who had gotten well ahead of us.
“You two didn’t seem very close. Is he really your uncle?”
“Hey. Hey, can’t you hear me?”
“If someone calls you, you’re supposed to answer. Do you want to see the burning pasture? Huh? Want me to start a nice fucking fire on the way back?”
“Oh, this bastard is ignoring me to the very end. Fine, I get it. You have to see fire, not a coffin, before you’ll cry.”
As a trash talker, I had a hundred percent win rate. This time was no different.
“...Please stop spouting bullshit I can’t understand.”
“Oh, then behave yourself. If you answered promptly, none of this would happen.”
Yayul Mok glared at me for a moment, then sighed.
“Think before you ask. Would we belong to different tribes if he were my uncle by blood?”
“Fair point. So why call him Uncle?”
“He and my father are sworn brothers. They became close when they were young, and I’m told they always fought together during the Great Faction War.”
My eyes widened.
“What? Really?”
“I’d heard you Han Chinese bastards were suspicious, but I didn’t expect it to be true. What, don’t you believe me?”
“It’s not that, but... I was a little surprised.”
“Is it so surprising that they’re sworn brothers?”
“No, not that.”
“Great Hero Yayul Cheok was your father? Not your grandfather or great-grandfather?”
Yayul Mok’s eyes went cold, but I couldn’t help being surprised. The guy looked twenty-five at most, and he was the son of the Beast Miao King, who was well past eighty.
Martial artists tended to marry late, but this was impressive in a whole different way.
“Um, Pavilion Master?”
I waved off Ju Hwaran’s cautious call.
“Just a second. One last question. You’re not the eldest son, are you?”
Tap tap tap.
Yayul Mok suddenly walked faster. He forced the words through his teeth.
“I’m the only son in three generations.”
“Wow. Yayul Only Son. Omniscient Nanman Reader’s Viewpoint—totally doable.”
“What does that mean? Are you actually insane?”

“I say things people can’t understand sometimes. Anyway, that Baeksang fellow seems to be against the Nanman Beast Palace joining the alliance, right? Whatever happened back then, you two aren’t on great terms now?”
“That’s no concern of an outsider like you—!”
This was why the flow of a conversation mattered.
Yayul Mok had answered with his face flushed in anger, but he caught himself and trailed off. Too late. The water was spilled, and the fire had spread.
Having baited him perfectly, I smiled warmly and patted his shoulder.
“You bastard. Why’d you stop? My guess was right, then?”
“That’s enough for now. I’ll ask again if I need to. Thanks. Oh, this is our lodging, right? Thanks for showing us the way.”
I left Yayul Mok glaring at me like he wanted to kill me and turned around. Namho was staring at me like a caveman who had just discovered fire.
“Ever thought of joining the Hidden Shadow Pavilion?”
“The Hidden Shadow Pavilion? Forget it. Anyway, you heard all that, didn’t you?”
“Of course. The way you lured him in and hooked him—you’re at least as good as Jiang Taigong.”
I answered solemnly.
“A fisherman who catches people. Please call me Jindro.”
“Jindro...!”
Ju Hwaran and Hyuk Mujin clenched their fists, their faces alight with excitement.
“Pavilion Master, that was incredible. I really thought you’d lost your mind at first.”
“Young Lady Ju is right. I was so frustrated that I wanted to tear Captain’s mouth open and kill him.”
That felt like a strange sort of praise, but I’d gotten the job done. I smiled with satisfaction.
“Thank you, Young Lady Ju. Mujin, head down.”
“Yes, sir.”
Thud.
Hyuk Mujin planted his head on the ground as naturally as breathing, and I sat on his back.
Song Ilseom and Sama Pyo watched us in disbelief.
“That was absurd, but... we did learn something important.”
“Pavilion Master, what do you intend to do now?”
I shrugged.
We had new information, but the Great Chieftain of the Bai people opposing the Nanman Beast Palace’s entry into the Murim Alliance was hardly good news.
What bothered me more was why.
Why? Why?
Why would a man who had fought in the Great Faction War—the Beast Miao King’s childhood friend and sworn younger brother—oppose joining the alliance?
And what had that coldness in Baeksang’s eyes meant during our brief encounter? Why had he studied me so closely?
I couldn’t stop thinking about it.
Grrrrrrk.
“Taishan. Hungry.”
That fucking bastard.
The Beast Miao King sat in a high-backed chair draped with leopard and tiger hides, his chin propped on one hand. He picked up the wine bottle before him.
Trickle.
Cloudy liquor poured from the rough stone bottle he had carved himself, filling a large wooden bowl. He filled a second and offered one to his guest.
“It’s the fruit wine you like. Have some, Baeksang.”
Baeksang. The name meant white elephant.

But the middle-aged man who caught the slowly flying bowl looked nothing like one. He was lean, unlike the Beast Miao King, with eyes as cold as ice and a mouth held stiff. His answer was just as rigid.
“No, thank you. I’ll pass today.”
Clack.
Baeksang set the bowl down with a clack. The Beast Miao King smiled bitterly.
“...I see. That’s fine.”
It wasn’t fine. His heart ached.
In memories grown hazy with time, his one sworn brother had laughed and talked with him for days and nights, their cups never still. For decades now, that brother had given him the same answer.
I’ll pass today.
It wasn’t only today. He had said it the day before yesterday and yesterday. Tomorrow and the day after would be the same.
The Beast Miao King knew the answer so well he could predict it. Knowing he would be right hurt all the more.
“So, what brings you to see your older brother today?”
Baeksang’s voice did not waver.
“You know why.”
“Because of them.”
“I heard they came from the Murim Alliance.”
“That’s right. Sword Saint Mae Jonghak, the new Alliance Leader, sent them.”
The Beast Miao King admitted it readily. There was no reason to hide it, and Baeksang would hear about it regardless. Plenty of Bai people belonged to the Nanman Beast Palace’s Inner Hall.
He may even know exactly who they are.
The Baeksang he knew had always been meticulous. This time would be no different.
Baeksang’s cold eyes settled on the Beast Miao King as he silently raised his bowl.
“You haven’t forgotten the result of the last tribal council, have you?”
Of course not.
As the Beast Miao King answered inwardly, Baeksang’s rigid voice pierced his ears.
“We—the Nanman Beast Palace... will never join the alliance.”

chapters.title: Chapter 627
paragraphs: The temporary lodging we’d been assigned was decent enough. It wasn’t as lavish as the accommodations in the Central Plains, but it was clean and had everything the Fire Dragon Pavilion and I needed for our stay.
That didn’t mean we’d been welcomed without reservation.
“Hmm. Does anyone know what’s stuck between my chopsticks?”
Hyuk Mujin shot his hand up at the surprise quiz I’d sprung on everyone in the middle of the meal.
“Okay, Mujin. Let’s hear it.”
“A bug!”
“Correct. A centipede, to be precise. So why is it in our food?”
“Hmm. Perhaps it’s a custom of the non-Han people of Nanman?”
Namho, who had eighty years of experience being one of those people, picked out something that looked like a pine caterpillar and muttered, “First I’ve heard of it...”
I could have understood roasted locusts, more or less. But it looked as though someone had dumped live insects into the food. I couldn’t defend that.
Sama Pyo sighed as he watched Taishan, who was still determined to bury his face in his plate.
“So we aren’t welcome after all.”
There was no way we could eat this. Song Ilseom set down his chopsticks and answered calmly.
“It’s probably because of the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau incident.”
I agreed. But I didn’t think Yayul Mok had personally ordered it. Someone who was Young Palace Lord wouldn’t resort to anything this petty.
So this was the work of other non-Han people within the Nanman Beast Palace.
We’d been hated ever since we entered Nanman. Even the ugly duckling hadn’t had it this bad, I thought, just as Ju Hwaran quietly appeared. She’d gone upstairs before the meal to wash up.
“Huh? You’re done already?”
How long had she been up there? Not even Recruit Number 54 at the Nonsan training center could wash that fast.
She gave me an uneasy smile. “Ah, yes.”
I had a bad feeling. I kept looking at her, and after a moment’s hesitation, she spoke.
“Actually...”
By the time I’d heard the whole story, all I could do was laugh in disbelief.
“They gave you boiling-hot water in this weather? With something like filth mixed into it?”
Hwaran nodded, looking uncomfortable.
“I wasn’t going to say anything. It could have been a mistake, and I didn’t want it to cause trouble...”
“It wasn’t a mistake. And don’t worry about causing trouble. We’ve already got another problem.”
Only then did she notice what had happened to our meal. She offered a brief assessment.
“Ugh.”
“Just checking—you’re not going to eat it, are you?”
“No. Of course not.”
I’d never heard Hwaran answer so firmly. I clicked my tongue and stood.
“Captain, where are you going?”
“To make a scene.”
Sit still and people take you for a sack; let them get away with enough and they’ll take you for wrapping cloth. That was how the world worked.
We were here to persuade the Nanman Beast Palace, so I’d keep it within reason. But I had to raise hell at least once if I didn’t want this to happen again.
I was about to fling open the door when I remembered something and stopped.
“Oh. One more thing.”
“Yes?”
“Make him stop eating.”
No one had to ask who I meant. Only one person was wolfing down his third bowl of colorful insect fried rice.
Sama Pyo looked at Taishan with sorrow in his eyes.
“Taishan. Stop...”
Yeah. Please stop.
It was the largest tree I’d ever seen.
Dozens of grown men would have needed to stretch their arms out to encircle its trunk. It towered at least several dozen jang above me.
The sight drew a silent gasp from me, but I hadn’t come to admire the tree. I’d come to see someone.
“Hey. Get down.”
Rustle.
The thick leaves shook. A beast growled low, and Yayul Mok’s displeased voice came from above.
“You again. How did you find this place?”
“I asked. Someone told me you come here a lot.”
“Who?”
“The guy who manages the pavilion.”
“Hwang Gae?”
“Maybe it was Hwang Gae or Ddong Gae. Something like that.”
“He’s not the sort to tell a Han Chinese where I am.”
“Maybe not a Han Chinese. He was pretty forthcoming with my fist.”
“Come down. My neck hurts.”
I doubted he’d come down just because my neck hurt, so I kindly added, “Before I break the tree.”
“My ancestors’ ancestors planted this tree. It took root here a thousand years ago.”

“Then, sometime far in the future, your descendants will say, ‘There used to be a thousand-year-old tree here, but some Han Chinese bastard came and ripped it out by the roots.’ And when the child asks, ‘Why, Mom?’ she’ll say, ‘Because our ancestor wouldn’t come down from the tree when asked nicely.’”
“So get down before I destroy the environment.”
I wondered if I’d really have to pull it out if he refused again, but Yayul Mok loved nature more than I’d expected.
Rustle. Tap.
The White Tiger stepped from branch to branch and landed smoothly, letting out a low growl at me. Yayul Mok gave its neck a light stroke and glared.
“Madman.”
“Come on. You’re only noticing now?”
I scratched the back of my head bashfully. Yayul Mok’s face reddened, and he snarled like a wild beast.
“What happened to Hwang Gae?”
“Oh, him? All four limbs are fine. He’s a little scared, though.”
“You’re out of your mind. You come here asking for help, then bully the people of Nanman?”
“You’ve got the wrong idea. I didn’t lay a finger on him. I did grab him by the collar, though.”

I wasn’t some neighborhood thug. I hadn’t gone around acting like that even in the Central Plains. I always started by asking nicely and only used my fists when that didn’t work. This time, I’d had plenty of reason.
“Insect fried rice. Bathwater mixed with filth.”
“What?”
“If that isn’t a traditional custom, then the Nanman Beast Palace’s treatment of its guests is pretty terrible. Don’t you think?”
Yayul Mok frowned. After a moment, he let out a sigh.
“I think I have a general idea of what happened.”
“If you had a general idea, you should have warned them beforehand.”
“I didn’t think they’d show their hostility quite so openly...”
He stopped mid-sentence, then dipped his head toward me.
“I’m sorry. I sincerely apologize.”
“What’s that reaction?”
“Nothing.”
I was a little surprised. We hadn’t known each other long, but Yayul Mok seemed too proud and rough-edged to bow his head so readily.
The type to admit when he’s wrong and not hold a grudge?
It was easy to make a mistake, but hard to admit it and apologize sincerely.
In that sense, the young Young Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace had a better personality than I’d expected.
“I’ll replace the people responsible as soon as I get back. Hwang Gae and everyone else involved. Nothing like this will happen again.”
“Well, if you’ll do that...”
“It was my mistake. Again, I apologize. I’d appreciate it if this didn’t reach my father’s ears.”
“Why? Does he hit you when you do something wrong?”
Yayul Mok bristled. “What kind of nonsense is that?”
“If not, never mind. You went so far as to ask me not to tell him, so I thought you might get beaten for three days and three nights.”
“My father has never laid a hand on me even once.”

Well, if your father was the Beast Miao King, you’d probably grow up fine without him laying a hand on you. At that size and with that martial power, he could probably get his son, grandson, and maybe even his great-grandson through puberty without any trouble.
While I was thinking that, Yayul Mok hesitated, then added quietly, “I’ll be fine. The others won’t. If my father finds out, he’ll come down on them like thunder.”
“Ah.”
“You’re guests my father welcomed. You Han Chinese have every right to protest how you’ve been treated. But I don’t want Hwang Gae or the others punished for it.”
“Because they’re pissed off about that fucking Dick Demon Escort Bureau?”
“...You’ve got the name a little wrong, but yes. That’s one reason.”
“One reason. Sounds like there’s another.”
Yayul Mok stared at me silently for a while. Then, as he stroked the chin of the now-quiet White Tiger, he opened his mouth.
“The Great Faction War.”
“Hmm?”

“We shed far too much blood in the Central Plains. Under my father’s leadership, all of Nanman’s tribes joined forces, and as many as ten thousand warriors went to the battlefield. But the number of those who returned home alive was less than a quarter of that.”
Grrr.
The White Tiger accepted his touch, then looked up at its master with worried eyes.
Yayul Mok went on, his voice heavy with conflicting emotions.

“Someone’s parents. Someone’s children. Friends and relatives who had grown up together since childhood. Most of them left for the battlefield with smiles on their faces and never returned. Even I, who was born long afterward, wasn’t exempt.”
“You did?”
“Under ordinary circumstances, I’d never have become Young Palace Lord. That’s the real answer to the question you asked earlier.”
I thought back to our conversation just after we’d left the Beast Miao King. Then I understood.
“You had older siblings.”

“Three. One of them was my elder sister. She was young, and she was a woman, but I heard she was as brave as any warrior. If she hadn’t participated in the Great Faction War, she would have married the man she loved. My father and Uncle Baeksang would have become in-laws as well as sworn brothers.”
“Wait. Then...”

“What you’re thinking is right. In the war between Han Chinese that they called the Great Faction War, my father lost two sons and a daughter. Uncle Baeksang lost the son he treasured more than his own life.”
Yayul Mok smiled bitterly and added, “Don’t blame Hwang Gae too much. He lost his parents and all his relatives.”
I had nothing to say, so I simply closed my mouth.
I’d heard about the Great Faction War so many times my ears practically rang with it, but I hadn’t known Nanman had suffered losses like these.
No. If I was honest, I hadn’t thought I needed to know. Nanman was in the Outer Lands, tens of thousands of ri from the Central Plains. I’d thought of it as a separate land, far removed from Murim.
The others who still talked about the war probably thought the same way. Only Jeok Cheongang and a tiny handful of others had even mentioned that Nanman had suffered heavy losses.
So they must have all been carrying old resentment. The Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau incident from recently must have been the flashpoint.
Whatever Reward they’d received after the war, the wound was still there. It had only just begun to heal, barely forming a scab, when this happened.
“Only a few decades ago, we united and risked our lives fighting for the Han Chinese. And now, you killed some of us.”
Yayul Mok’s voice reached me, cold and seething.

chapters.title: Chapter 628
paragraphs: “Only a few decades ago, we stood together and risked our lives fighting for the Han Chinese. And now, you’ve turned your swords on us.”
At that moment, Yayul Mok was genuinely furious.
More than two hundred people had been massacred in the recent tragedy. Most of the victims had been powerless old men, women, and children.
They were Miao people, just as he was. And after doing that to them, the Han Chinese still had the nerve to ask for help.
“We’ve already shed enough blood. Not for ourselves, but for you Han Chinese.”
His voice trembled with anger.
“Nanman will not shed blood in vain again. Stop causing trouble and go home.”
The words came out sharp and firm as a blade. Having finally said everything he’d been holding back, Yayul Mok felt a weight lift as he looked at the Han Chinese man before him.
Jin Taekyung, was it?
Half a day ago, Yayul Mok had known almost nothing about him. He’d heard in passing that Jin Taekyung was a renowned young prodigy from the Central Plains, but that was all.
If the absurd rumor that he was a Supreme Peak master was true, though, he might rank among the three greatest warriors even here in Nanman, where Yayul Mok had been born and raised.
He blocked Father’s punch. Maybe the rumor is true.
Yayul Mok knew better than anyone how formidable his father, Yayul Cheok, was.
Before turning forty, his father had become Nanman’s greatest warrior. He had made the Miao people its strongest tribe and, with the recognition of all, become lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.

Nor was that all. His martial power had won the admiration of even the Han Chinese of the Central Plains, who treated the people of Nanman as barbarians. Yayul Mok had heard that was when his father earned the name Beast Miao King.
I thought Uncle Baeksang was the only one who could exchange blows with Father.

Yet Jin Taekyung’s martial arts were astonishing, especially for someone no older than Yayul Mok himself. He had blocked a punch from Yayul Cheok without much difficulty—a punch Yayul Mok could barely see, let alone stop.
True, its force had driven Jin Taekyung back nearly one jang. That was hardly a reason to underestimate him.
And besides...
He was big. A head or two taller than an ordinary grown man, with broad shoulders and a muscular build his clothes couldn’t hide.
Facing him at close range now, Yayul Mok felt as though he were looking at a beast standing on two legs.
Maybe it was his size. Or maybe it was the way the eyes and mouth that always seemed to be smiling had gone still. Either way, Yayul Mok swallowed hard without meaning to.
Then Jin Taekyung spoke.
“Hey.”
“Why’d you jump? I just called you.”
Yayul Mok flinched at the sudden low voice. “Wh-why did you call me?”
“Why are you stuttering?”
Because you’re looking at me like that, you bastard.
Until now, Jin Taekyung had always seemed lighter than a feather. With the smile gone from his face, he felt more like a boulder weighing ten thousand geun.
—Grrr...
The white tiger beside Yayul Mok seemed to feel its master’s unease. Pretending to be calm, Yayul Mok stroked his beloved tiger’s neck as it shrank back beside him.
“I-I didn’t stutter.”
“Why did you call me? If you’ve got something to say, say it.”
“Hmm. Nothing much.”
Jin Taekyung gave him an odd look, scratched the back of his head, and said, “Thanks for telling me.”
“Huh?”
“Thanks for being honest. There were things I didn’t know, and you’ve cleared up quite a bit for me. I understand what’s going on around here a little better, too.”
What is he talking about?
This was nothing like the reaction Yayul Mok had expected. He stared at Jin Taekyung for a moment, then asked, “So you mean... you’re going back?”
“Hm?”
Jin Taekyung tilted his head. “How did you get that from what I said?”
“No, but you said you understood.”
“Yeah. Of course I understand. It’s not like I’m incapable of empathy.”
“Then?”
“That’s a separate matter.”
“What?”
“This’ll take too long if I explain everything, and my mouth hurts. So let’s cut to the chase and ask one thing.”
Jin Taekyung leaned back against a tree and lowered his voice.
“Do you honestly think the Great Faction War was fought only for the Han Chinese?”
“And since we’re on the subject, do you think the Nanman people who died in that war died like dogs for no reason?”
“That’s...”
“That’s what?”
Yayul Mok found himself at a loss for words. For some reason, the answer wouldn’t come. As he searched his muddled thoughts for one, Jin Taekyung’s quiet voice reached him again.
“There are two reasons you can’t answer. First, you know I’m right, but you don’t want to admit it. And second...”
Jin Taekyung held up two fingers.
“Because you’re still a brainless brat.”
“What is that supposed to—”

“Don’t ask me. Think about it yourself. Why did the Nanman Beast Palace take so many warriors tens of thousands of li to help the Central Plains? Just because an ancestor of the Fire Gate Clan brought order to Nanman ages ago? Even that white tiger beside you would laugh at that.”
“Most people in Nanman probably oppose joining the alliance for the first reason. They think all that blood was shed for nothing, and they don’t want to repeat it.”
Jin Taekyung went on with a sigh.

“If you look at it that way, it isn’t entirely wrong. Who the fuck wants war? So what if you fight like hell and gain land, gold, and silver treasures? People are dying like ants in every direction. And some of those ants might be my friends, my family, or my lover. They could even be me—or you. By the way, do you have a girlfriend?”
Yayul Mok shook his head before he could think.
“An ex-girlfriend?”
“What exactly do you mean by ‘girlfriend’?”
“A lover. A woman you date and have feelings for.”
“Uh, no.”
“Oh. So you had one?”
“No.”
“Right. So you had one?”
“...I’ve never had one. Not even once.”
“How old are you?”
“Twenty-six.”
“What a guy. A promising candidate for the virgin-boy technique. If you hold out like this for fifty years, you might even become a Martial God. Fine, let’s take lovers off the list of victims.”
Jin Taekyung smiled, looking pleased for some reason. Yayul Mok felt his mood sour as the tension went out of him.
The man was impossible to get a read on. So was this conversation.
“What the hell are you trying to say? Why did you suddenly go off on a tangent about lovers?”
“Who knows? I’m not entirely sure myself. But I do know one thing.”
The faint smile left Jin Taekyung’s face.

“The people of Nanman who left home and died in the Central Plains all those years ago did not die for nothing. And if the same thing happens again, their deaths won’t be for nothing this time, either.”
“I’m sincerely sorry about what happened with the Heavenly Demon Escort Bureau. But if there were people crazy enough to do something like that... I would have killed them myself.”
“Even though they were Han Chinese, like you?”
“What does that have to do with it?”
Was it his imagination, or had Jin Taekyung left him speechless several times today?
Yayul Mok pressed his lips together and stared at him before saying, “No matter how good your words sound, Nanman won’t help the Central Plains.”
“It’ll be hard to convince you. I still have to try.”
“It’s pointless.”
“What?”
“It’s as good as decided. The first tribal council reached a conclusion fifteen days ago.”
“First? Sounds like there’s going to be a second.”
“Nanman is vast. Gathering all thirty-two tribes in one place takes time, so the four great chieftains, including my father, consider matters first.”
“And they decided against joining the alliance? Go on.”
“In three days, every tribe in Nanman will gather for a council. But the other great chieftains have already made up their minds. I doubt anything will change.”
Yayul Mok was telling the truth. The Nanman Beast Palace was a symbol of unity, but that didn’t make the tribes equal.

If the three great chieftains led by Baeksang, the Great Chieftain of the Bai people, stood together, even the Beast Miao King—Nanman’s greatest warrior and lord of the palace—could not decide on his own to join the alliance.
Those are the rules here.
Yayul Mok watched Jin Taekyung closely. How would this young, powerful Han Chinese from the Central Plains react now that Nanman’s joining the alliance was all but impossible?
He’ll probably be disappointed. If not, he’ll surely exhaust himself trying to persuade us somehow...
“I’ll do what I can. If it doesn’t work, it doesn’t work.”
“Huh?”
Yayul Mok couldn’t hide his surprise. Jin Taekyung sounded far calmer than he’d expected.
“B-but the result is already decided, isn’t it?”
“Yeah. You also said it isn’t over yet.”
“That’s true, but...”
What is with him?
Yayul Mok frowned. “Don’t you have to persuade us somehow?”
“That’s what I said I’d try to do. If I can’t, I’ll go home. After I deal with something more important, of course.”
“More important?”
“You’ve got the wrong idea.”
Jin Taekyung scratched his chin.
“I didn’t come here as a diplomat. I’m more like a firefighter.”
“A firefighter? What’s that?”
“Someone who puts out fires.”
“Didn’t you set fire to the pasture as soon as you arrived?”
Jin Taekyung fell silent at the earnest question.
“...It’s a metaphor. What I mean is, persuading people isn’t exactly my greatest talent.”
“That seems true.”
“...You fucking bastard. Now I’m getting annoyed for no reason. Anyway, it’d be a shame if Nanman didn’t join us, but if trying doesn’t work, there’s nothing we can do.”
“But you’re Han Chinese. And you belong to the Murim Alliance.”
“So?”

Jin Taekyung let out a quiet laugh at the way Yayul Mok looked at him, as though he were some strange creature.
“What would you do if the pasture caught fire again?”
“Put it out at once.”
“Why?”
“If we don’t put it out, the flames will spread in every direction.”
“Good. There’s your answer.”
“Don’t make it complicated. There’s a fire, so I’m trying to put it out. Just like the people of Nanman who left this land for the Central Plains decades ago.”
Yayul Mok was silent for a moment. Then, with a troubled look, he asked, “So you came here just to help us... without expecting anything in return?”
“What if I did?”
“I don’t believe you.”
“Believe what you want. But before any of that...”

“At least feed me properly, asshole.”

sentences.text: “Only a few decades ago, we stood together and risked our lives fighting for the Han Chinese.
And now, you’ve turned your swords on us.”
At that moment, Yayul Mok was genuinely furious.
More than two hundred people had been massacred in the recent tragedy.
Most of the victims had been powerless old men, women, and children.
They were Miao people, just as he was.
And after doing that to them, the Han Chinese still had the nerve to ask for help.
“We’ve already shed enough blood.
Not for ourselves, but for you Han Chinese.”
His voice trembled with anger.
“Nanman will not shed blood in vain again.
Stop causing trouble and go home.”
The words came out sharp and firm as a blade.
Having finally said everything he’d been holding back, Yayul Mok felt a weight lift as he looked at the Han Chinese man before him.
Jin Taekyung, was it?
Half a day ago, Yayul Mok had known almost nothing about him.
He’d heard in passing that Jin Taekyung was a renowned young prodigy from the Central Plains, but that was all.
If the absurd rumor that he was a Supreme Peak master was true, though, he might rank among the three greatest warriors even here in Nanman, where Yayul Mok had been born and raised.
He blocked Father’s punch.
Maybe the rumor is true.
Yayul Mok knew better than anyone how formidable his father, Yayul Cheok, was.
Before turning forty, his father had become Nanman’s greatest warrior.
He had made the Miao people its strongest tribe and, with the recognition of all, become lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.
Nor was that all.
His martial power had won the admiration of even the Han Chinese of the Central Plains, who treated the people of Nanman as barbarians.
Yayul Mok had heard that was when his father earned the name Beast Miao King.
I thought Uncle Baeksang was the only one who could exchange blows with Father.
Yet Jin Taekyung’s martial arts were astonishing, especially for someone no older than Yayul Mok himself.
He had blocked a punch from Yayul Cheok without much difficulty—a punch Yayul Mok could barely see, let alone stop.
True, its force had driven Jin Taekyung back nearly one jang.
That was hardly a reason to underestimate him.
And besides...
He was big.
A head or two taller than an ordinary grown man, with broad shoulders and a muscular build his clothes couldn’t hide.
Facing him at close range now, Yayul Mok felt as though he were looking at a beast standing on two legs.
Maybe it was his size.
Or maybe it was the way the eyes and mouth that always seemed to be smiling had gone still.
Either way, Yayul Mok swallowed hard without meaning to.
Then Jin Taekyung spoke.
“Hey.”
“Why’d you jump?
I just called you.”
Yayul Mok flinched at the sudden low voice.
“Wh-why did you call me?”
“Why are you stuttering?”
Because you’re looking at me like that, you bastard.
Until now, Jin Taekyung had always seemed lighter than a feather.
With the smile gone from his face, he felt more like a boulder weighing ten thousand geun.
—Grrr...
The white tiger beside Yayul Mok seemed to feel its master’s unease.
Pretending to be calm, Yayul Mok stroked his beloved tiger’s neck as it shrank back beside him.
“I-I didn’t stutter.”
“Why did you call me?
If you’ve got something to say, say it.”
“Hmm.
Nothing much.”
Jin Taekyung gave him an odd look, scratched the back of his head, and said, “Thanks for telling me.”
“Huh?”
“Thanks for being honest.
There were things I didn’t know, and you’ve cleared up quite a bit for me.
I understand what’s going on around here a little better, too.”
What is he talking about?
This was nothing like the reaction Yayul Mok had expected.
He stared at Jin Taekyung for a moment, then asked, “So you mean... you’re going back?”
“Hm?”
Jin Taekyung tilted his head.
“How did you get that from what I said?”
“No, but you said you understood.”
“Yeah.
Of course I understand.
It’s not like I’m incapable of empathy.”
“Then?”
“That’s a separate matter.”
“What?”
“This’ll take too long if I explain everything, and my mouth hurts.
So let’s cut to the chase and ask one thing.”
Jin Taekyung leaned back against a tree and lowered his voice.
“Do you honestly think the Great Faction War was fought only for the Han Chinese?”
“And since we’re on the subject, do you think the Nanman people who died in that war died like dogs for no reason?”
“That’s...”
“That’s what?”
Yayul Mok found himself at a loss for words.
For some reason, the answer wouldn’t come.
As he searched his muddled thoughts for one, Jin Taekyung’s quiet voice reached him again.
“There are two reasons you can’t answer.
First, you know I’m right, but you don’t want to admit it.
And second...”
Jin Taekyung held up two fingers.
“Because you’re still a brainless brat.”
“What is that supposed to—”
“Don’t ask me.
Think about it yourself.
Why did the Nanman Beast Palace take so many warriors tens of thousands of li to help the Central Plains?
Just because an ancestor of the Fire Gate Clan brought order to Nanman ages ago?
Even that white tiger beside you would laugh at that.”
“Most people in Nanman probably oppose joining the alliance for the first reason.
They think all that blood was shed for nothing, and they don’t want to repeat it.”
Jin Taekyung went on with a sigh.
“If you look at it that way, it isn’t entirely wrong.
Who the fuck wants war?
So what if you fight like hell and gain land, gold, and silver treasures?
People are dying like ants in every direction.
And some of those ants might be my friends, my family, or my lover.
They could even be me—or you.
By the way, do you have a girlfriend?”
Yayul Mok shook his head before he could think.
“An ex-girlfriend?”
“What exactly do you mean by ‘girlfriend’?”
“A lover.
A woman you date and have feelings for.”
“Uh, no.”
“Oh.
So you had one?”
“No.”
“Right.
So you had one?”
“...I’ve never had one.
Not even once.”
“How old are you?”
“Twenty-six.”
“What a guy.
A promising candidate for the virgin-boy technique.
If you hold out like this for fifty years, you might even become a Martial God.
Fine, let’s take lovers off the list of victims.”
Jin Taekyung smiled, looking pleased for some reason.
Yayul Mok felt his mood sour as the tension went out of him.
The man was impossible to get a read on.
So was this conversation.
“What the hell are you trying to say?
Why did you suddenly go off on a tangent about lovers?”
“Who knows?
I’m not entirely sure myself.
But I do know one thing.”
The faint smile left Jin Taekyung’s face.

I would have killed them myself.”

chapters.title: Chapter 629
paragraphs: After parting ways with Yayul Mok, I headed back toward the temporary lodging where the Fire Dragon Pavilion members were waiting.
With my martial prowess, I wasn’t in danger of anyone trying to harm me. Still, wandering around alone in this atmosphere wouldn’t do me any good.
Somehow, I found myself in the Nanman Beast Palace’s Outer Hall.
“Huh. When did I get here?”
I muttered to myself and looked around.
Perhaps because it was hidden among the thick, overgrown grass, I couldn’t see a single rat anywhere...
Well, not quite. Two or three monkeys were milling around—Nanman’s mascots, much like Gukkeoni was for the Ministry of National Defense.
—Screech?
Why’s that Han Chinese bastard crawling around out here instead of staying put in his lodging?
That seemed to be the question in the monkey’s curious eyes. But I had nothing to be ashamed of before the heavens.
I got lost. What do you want me to do about it?
Of course, I’d followed the advice of the greatest assassin of all time disguised as the Divine Physician: conceal my breathing and move stealthily so no one would spot me.
But one thing was certain. I was lost.
The lodging was less than fifteen minutes away, and there were only two roads, but that was beside the point. If I said I was lost, I was lost.
Still, I’m here representing the Murim Alliance. I should be able to figure out this much on my own.
Back at the Hunter Training Center, a fellow recruit had once said that a perfect lie was a true story.
In the end, all that mattered was not getting caught. Though in this atmosphere, I did need to make an effort to avoid it.
Rustle.
I steadied my breathing, slipped out of the grass, and blended into the people gathered nearby.
I suppressed my presence, reined in my aura, and bent slightly at the waist to make myself look shorter. Just as Mungyeong had taught me.
Do you know who the most frightening assassin in the world is?
Sure. The person standing right in front of me.
I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. I’ve committed a crime worthy of death. Please put the dagger in your sleeve away and teach this fool.
Mungyeong had glared at me as though deciding whether to kill me, then answered.
An ordinary person.
Ordinary?
Someone more ordinary than anyone else, who blends naturally into any place. That is the most frightening assassin.
What Mungyeong taught me that day wasn’t useful only to assassins.
He’d mentioned it in passing, calling it a simple trick that couldn’t even be considered martial arts. But I hadn’t forgotten it, and it had come in handy more than once.
Just like now.
This really is different from the Central Plains.
I turned my head without drawing attention and looked around the Outer Hall.
Even on a second look, the Nanman Beast Palace was a distinctive place. It was less like a sect than a small city, with all kinds of peoples living together.
Compared to the Central Plains, where the Han Chinese made up the majority, Nanman was practically a melting pot of races.

A Miao woman draped in colorful jewelry strode through the market, enjoying the attention of the people around her, while a Bai merchant in white traditional clothing tried to conduct a trade with a monkey perched on his shoulder.
And an old man was limping straight toward me.
No, sir. Why are you coming this way?

“Excuse me. I’m trying to buy some cloth at the market. Which shop would you recommend? If I were ten years younger, I could have found it with my eyes closed, but perhaps it’s because I’m old that I can’t remember anything these days.”
Had I blended in too well? I hadn’t expected this.
The non-Han old man had blocked my path with his cane and asked me the question. I hesitated for a moment, then answered as shamelessly as possible.
“Go straight ahead, then take the alley on the right.”
“The alley on the right? Was there a cloth shop there?”
How would I know, sir?
But contrary to my thoughts, I nodded.
“Yes. Plenty of them. More than the hairs on your head. They’re springing up everywhere.”
“Really? What’s one of them called?”
Why do you need the name, too?
Hesitating now would make him suspicious, so I blurted out the first name that came to mind.
“Hyuk Family Textile Shop. Their cloth is pretty good.”
“Hyuk Family Textile Shop? I don’t think I’ve heard of it...”
I’d underestimated how well a local knew his own market.
It was clearly an unreasonable answer, but in situations like this, the shameless person won. With an expression utterly free of shame, I spoke firmly.
“It’s been there for over ten years.”
“Really? That’s strange. I could’ve sworn...”
“Isn’t your memory getting hazy? That’s why you asked me, right?”
“Well, yes, but...”
“Sir, if you don’t mind my asking, how old are you?”
“Me? Eighty-two.”
“I’m twenty-two. I can still vividly remember moving from my father’s side to my mother’s.”
“You remember that?”
“I’m only twenty-two, so I remember everything. Trust me.”
“Ah. All right, then. Thank you.”
Defeated by sheer force of confidence, the old man turned to leave. I suddenly remembered something and called after him.
“Sir?”
“Hmm? What is it?”
“Where is the place with the biggest crowd right now? I was supposed to meet someone, but that bastard isn’t showing up anywhere, so I’m going to look for him myself.”
“Try over there.” He pointed with his cane. “I caught a glimpse of it on my way here. No idea what’s going on, but it was awfully noisy. Probably something to do with the festival in a few days.”
Then he paused and studied my face with his cloudy eyes.
“By the way, which tribe are you from?”
“What?”
“You don’t look Yao, like me. Yet you speak our language so well. How strange...”
“Oh, I can see it over there. Please be careful on your way.”
“Hey. Wait.”
I left the old man behind and walked away quickly.

No matter how naturally I blended in, anyone who had enough time to study my face would notice. The differences between the Han Chinese and Nanman’s other peoples weren’t so pronounced that I’d stand out at a glance, but they were there.
Fortunately, there was a solution.

My hands were very fast. And as luck would have it, the market was packed with non-Han people, while the merchant selling traditional animal masks was too busy dealing with customers pouring in from every direction to pay attention to anything else.
In short, slipping one mask away was no trouble at all.
Open Inventory. Store.
Ding.
System You have acquired Crudely Made Tiger Mask!
The hand wasn’t faster than the eye. The System was.
I put the mask in my Inventory. By the time I’d passed a couple of people, the tiger mask, painted with crude dye, was on my face.
This should do. It won’t stand out around here.
Maybe it was because of the festival the old man had mentioned. Two or three out of every ten people I saw were wearing similar masks.
I headed in the direction he’d pointed and listened to the voices around me.
“Did you hear? The great chieftains of the Yi and Yao peoples are back.”
“Really? I heard they went to subdue man-eating beasts about fifteen days ago.”
“They mobilized around five hundred warriors, so they must have finished quickly. Unlike the Yao people, it seems the great chieftain of the Yi people didn’t achieve any noteworthy results, though.”
“Just what I expected. Not that I expected much.”
I didn’t miss the familiar information exchanged in their conversation.
The Yi and Yao peoples.

Together with the Miao and Bai peoples—led respectively by the Beast Miao King, lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, and Baeksang, whom I had briefly encountered earlier—the Yi and Yao peoples made up Nanman’s four most powerful tribes.
I remembered what Namho had told me on our way to the Nanman Beast Palace.
Nanman’s four great tribes are the Miao, Bai, Yi, and Yao peoples. The Miao are the strongest, followed by the Bai.
What about the Yi and Yao?
Twenty or thirty years ago, the Yi would have been ahead.
Sounds like they aren’t anymore.

Times have changed. Many say the Yi great chieftain, who inherited the position from his late father, lacks resolve. The Yao, on the other hand, have grown considerably. They gained an exceptional leader. I doubt any man they put in her place could have done as much.
Wait. Are you saying...?
You’ve guessed right. The Yao great chieftain is a woman. Extremely intelligent, and extraordinarily beautiful.
My thoughts broke off. Not because I chose to stop thinking, but because a clear note from a distant instrument reached my ears.
Fwoooosh.
A gentle melody rode Nanman’s hot, humid wind across the open space.
The noisy market fell silent in an instant, and a short exclamation escaped someone’s lips.
It was impossible to hold back. The melody was that pure, and the procession revealed as people hurriedly stepped aside was splendid and beautiful.
Thump. Thump. Thump.
Hundreds of men and women marched to the low beat of drums.
The Yi men wore black tops trimmed with floral cloth and wide, pleated trousers. The Yao women, in conical hats, walked slowly in two lines.
“Wow.”
“The Yi and Yao have arrived!”
Cheers rose all around me.
But while everyone else admired their beauty and finery, I watched the weapons strapped to their waists and shoulders.
Every one of them is a warrior.

A warrior of Nanman was equivalent to a Murim practitioner in the Central Plains. Since these people belonged to their respective tribes, it would be more accurate to call them members of a martial sect.
And if the Yi and Yao great chieftains are back from subduing those beasts...
This was more than a procession. It was a victory parade, and a victory parade needed the generals who had led the battle.
In this case, those generals were the two great chieftains.
“Oh!”
“Th-there...!”
Cries rang out almost as soon as the thought occurred to me. Gazes and voices turned in one direction, and then the whole crowd erupted into cheers.
“Waaaaah!”
Amid the roar that seemed capable of shaking all of Nanman beyond the Outer Hall, two people finally appeared at the center of the procession and waved their hands.
A man riding an enormous black bear—presumably the Yi great chieftain. And...
“Yohi! Great Chieftain Yohi!”
A woman smiling brightly as the crowd lavished her with far more attention and affection than they had the man.
Even without hearing them call her name, I would have known she was the Yao great chieftain.
The Yao great chieftain is a woman. Extremely intelligent, and extraordinarily beautiful.
Namho had been right. Yohi was beautiful—almost bewitchingly so.
Whenever her deep gaze swept over the crowd, people gasped in admiration.
That was probably why I stood out. Amid all those cheers and admiring faces, I was standing there like a block of wood.
Yohi’s eyes lit up when she spotted me.
