The Beast Miao King, his face flushed, spread both arms toward me.
“Uh, that’s really crossing the line—”
Grab!
Crack!
“What an incredible bastard!”
“Argh!
Aaaagh!”
“How did you do that?
Was it the Fire Gate Clan’s unique martial art?
Or the final ultimate technique Old Man Jeok learned?”
Whap!
Whap!
“Uuuugh!”
“What a monster!
I couldn’t believe it even while watching!”
“Aaaaaagh!
You crazy bastard!”
“What?
Crazy bastard?
Yes!
That’s exactly what you are—a madman born of the Central Plains!”
I nearly died far from home.
I wasn’t joking.
When the madman born of Nanman finally let go of me, a mournful notification sounded in my ear.
Beep.
System Status abnormality Mild Ligament Tear applied!
Strength decreases by 20 until recovery!
Agility decreases by 20 until recovery!
This was why Doctor Octopus was a villain.
I didn’t have the strength to say anything else.
Gasping through the pain, I glared at the Beast Miao King and barely managed to speak.
“Spider.
Spider.”
“Spider?
Oh, the Thousand-Year Spider?”
“Quick.
Hurry.”
At my pitiful gestures, the Beast Miao King nodded in admiration.
“I wondered if that was what you meant, but are you planning to use the Thousand-Year Spider to figure out the Poisonblood Grounds?
You really are something.”
“Ah, please.”
“Ha, all right.
Just as you asked, I brought it here alive and unharmed—”
Before he could spout any more nonsense, I squeezed out what little strength I had left.
“Gnnngh!”
I wrenched White Flame free and drove it straight into the Thousand-Year Spider’s head, like a patient collecting a random insurance payout.
Thud!
—Ssssit!
Kieeeek!
The monster gave a brief death cry.
Then heavenly bells rang from somewhere.
Ding.
Ding.
Ding.

System You defeated Level 119 Thousand-Year Spider! - Additional EXP has been awarded for defeating a rare entity! - Level Up! - The damaged body has been substantially restored! - All status abnormalities have been removed! - Warning!
Your physical condition is not yet perfect!
A little treatment and rest are required!
Ah, this was why I took out insurance.
If the EXP from one venomous beast was an ant’s tear, the Thousand-Year Spider was a downpour from heaven.
Add its EXP to what I’d earned killing thousands of venomous beasts at once, and life immediately surged back into my dying body.
“Buuuurp.”
Last hit.
Sweet.
As the ancient sages said, one Level Up made the five loaves and two fish look like nothing.
I couldn’t tell you which sage said it, but someone did.
It was true, too.
Whew.
I almost died.
Having barely made it back from the nursing home’s doorstep, I rubbed my stomach, feeling a satisfying fullness spread through my body.
Then I looked up and met the eyes of someone staring at me with a distinctly unimpressed expression.
“Why?”
“What is it?”
After a moment, the Beast Miao King spoke, his expression gone cold.
“Why did you tell me to keep it alive if you were going to do that?”
Why else?
To get the EXP, obviously.
But years of working for a shitty small Guild had given me something I had never possessed before: social awareness and people skills.
I answered with a mournful, rigid expression.
“I wanted to take revenge with my own hands.”
“What?”
“For the Nanman warriors who died at the hands... no, the slime and webs of those bastards.
Tearing them apart wouldn’t have been enough.”
The Beast Miao King’s eyes widened, emotion stirring in them.
He stared at me, his gaze trembling, then spoke in a choked voice.
“I... don’t know what to say.”
“Shh.
Don’t say anything.
I already know.”
“You... you little bastard!”
What a romantic moment...
Like hell.
Fuck off.
I was going to gag.
But one thing was certain: the Beast Miao King couldn’t hide how moved he was.
Well, the result’s good.
That’s what matters, right?
I didn’t need to feel guilty.
I genuinely mourned the Nanman warriors, and I genuinely needed the EXP to recover.
More importantly, my quick excuse had made things better.
If word of this gets around Nanman, maybe the odds of the Nanman Beast Palace joining the Murim Alliance will go up ten percent.
Even so, a weight remained in my chest.
I felt guilty because I hadn’t been able to prevent hundreds of people from being massacred less than two shichen away.
...Damn it.
A bitter taste filled my mouth.
Even now, countless people were probably dying across both the modern world and Murim.
Some in traffic accidents.
Some at the hands of monsters.
A martial artist might get into a quarrel at an inn, draw a sword, and die on the spot.
Somewhere, a nameless hero might lose their life fighting an evildoer.
I knew I couldn’t save them all.
But I was human, and I hated seeing other people die.
And I felt regret, too.
Regret that if I had been there, perhaps I could have saved innocent people.
Great power comes with great responsibility.
At some point, that line from a superhero movie had become a boulder weighing on my body and mind.
It weighed on me even while I circulated my qi, when I needed to give it my full concentration.
Maybe this is a Heart Demon, too.
I sighed softly, shook my head, and started walking again, leaving the Thousand-Year Spider’s corpse behind.
We headed deeper into the hidden reaches of the Poisonblood Grounds.
Splash.
Splash.
The Beast Miao King and I watched our steps more carefully now.
Killing five Thousand-Year Spiders and an enormous number of venomous beasts had left the area quiet, but it was too soon to let our guard down.
That bastard is the biggest problem of all.
Ailao Mountain’s Wraith.
The Black Tiger fit the name the System had given it perfectly.
It was the one thing we had to watch for above all else.
Its enormous body moved like the wind.
The powerful, eerie qi I’d sensed from it, however briefly, proved it was far beyond any ordinary spiritual creature or venomous beast.
—Where do you think it is now?
It was useful having someone beside me who was thinking the same thing.
I moved my lips in answer to the Beast Miao King’s Sound Transmission.
—Who knows?
But I’m sure it’s still in the Poisonblood Grounds.
—That’s what I don’t understand.
Why lure us all this way and then fail to appear?
Fifteen minutes ago, we would have been at a clear disadvantage.
He was right.
Despite their reputation, the five Thousand-Year Spiders had been easier to handle than I’d expected, and so had the thousands of venomous beasts.
But if Ailao Mountain’s Wraith had joined them, things would have been different.
If it had joined the fight from the beginning, we could probably have put up a decent fight.
But if it had appeared right after I used One Annihilation...
Even if we’d done everything right, it would have been a brutal fight.
Its teeth could withstand Force.
It was unbelievably fast, and, true to its name, its presence was as impossible to sense as a wraith’s.
One of us might have died.
Or left a limb behind.
At worst, we’d both be dead.
But why?
Why didn’t it appear even under those circumstances?
I didn’t know.
Only two remotely plausible explanations came to mind.
First, a classic island-nation plot twist:
Heh heh.
The Thousand-Year Spider is merely the weakest of our Four Great Venomous Beasts.
And second:
Ailao Mountain’s Wraith has no intention of hurting us.
I took a few cautious steps and discarded the second theory.
However I looked at it, it seemed too unlikely.
Before I could think any further, the Beast Miao King, who had been following behind and watching our flanks and rear, put his broad hand on my shoulder.
Tap.
Oh, shit.
That scared the hell out of me.
My heart nearly fell out of my chest.
I steadied myself and turned to look where his finger was pointing.
Beyond the Poison Mist, growing thicker with every step, and the dark jungle crowding in on all sides, a faint, unfamiliar light shone through.
Could it be?
We didn’t need to say anything.
My instincts had reached the answer before my thoughts had.
Rustle.
Crackle.
We pushed through grass that carried a faint trace of poison and came to the source of the light.
At last, we saw what lay before us.
Both of us stopped, mouths hanging open.
“This is...!”
A vast swamp lay under the faint moonlight.
Waiting there were countless shapes hanging, each bound tight in transparent spiderwebs—and white eggs.

chapters.title: Chapter 641
paragraphs: Sometimes, the mere sight of something sends a chill down your spine and makes your hair stand on end.
Like everything in front of me now.
Fwoosh.
Faint moonlight spilled through the swaying leaves, as mysterious as a scene from a myth. But it wasn’t shining on a peaceful blue lake.
What is this...?
A dark, desolate swamp. Hundreds of large shapes hung there, wrapped in layer upon layer of spiderwebs like silkworm cocoons. Around them were white eggs, smaller but several times more numerous.
What the hell are they?
An ominous question weighed on me, one I felt I shouldn’t learn the answer to.
Even so, I’d instinctively reached out. My hand was already touching the nearest cocoon.
Tap.
An unpleasant sensation ran through my fingertip. At the same moment, a System notification sounded in my ear.
Beep. Ding.

System You have been Poisoned by the Thousand-Year Spider’s Paralysis Poison! - If you are not detoxified quickly, you may enter Full-Body Paralysis and Unconsciousness! - The potential effect of the Myriad-Poison Ring has been activated! - All status abnormalities related to Poison have been removed!
My fingertip went numb for a moment, then felt cool and clear again.
The Myriad-Poison Ring was a divine artifact capable of absorbing even Formless Ultimate Poison. However unusual a venomous beast the Thousand-Year Spider might be, its poison couldn’t harm me.
If this is a Thousand-Year Spider’s web...
A possibility struck me. I tightened my grip and tore the webbing apart.
Crack. Riiiip.
Hundreds of layers of webbing gave way under my grip. When the shape concealed inside was revealed, the Beast Miao King, who had been watching from beside me, muttered like he was groaning.
“A person?”
He was right.
The man’s face was as white as paper, and his body lay perfectly still. The Beast Miao King checked the unknown man’s faint pulse and breathed a sigh of relief.
“Thank goodness. He’s still alive.”
I had expected as much. According to what the System had told me earlier, the Thousand-Year Spider’s webs did not contain poison powerful enough to kill their victims.
The reason was probably...
To keep them fresh. So the spiders can eat whenever they want.
Now I understood why the sight of this place had made my hair stand on end.
A slaughterhouse.
Before it was the Thousand-Year Spiders’ home, this swamp was a slaughterhouse and an enormous food store.
Only then did I detect the heavy smell of blood beneath the stench coming from all around us.
“Spider bastards. They’ve sure been stuffing their faces for a long time.”
Hundreds. No, perhaps thousands.
If the Nanman Beast Palace’s records were right and the Five Poisons Sect had created the Poisonblood Grounds, there was no telling how many people had died here over the years.
Ironically, the spiders’ habit meant we could save many of their captives today.
It did seem strange. More warriors had disappeared than died.

About three hundred elite warriors had been stationed at Ailao Mountain. The five Thousand-Year Spiders had killed roughly a hundred on the spot, eaten their fill, then dragged the rest into the Poisonblood Grounds. Before long, they would have eaten those warriors one by one.
Instead, we’d found them.
“Would you look at these goddamn bastards! They deserve to die!”
The Beast Miao King’s eyes were red with fury. I tried to calm him down.
“Uh, sorry to interrupt, but you already killed them.”
“Tearing them to pieces wouldn’t be enough!”
Well, I couldn’t argue with that. But for now, we needed to deal with the situation, not dwell on our anger.
After calming down a little, the Beast Miao King looked around with a devastated expression.
“To think they dared to do something like this.”
“You said there hadn’t been any major losses before now, didn’t you?”
“It’s true. At least during my time as Palace Lord, we’ve had no trouble like this.”
“Strange, then. Five Thousand-Year Spiders suddenly show up and attack your warriors at a time like this.”
He was silent for a moment at my pointed words. Then he said, “Dark Heaven... Do you think this was their doing?”
I nodded without hesitation.

“I don’t know if they were directly involved, but I’d bet they had a hand in it. There’s nothing strange about Thousand-Year Spiders attacking people. The timing, though? Of course I suspect Dark Heaven.”
“But if they are behind this, they could have waited until after you left. Doing it on the final day of the Tribal Grand Council only hurts their cause.”
“Well...”
My voice trailed off. His point was sharper than I’d expected, and I couldn’t easily dismiss it.
He’s right. If I were the Southern Heaven Demon Empress—that bitch—I wouldn’t have bothered.
Even without any interference, it was practically certain that the Nanman Beast Palace’s entry into the Murim Alliance would fall through. Dark Heaven had no reason to stir up Nanman for nothing.
So why?

Nothing about it made sense. Ailao Mountain’s Wraith had appeared out of nowhere and still hadn’t shown itself. Five Thousand-Year Spiders had suddenly begun a massacre. And there was the question of whether they were connected to Dark Heaven.
I was still frowning over it when the Beast Miao King’s voice brought me back.
“Right now, the problem is moving these people. It’s a blessing they’re alive, but getting them out of the Poisonblood Grounds is another matter.”
I set those thoughts aside. “If you ask me, we should leave the others as they are.”
“Leave them? Here?”
“...Do I look insane? Of course we’re taking them back to the Nanman Beast Palace. I told White Tiger to bring people here, so we should wait for them. Assuming he understood me.”
“You mean Muyaho. He’s cleverer than most people. I’m sure he understood.”
“What’s that look for?”
“Oh. Nothing.”
I nearly burst out laughing.
Muyaho. The more I heard that name, the harder it was to get used to. I managed to straighten my face and went on.
“And we should leave the webs intact.”
“Because of the poison.”
“Yes.”

Getting here had been difficult. Getting back would be far worse. We’d have to take some two hundred patients through the Poison Mist after they woke from several shichen of full-body paralysis and unconsciousness.
I’m not even sure how much the Myriad-Poison Ring can cover.
The Myriad-Poison Ring certainly possessed mysterious power, but I couldn’t put two hundred lives through a fifty-fifty gacha roll just by trusting in this one item.
They were safer staying wrapped in the webs.
“At least the Poison Mist doesn’t seem to affect them in there. Otherwise, they’d have died on the way here.”
“True. Perhaps the Thousand-Year Spider’s poison in the webs keeps other poisons out.”
In a sense, it was poison countering poison. The webs had been coffins on the journey here. Now they could serve as cryogenic capsules, keeping the warriors safe from the Poison Mist.
Besides, even if I unwrapped and detoxified them one at a time, there was only so much I could do. Our conversations would probably go something like this:
All right, patient. Slowly open your eyes. Can you see the fingers I’m waving in front of you? If you can, tell me how many there are.
“Uhh... One. One.”
Which finger?
“The middle one.”
Right. It means fuck you.
“Huh? What are you talking about all of a sudden...?”
It was a simple test. Anyway, good. You can see and hear clearly now. Both your sight and hearing have recovered.
“Thank you. Thank you so much, Han Chinese sir.”
Ha ha. Don’t mention it. The paralysis should be gone now that you’ve been detoxified. Can you move your fingers?
“Of course. I can move them just fine.”
Good. I have something for you to do with them. First, what’s your name?
“Me? Jang Sam.”
Excellent. Here’s a dagger. Write what I dictate on this wooden tablet.
“Yes, all right.”
Write exactly what I say. Jang Sam.
“Jang. Sam.”
Lies here.
“Lies here. Wait, what?”
I didn’t want to alarm you, but we have to go back the way we came. And we’re out of poison-warding pearls. Oh, I’ll be fine. I have the Myriad-Poison Ring.
I’m ‘invincible.’ The Myriad-Poison Ring is a ‘god.’
Hmm.
That would turn into a two-hundred-against-one battle to the death over the Myriad-Poison Ring.
Or two hundred against two. The Beast Miao King had a big, beautiful top-grade poison-warding pearl of his own.
“...Why are you looking at me like that?” he asked.
“It’s nothing.”
“Is it Dark Heaven?”
“No. Heaven as in the sky.”
His expression hardened. “Are you actually insane...?”
If my department head had been here, he would have laughed. But it seemed the Palace Lord didn’t get the joke.
The Beast Miao King looked me over with an expression like he was staring at a Thousand-Year Spider walking on two legs, then began gathering the warriors wrapped in webs into one place.
Slice. Slice.
Every time his straightened palm moved, the people hanging in midair were neatly stacked together.
There were two hundred of them—almost exactly the number of warriors who had gone missing from Ailao Mountain.
Wait. What about the ferocious beasts?
As I helped the Beast Miao King move the survivors, I remembered one of the questions I’d had while searching Ailao Mountain: the missing ferocious beasts were nowhere to be seen.
The Beast Miao King soon noticed it as well and wore a puzzled expression.
“That is strange. There is no sign of the ferocious beasts.”
“Are they timid, by any chance? Do they tuck their tails and run when they meet strangers?”
“I’m asking because I’m curious, but do you perhaps not know what ‘ferocious beast’ means?”
Of course I did. Ferocious. Beast.
That was why it was strange. So many of them wouldn’t have abandoned their masters and run away.
And it’s not as if Thousand-Year Spiders are picky eaters.
I knew spiders. Hope Goshiwon, where I’d lived for nearly seven years, had more spiders than hope. I’d even grown fond enough of them to share my ramen.
Then where the hell did the beasts go?
We’d have to search more of the Poisonblood Grounds to find out, but I doubted Thousand-Year Spiders were meticulous enough to sort their food by type.
Just as the Beast Miao King and I were looking around in confusion—
Rustle.
A small sound came from more than ten zhang away. With it, I sensed a faint presence.

paragraphs: Rustle.
A faint noise came from the distance, followed by a presence closing in fast. I whipped White Flame toward it.
The Beast Miao King immediately drew up his internal energy. The same thought must have crossed his mind.
The Wraith of Ailao Mountain.
But we were both wrong. I caught a glimpse of white beyond the dark grass and lowered my spearhead with a sigh.
“Muyaho?”

That night, the darkness over Nanman seemed unusually deep and long. But everything has a beginning and an end.
Deep in the night, while everyone slept, a hundred elite warriors hurried to Ailao Mountain. They returned to the Nanman Beast Palace near dawn, and plenty of people saw them arrive.
“Did you hear? Something huge happened last night.”
“What happened?”
“Well, old man Mong, who lives near the West Gate of the Outer Palace, told me...”
“Gasp!”
“What? I haven’t even started.”
“He’s still alive? I was sure he died last year.”
“Ah, fuck.”
By morning, the gist of the rumor was spreading fast.

Something major had happened somewhere in Nanman the night before. Baeksang, Great Chieftain of the Bai people, and Young Palace Lord Yayul Mok had led a hundred elite warriors out of the Outer Palace. When they returned a few shichen later, the Beast Miao King and Jin Taekyung were at the head of the party.
The Nanman Beast Palace did not normally intervene by force in disputes between tribes. For the Palace Lord himself to have gone out meant it was a serious incident.
But the rumor didn’t stop there.
“And the trouble was at Ailao Mountain, of all places.”
“Ailao Mountain? That Ailao Mountain?”
“Is there another Ailao Mountain in Nanman? Yao merchants from a village a hundred li from the mountain told us at first light. They happened to see it while working late on their ledgers.”

To the people of Nanman, the name Five Poisons Sect was a burden they could never cast off. Their ancestors had fought the sect, and only after countless sacrifices had they established the order and laws they lived by today.
And yet, of all places, the incident had occurred in Ailao Mountain, the Five Poisons Sect’s former headquarters.
Ordinarily, it was a forbidden place they didn’t even want to mention. Trouble there was another matter.
“What the hell? Go on. Hurry!”
Through markets lined with stalls, back alleys, and busy inns, the story passed from mouth to ear and from one mouth to the next.

The chieftains gathered for that day’s Tribal Grand Council knew all about the commotion. They also knew the rumors circulating through the Outer and Inner Palaces were more accurate than anyone might have expected.
“The whole place is in an uproar. Everyone’s heard.”
“The bigger problem is that it isn’t just a rumor. Isn’t that right?”

They had gathered for the first time in a year, but there was no time to exchange pleasantries. Seated early in the Inner Palace’s vast main hall, the chieftains continued their discussion with grave expressions.

“You all received word in advance, so you know this is no ordinary matter. Nearly a hundred elite warriors have already died at Ailao Mountain because of creatures that should have stayed in the Poisonblood Grounds.”
“I heard Thousand-Year Spiders appeared. Frankly, I find that hard to believe. Five of them, no less.”

“Hard to believe, but true. Their corpses are still there. Enraged by the deaths of the warriors stationed at Ailao Mountain, the Palace Lord pursued the creatures into the Poisonblood Grounds and hunted them down.”
The middle-aged chieftain who had answered so readily added in a low voice, “That young Han Chinese man from the Murim Alliance was with him, too. Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung.”
Every chieftain in the hall governed some part of Nanman, large or small. Naturally, they knew of the young outsider. Their reactions varied.
“Oh.”
“Hmm.”
“Ahem.”
One nodded with an exclamation of admiration. Another cleared his throat uneasily and stared at nothing.
But the mood had changed since a few days earlier. This time, no one called him a “damned Han Chinese bastard.”
Even the chieftains who normally disliked Han Chinese people knew Jin Taekyung had played no small part in resolving the incident.
“Without him, it might not have ended so quickly. The Palace Lord went after those creatures in haste. Perhaps he might even have been hurt—”
Bang!
A sudden boom drowned out the rest.
Some thirty pairs of eyes turned to one chieftain. He had looked displeased ever since Jin Taekyung’s name came up, and now he had slammed a hand on the stone table.

“I tried to hold my tongue, but I can’t listen to this anymore. Watch what you say, Chief Jang. The Palace Lord is far stronger than you think. The same goes for everyone in Nanman. We don’t need help from some weak Han Chinese bastard!”
The middle-aged chieftain frowned.

“What brave and prideful words. Truly moving. But didn’t you hear that weak Han Chinese bastard dealt with two Thousand-Year Spiders and thousands of venomous beasts in the Poisonblood Grounds? That he is a renowned warrior of the Central Plains who inherited the Fire King’s legacy?”
“Th-that...”

“And five years ago, who invaded our tribe’s territory even after the Palace Lord personally mediated the dispute? Wasn’t it you? Even if a venomous snake’s bitten your mouth, speak straight. Your loyalty isn’t to the Palace Lord. It’s to Great Chieftain Baeksang. All of Nanman knows you’re his loyal dog.”
“What? Loyal dog? You son of a bitch!”
“Son of a bitch? You piece of poisonous refuse left behind by the Five Poisons Sect—how dare you...”
Bang!
The two chieftains sprang to their feet, snarling as if they were about to draw their swords on each other.
Rumble...
The enormous stone gate swung open. Three figures stepped into the hall.
Step. Step.
Footsteps echoed through the sudden quiet. The man in front stopped, and his voice came cold as ice.
“Looks like I interrupted your conversation.”
“Don’t mind me. Carry on.”
No one said a word.

As if nothing had happened, the shouting that had filled the hall only moments ago vanished in an instant, replaced by a heavy silence that pressed down on everyone. At the same time, the expressions of the two opposing chieftains split between joy and sorrow.
“Welcome, Great Chieftain Baeksang.”
Baeksang glanced at the groveling loyal dog, then fixed his eyes on the middle-aged chieftain.
“That was an interesting conversation. I’d like to hear the rest.”
“You’ve grown quiet since I last saw you, Chief Jang.”
Chief Jang bit his lip and lowered his head.
“I greet Great Chieftain Baeksang.”
Yohi, Great Chieftain of the Yao people, stood to Baeksang’s right. She gave a quiet laugh.
“We must be invisible. Don’t you think, big brother Heugung?”
“Hm? Oh. Yes, that won’t do. Failing to show proper courtesy with our lovely Yohi right here? No, that won’t do.”
Heugung had been grinning foolishly at Yohi. He put on a stern face, but Baeksang’s chilly glance made his plump body shrink back.
“S-sorry, Uncle Baek. But did I do something wrong...?”
“Oh, what could you have done wrong? Our kind, handsome big brother Heugung hasn’t done anything wrong. Has he?”
“R-right. Yohi’s right.”
Baeksang watched them in silence, clicked his tongue, and resumed walking.
The table was large enough to seat several dozen people. It had one head seat, and the three seats nearest it belonged to the great chieftains, second only to the Palace Lord.
Scrape. Clack.
Twenty-eight chieftains had arrived before them. With the three great chieftains now seated, thirty-one places had found their owners.
Baeksang had seen this arrangement year after year. Yet something felt wrong.
“Two seats are empty.”
At first, no one understood what he meant. Then Yohi spoke with laughter in her voice, and the chieftains’ puzzlement gave way.
“You’re right. How strange. Why are two seats empty?”

Only thirty-two seats were ever prepared for the Tribal Grand Council. That had been true a hundred years ago, and it was true now. Anyone who was not a chieftain—even the Young Palace Lord—had to stand in attendance.
There should have been only one empty seat left.
Today, there were two.
“Why would...”
And just as a puzzled murmur escaped someone’s lips—
Rumble...
The enormous stone gate moved again. Two figures appeared beyond it at last.
The moment Baeksang saw them, his eyes darkened.

chapters.title: Chapter 643
paragraphs: Rumble!
The stone gate descended behind me with a heavy rumble.
Inside the spacious main hall, illuminated by spreading lamplight, thirty-one pairs of eyes flew toward my face like arrows and lodged there amid a silence in which no one spoke.
What are you doing coming out of there?
That was the look they gave me. But it held more surprise than hostility toward a Han Chinese man, and several chieftains even looked pleased to see me.
Of course, there was one absolute exception.
“One of two things must be true. Either my eyes deceive me, or the rules of the Tribal Grand Council have changed without anyone—including me—knowing.”
The middle-aged man who broke the silence was Baeksang, the Great Chieftain of the Bai people. He continued in a cold voice.
“Explain why you’ve brought a mere Han Chinese man here. He is neither a chieftain nor a Nanman.”
Baeksang wasn’t asking the Beast Miao King, who had yet to arrive. He wasn’t asking me, either.
Yayul Mok stood to my right. He answered calmly.
“Because he has the right to be here.”
“The right.”
Baeksang repeated the words under his breath.
“That sounds like the rash judgment of a brat who isn’t even thirty.”
“It is also the judgment of someone else who has yet to arrive.”
“My father. No—the Palace Lord said he has the right to attend the Tribal Grand Council.”
Baeksang’s eyes darkened. After a moment’s silence, he asked, “Why hasn’t the Palace Lord come?”
“He’ll be here soon. By then, there will be only one empty seat left.”
“Unacceptable.”
Baeksang tapped the table with a finger pierced by a nail.

“The Tribal Grand Council is a solemn gathering where the chieftains representing all of Nanman come together to exchange their views. If one is not a chieftain, no one may take a seat here except the Young Palace Lord. This man’s qualification is merely the will of the Palace Lord alone. We will not permit it.”
I watched for a moment, then muttered, “That’s funny. Isn’t that just your opinion?”
I was clearly talking to myself, but none of the chieftains gathered here were so lacking in martial arts that they couldn’t hear me.
That went without saying for Baeksang, whose martial arts were particularly formidable.
He turned a cold gaze on me. “What did you say?”
“Oh, you heard me?”
“Did you think I wouldn’t?”
“No. I said it so you would. Glad you caught that.”
I shrugged at his frozen expression.

“Since the subject has come up, let me say this. We may call ourselves ‘we,’ but isn’t this ultimately just your personal opinion as well? You haven’t even asked what the other chieftains think, yet you say you won’t permit it. What exactly are we supposed to do with that?”
As my words continued to flow smoothly, I could feel an invisible stir spreading among the seated chieftains.
Baeksang was the Great Chieftain of the Bai people, the most powerful tribe in Nanman after the Miao people, as well as a Supreme Peak master who represented Nanman alongside the Beast Miao King.
I doubted anyone had ever dared speak to him so openly.
Anyone but me.

“When Great Hero Yayul sent me ahead, he told me this: ‘Yayul Cheok, Great Chieftain of the Miao people, recognizes your right to attend. But Yayul Cheok, Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, cannot decide this alone. Gain the other chieftains’ consent.’”
Nanman was hardly a welcoming place for outsiders. Even breathing here felt like a privilege. And the Tribal Grand Council, held once a year, was so rigid a needle couldn’t slip through its rules.
If the Beast Miao King hadn’t done me this favor, they’d have stopped me at the door.
His help had gotten me past those rules. Now I intended to claim a seat—by winning the other chieftains’ support.
“So that’s what I’d like to ask.”
I met their eyes one by one.
“What do the rest of you think?”
Fwoosh.
A breeze from somewhere made the torches flicker. In their reddish light, some faces tightened with discomfort, others looked troubled, and more than I’d expected looked receptive.
Including the middle-aged chieftain who had just opened his mouth.
“Everyone here, including my Zang people, knows what happened at Ailao Mountain last night.”
From what I’d seen and heard in Nanman, the Zang people weren’t one of its four great tribes, but they had enough strength to stand just behind them.
The man who appeared to lead them continued slowly.

“An unexpected disaster cost us much blood. Swift action kept the loss from becoming greater. We owe that to our wise Palace Lord, Great Chieftain Yayul, and to a young Han Chinese man who helped him.”
His strong voice carried through the hall. He watched the other chieftains’ expressions shift, then turned to me with a faint smile.
“It’s late, but I want to thank you here. Because of your help, twenty-two brave, fine warriors of the Zang people are alive. One of them is my own kin.”
“Ah.”
Around two hundred warriors had been dragged into the Poisonblood Grounds. I hadn’t learned all their names or who they were.
I hadn’t known, and couldn’t have known. But what I’d done last night was coming back to me now as goodwill and gratitude.
“On behalf of the Zang people, I welcome Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung to the Tribal Grand Council.”
He finished with a respectful salute—not one from the land where he’d been born and raised, but a cupped-fist salute from the Central Plains.
And that was only the beginning.
Scrape. Scrape.
Unfamiliar chieftains rose one after another. Their faces and clothing differed, but they spoke with the same goodwill.
“We can’t accept a kindness and pretend it never happened. The Hui people support his attendance.”
“The Man people have no objection. I only wish to thank him for saving my good-for-nothing son.”
Each of them ruled a tribe, large or small.
But they were also heads of families. Fathers and mothers with children they loved.
One by one, they offered me their thanks with painfully awkward cupped-fist salutes. The warriors I’d rescued from the Poisonblood Grounds last night were their people. Their families.
Not everyone who supported me was doing it because of last night’s rescue, though.
“The Bouyei people also support him. He is more than qualified.”
At the words of the middle-aged female chieftain, one of the chieftains who still had not risen from his seat frowned.
“Wait. What reason do the Bouyei people have? None of your warriors were stationed at Ailao Mountain, were they?”
“Nanman is my homeland.”
“What does that have to—”
“Even beasts that cannot speak repay a kindness. Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung risked his life fighting for my homeland last night. Isn’t that reason enough to let him attend?”
“...Ahem.”
The chieftain who had questioned her fell silent after an uncomfortable cough. Warm smiles appeared on other faces.
And amid this atmosphere, so clearly different from the one only a few days ago, I felt a tickle in one corner of my chest.
Repaying someone who helped you. It should be the most natural thing in the world.
But sometimes, in this world, it wasn’t.
I hadn’t gone into the Poisonblood Grounds looking for repayment. Yet here the chieftains were, giving me their gratitude and trust.
Some because I’d helped them last night. Others because of something that had happened long ago.

“My late father, who was once a Great Chieftain, often said things like this after returning from the Great Faction War. ‘If it hadn’t been for the Fire King, I would have gone to the Nine Springs instead of returning to Nanman.’ I had completely forgotten those words after his death, but they have finally come back to me.”

“My ancestor destroyed the Five Poisons Sect alongside the Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan at the time. If it hadn’t been for him, our tribe would not have survived to this day. I support him as well.”
Still water began to flow.
Chieftains who had sat in silence rose with the current, one after another, and spoke. Soon more of them were standing than seated.
Then the last person—the one who would put an end to this—finally appeared.
Rumble, rumble—boom!
A giant eight cheok tall lifted the stone gate, heavy as a thousand geun, with one hand.
The Beast Miao King cast a long, enormous shadow across the hall. He spoke in a low voice.
“Looks like a conclusion has been reached.”
At the end of his gaze, Baeksang slowly rose and offered him a cool, formal salute.
“I greet you, Palace Lord.”
“Unless my eyes and ears deceive me, he seems more than qualified. Don’t you agree, little brother?”
“It is the wrong choice. You are breaking the rules of a Tribal Grand Council with a long and venerable tradition.”
“More than half the chieftains have agreed to his attendance. Scholars in the Central Plains call that a consensus.”
Baeksang closed his eyes instead of answering. The Beast Miao King did not wait.

“I, Yayul Cheok, Great Chieftain of the Miao people and Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, permit Jin Taekyung—Fire Dragon Pavilion Master of the Murim Alliance and successor to the Fire Gate Clan—to attend the Tribal Grand Council.”
At that moment, a clear bell sounded in my ears.
Ding.
System Quest: Tribal Grand Council has been created!
Somewhere damp and sweltering.
In a darkness that lay somewhere between pitch-black and the abyss, voices no one could hear passed back and forth.
—The grand council has begun in the Inner Palace.
—And him?
—He attended as well. But...
—Go on. Don’t hesitate.
—Th-that is...
A moment’s hesitation.
The man sending the Sound Transmission could never have guessed it would cost him his life.
Swish. Slice.

—Jin Taekyung. Jin Taekyung attended the grand council.
—Who? Jin Taekyung?
—Yes! Apparently he gained permission with the support of the Beast Miao King and the other chieftains.
After a moment’s silence, someone in the darkness clicked their tongue.
—Those barbarian bastards... And you? You just stood there and watched?
—W-what?

sentences.text: Rumble!
The stone gate descended behind me with a heavy rumble.
Inside the spacious main hall, illuminated by spreading lamplight, thirty-one pairs of eyes flew toward my face like arrows and lodged there amid a silence in which no one spoke.
What are you doing coming out of there?
That was the look they gave me.
But it held more surprise than hostility toward a Han Chinese man, and several chieftains even looked pleased to see me.
Of course, there was one absolute exception.
“One of two things must be true.
Either my eyes deceive me, or the rules of the Tribal Grand Council have changed without anyone—including me—knowing.”
The middle-aged man who broke the silence was Baeksang, the Great Chieftain of the Bai people.
He continued in a cold voice.
“Explain why you’ve brought a mere Han Chinese man here.
He is neither a chieftain nor a Nanman.”
Baeksang wasn’t asking the Beast Miao King, who had yet to arrive.
He wasn’t asking me, either.
Yayul Mok stood to my right.
He answered calmly.
“Because he has the right to be here.”
“The right.”
Baeksang repeated the words under his breath.
“That sounds like the rash judgment of a brat who isn’t even thirty.”
“It is also the judgment of someone else who has yet to arrive.”
“My father.
No—the Palace Lord said he has the right to attend the Tribal Grand Council.”
Baeksang’s eyes darkened.
After a moment’s silence, he asked, “Why hasn’t the Palace Lord come?”
“He’ll be here soon.
By then, there will be only one empty seat left.”
“Unacceptable.”
Baeksang tapped the table with a finger pierced by a nail.
“The Tribal Grand Council is a solemn gathering where the chieftains representing all of Nanman come together to exchange their views.
If one is not a chieftain, no one may take a seat here except the Young Palace Lord.
This man’s qualification is merely the will of the Palace Lord alone.
We will not permit it.”
I watched for a moment, then muttered, “That’s funny.
Isn’t that just your opinion?”
I was clearly talking to myself, but none of the chieftains gathered here were so lacking in martial arts that they couldn’t hear me.
That went without saying for Baeksang, whose martial arts were particularly formidable.
He turned a cold gaze on me.
“What did you say?”
“Oh, you heard me?”
“Did you think I wouldn’t?”
“No.
I said it so you would.
Glad you caught that.”
I shrugged at his frozen expression.
“Since the subject has come up, let me say this.
We may call ourselves ‘we,’ but isn’t this ultimately just your personal opinion as well?
You haven’t even asked what the other chieftains think, yet you say you won’t permit it.
What exactly are we supposed to do with that?”
As my words continued to flow smoothly, I could feel an invisible stir spreading among the seated chieftains.
Baeksang was the Great Chieftain of the Bai people, the most powerful tribe in Nanman after the Miao people, as well as a Supreme Peak master who represented Nanman alongside the Beast Miao King.
I doubted anyone had ever dared speak to him so openly.
Anyone but me.
“When Great Hero Yayul sent me ahead, he told me this: ‘Yayul Cheok, Great Chieftain of the Miao people, recognizes your right to attend.
But Yayul Cheok, Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, cannot decide this alone.
Gain the other chieftains’ consent.’”
Nanman was hardly a welcoming place for outsiders.
Even breathing here felt like a privilege.
And the Tribal Grand Council, held once a year, was so rigid a needle couldn’t slip through its rules.
If the Beast Miao King hadn’t done me this favor, they’d have stopped me at the door.
His help had gotten me past those rules.
Now I intended to claim a seat—by winning the other chieftains’ support.
“So that’s what I’d like to ask.”
I met their eyes one by one.
“What do the rest of you think?”
Fwoosh.
A breeze from somewhere made the torches flicker.
In their reddish light, some faces tightened with discomfort, others looked troubled, and more than I’d expected looked receptive.
Including the middle-aged chieftain who had just opened his mouth.
“Everyone here, including my Zang people, knows what happened at Ailao Mountain last night.”
From what I’d seen and heard in Nanman, the Zang people weren’t one of its four great tribes, but they had enough strength to stand just behind them.
The man who appeared to lead them continued slowly.
“An unexpected disaster cost us much blood.
Swift action kept the loss from becoming greater.
We owe that to our wise Palace Lord, Great Chieftain Yayul, and to a young Han Chinese man who helped him.”
His strong voice carried through the hall.
He watched the other chieftains’ expressions shift, then turned to me with a faint smile.
“It’s late, but I want to thank you here.
Because of your help, twenty-two brave, fine warriors of the Zang people are alive.
One of them is my own kin.”
“Ah.”
Around two hundred warriors had been dragged into the Poisonblood Grounds.
I hadn’t learned all their names or who they were.
I hadn’t known, and couldn’t have known.
But what I’d done last night was coming back to me now as goodwill and gratitude.
“On behalf of the Zang people, I welcome Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung to the Tribal Grand Council.”
He finished with a respectful salute—not one from the land where he’d been born and raised, but a cupped-fist salute from the Central Plains.
And that was only the beginning.
Scrape.
Scrape.
Unfamiliar chieftains rose one after another.
Their faces and clothing differed, but they spoke with the same goodwill.
“We can’t accept a kindness and pretend it never happened.
The Hui people support his attendance.”
“The Man people have no objection.
I only wish to thank him for saving my good-for-nothing son.”
Each of them ruled a tribe, large or small.
But they were also heads of families.
Fathers and mothers with children they loved.
One by one, they offered me their thanks with painfully awkward cupped-fist salutes.
The warriors I’d rescued from the Poisonblood Grounds last night were their people.
Their families.
Not everyone who supported me was doing it because of last night’s rescue, though.
“The Bouyei people also support him.
He is more than qualified.”
At the words of the middle-aged female chieftain, one of the chieftains who still had not risen from his seat frowned.
“Wait.
What reason do the Bouyei people have?
None of your warriors were stationed at Ailao Mountain, were they?”
“Nanman is my homeland.”
“What does that have to—”
“Even beasts that cannot speak repay a kindness.
Blazing Flame Divine Dragon Jin Taekyung risked his life fighting for my homeland last night.
Isn’t that reason enough to let him attend?”
“...Ahem.”
The chieftain who had questioned her fell silent after an uncomfortable cough.
Warm smiles appeared on other faces.
And amid this atmosphere, so clearly different from the one only a few days ago, I felt a tickle in one corner of my chest.
Repaying someone who helped you.
It should be the most natural thing in the world.
But sometimes, in this world, it wasn’t.
I hadn’t gone into the Poisonblood Grounds looking for repayment.
Yet here the chieftains were, giving me their gratitude and trust.
Some because I’d helped them last night.
Others because of something that had happened long ago.
“My late father, who was once a Great Chieftain, often said things like this after returning from the Great Faction War.

‘If it hadn’t been for the Fire King, I would have gone to the Nine Springs instead of returning to Nanman.’ I had completely forgotten those words after his death, but they have finally come back to me.”
“My ancestor destroyed the Five Poisons Sect alongside the Sect Leader of the Fire Gate Clan at the time.
If it hadn’t been for him, our tribe would not have survived to this day.
I support him as well.”
Still water began to flow.
Chieftains who had sat in silence rose with the current, one after another, and spoke.
Soon more of them were standing than seated.
Then the last person—the one who would put an end to this—finally appeared.
Rumble, rumble—boom!
A giant eight cheok tall lifted the stone gate, heavy as a thousand geun, with one hand.
The Beast Miao King cast a long, enormous shadow across the hall.
He spoke in a low voice.
“Looks like a conclusion has been reached.”
At the end of his gaze, Baeksang slowly rose and offered him a cool, formal salute.
“I greet you, Palace Lord.”
“Unless my eyes and ears deceive me, he seems more than qualified.
Don’t you agree, little brother?”
“It is the wrong choice.
You are breaking the rules of a Tribal Grand Council with a long and venerable tradition.”
“More than half the chieftains have agreed to his attendance.
Scholars in the Central Plains call that a consensus.”
Baeksang closed his eyes instead of answering.
The Beast Miao King did not wait.

“I, Yayul Cheok, Great Chieftain of the Miao people and Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, permit Jin Taekyung—Fire Dragon Pavilion Master of the Murim Alliance and successor to the Fire Gate Clan—to attend the Tribal Grand Council.”
At that moment, a clear bell sounded in my ears.
Ding.

chapters.title: Chapter 644
paragraphs: Ding. Ding. Ding.

System A new Quest, Tribal Grand Council, has been created! Quest Tribal Grand Council You have become the first outsider in the history of the Nanman Beast Palace to earn the right to attend the Tribal Grand Council. This is an achievement that even the Fire Gate Clan’s fifth Sect Leader failed to accomplish. Why? Because he destroyed the Five Poisons Sect and left before the council could even begin! At this momentous meeting, where the major and minor affairs of Nanman will be decided, you must achieve the best possible result you can right now! Grade: Supreme Peak Restriction: Jin Taekyung Mission: Nanman Beast Palace’s entry into the alliance (Incomplete) Reward: ??? Failure: ???
I stared at the Quest window and sighed inwardly.
Public opinion might have turned in my favor, but getting the Nanman Beast Palace to join the alliance? That was every bit as tough as the Quest’s Supreme Peak Grade suggested.
And what was that bit about the fifth Sect Leader...?
That was the Fire Gate Clan for you.

A venerable sect of thugs, passed down from one person to the next for hundreds of years. I’d heard that some of its Sect Leaders had lived long lives in seclusion, while others had gone out into Murim, burned like flames, and died young. But every last one of them had been a monster whose might placed him among the top five in the world.
That’s probably one reason I’m allowed to sit here.
It might have been over two hundred years ago, but the Nanman Beast Palace and the Fire Gate Clan had a fairly close connection.
By K-Murim logic, it was basically a sect founded by Grandfather Dangun’s best friend.
The problem was, I had a talent for beating people up and none whatsoever for persuading them.
Still, I have to do my best.
I straightened my back and looked around at the thirty-two chieftains seated at the table.

The Beast Miao King occupied the seat of honor. To his left and right sat the great chieftains Baeksang, Yohi, and Heugung, in that order. The others seemed to have been seated without regard to the strength of their tribes.
There weren’t many of them, but each chieftain commanded anywhere from several hundred to tens of thousands of tribespeople. In that sense, this gathering was Nanman itself.
As I studied their faces, the Beast Miao King broke the brief silence.
“Well, then.”
His expression was solemn, his gaze dignified. The moment he opened his mouth, the air in the hall drew taut as a bowstring.
Radiating all the authority of the master of the Nanman Beast Palace, the Beast Miao King delivered the historic words that would open the council.
“Did everyone eat before coming here?”
“We’ve had some unpleasant things happen lately, but you still shouldn’t skip meals. Chief Jang, you in particular look a little thinner than you did last year.”
Historic, my ass.
What did I just hear?
I was still doubting my ears when Chief Jang—the first to offer me a cupped-fist salute earlier—answered.
“As expected, nothing gets past the Palace Lord’s keen eyes. I have lost a little weight.”
No. He’s actually going along with this?
“I thought so. But a chieftain can’t neglect his health. You have to take care of yourself for your tribespeople’s sake. How old are you again?”
“Sixty.”
“You’re still in the prime of life. Eat more.”
“Jonmyeong.”
Now I was hearing things, too. Jonmyeong sounded like jonmang—“fucked.”
Nanman is fucked.
Was this really the Tribal Grand Council I’d imagined?
I stared at the thirty-two chieftains in disbelief.

These people represented all of Nanman. Yet the Beast Miao King’s opening words had apparently been their cue to start conversations all over the hall that made my spirit shrink just listening to them.
“Chief Gal, I heard the news. Your sixth child had their coming-of-age ceremony?”
“My seventh.”
“I got them mixed up. If only you’d stopped at one or two. I don’t care how vigorous you are—fifteen children?”
“Seventeen.”
“...You definitely had fifteen at last year’s council.”
“We had two more. Twins.”
“Oh.”
On one side, a super-sperm man seemed to be working toward founding a Nanman soccer league.
“Chief Gu. Return the livestock you stole a while ago.”
“What livestock?”
“The fifty-two dairy cows that vanished from the pasture. You think I don’t know your tribespeople took them?”
“I have never done such a thing.”
“Of course you’d say that. Return them while I’m asking nicely.”
“Oh, come on! I’m telling you, we didn’t take them!”
“I said hand over the cows while I’m asking nicely, you cow-udder bastard!”
On another, a furious argument raged over who had stolen all those cows.
“I remember it as if it were yesterday. The day you bastards trespassed on our tribe’s land.”
“Oh, this again? Every damn year. You’re barely forty. Why do you keep bringing up something that happened eighty years ago?”
“Because I inherited the spirits of my ancestors. So give me the land.”
“How does that make sense? Our predecessors settled this!”
“Give me the land.”
“No, seriously...”
“Give me the land.”
Elsewhere, a land ghost insisting he had been reincarnated continued his back-and-forth struggle.
As I watched it all in disbelief, someone’s Sound Transmission reached my ear.
—That’s a funny expression.
I turned my head slightly and met Yohi’s eyes. She was watching me with an amused smile.
—The Tribal Grand Council is always like this. Everyone’s scattered across Nanman and only gets together once a year, so I suppose it’s natural.
I thought for a moment, then answered honestly.
—Even so, this is a complete shitshow.
—The Tribal Grand Council handles all of Nanman’s affairs, major and minor. Minor means the small ones come up, too.
—...That matter is way too small, though.
—How else are thirty-two tribes supposed to live together in harmony? They settle things one by one when everyone’s gathered. It lets them clear up old grudges.
Crash!
“You son of a bitch!”
“Is this bastard out of his mind...?”
“You think your martial arts are that strong? Shut up and come outside.”
The two chieftains arguing over the cows had finally grabbed each other by the collars. Yohi looked at them and added:
—Of course, there are exceptions.
—It’ll be settled soon. The real grand council starts after that.
“Ah, give me the land. I said give it to me.”
“Oh, you Thousand-Year Spider bastard.”
“Come to think of it, a thousand years ago, our ancestors...”
“Stop! Stoooop!”
It’ll be settled soon, she said.
Hmm. I had my doubts.
Are these people really just a bunch of barbarians...?
I kept that thought to myself. But just as Yohi had said, the chaos began to subside, one dispute at a time, and new matters came up.

“Thirty Man warriors were wounded and twenty-two were killed in this year’s ferocious-beast hunt. The beasts seem to have become especially rampant lately, so before the losses grow any larger, we request that the Inner Palace take action...”
“Sudden torrential rain caused a flood. The pasture and around fifty nearby homes were submerged...”
“I report that the dispute between the Huang and Dong tribes has been resolved. Both sides have drawn up an official written agreement and will maintain peace for the next ten years...”
Ferocious-beast hunts. Floods. Tribal disputes.
The appetizers were over. Now the main dishes were coming out.
And among those reports was something that deserved serious attention.
“They say a strange figure has appeared in the northeast.”
A strange figure?
As the question arose in my mind, the Beast Miao King—who until then had merely nodded along with short replies—straightened his posture and spoke.
“A strange figure. This is the first I have heard of it.”
“W-well...”
The chieftain who had raised the matter looked uncertain.
“The information hasn’t been confirmed, so I can’t speak with confidence...”
“Where did it come from?”
“Three days ago, we captured a Han Chinese man who crossed the northeastern border. He told us an unidentified man had appeared out of nowhere and was leaving a trail of blood through Guizhou.”
Guizhou was a border region touching Nanman, along with Sichuan and Guangxi. With a little exaggeration, it was practically close enough to trip and bump your nose against.
But some strange man suddenly appeared in Guizhou?
Something felt off. More than off—it nagged at me. And I wasn’t the only one who sensed there was more to this than the stranger’s unknown identity.
“Tell me more.”
The chieftain swallowed at the sight of the Beast Miao King’s frown.

“Neither his name nor his age is known. They say he’s bald like a monk from the Central Plains and carries a Zen staff. He’s beaten several hundred people to death in Guizhou alone. That’s apparently why they call him the Blood Monk.”
“The Blood Monk?”
“Yes. The Han Chinese man we captured seemed to be a fairly skilled martial artist himself, but he couldn’t hide his fear when he spoke of him.”
The sobriquet was grim enough. Its owner had to possess astonishing martial arts.
Guizhou is orthodox faction territory. The Murim Alliance wouldn’t have just stood by.
Yet the Blood Monk had killed several hundred people and made a name for himself. Without at least Supreme Peak-level martial prowess, that would have been impossible.
It also bothered me that he’d appeared in Guizhou, right beside Nanman.
Could it be...?
An unidentified man appearing at such a strange time. Strong enough to rampage alone through Guizhou, a stronghold of the orthodox faction.

I couldn’t help thinking of Dark Heaven. He might not be a major figure on the Southern Heaven Demon Empress’s level, but the possibility was there. The Blood Lord and the Western Heaven Demon Lord had commanded Supreme Peak masters like the Yin-Yang Twin Ghosts and the Qilian Three Fiends.
And what if the Blood Monk is headed for Nanman?
For the first time, I spoke to the chieftain.
“Do you know where the Blood Monk is going?”
“I wanted to ask him myself, but there’s no way to know now.”
“What do you mean?”
The chieftain shook his head with a faint sigh.
“The man died.”
“What?”

“He died before I could ask anything else. He was badly injured to begin with, and I don’t think he adapted to the sudden change in environment. Then the heavy rain brought a flood, and we couldn’t take proper measures.”
The Blood Monk’s appearance. And the death of our only witness.
Silence settled over the hall. Then someone who had said nothing since the council began spoke up.
“Injury, endemic disease, and death. They happen often enough.”
Everyone turned toward the voice.
Baeksang.

“The Slaughter Saint appearing in the Central Plains is no different. Han Chinese have always been that way. Though they are one people, they’ve kept their world going by killing one another. In short...”
His tone and expression remained perfectly calm. His voice was cold.
“There’s no reason for Nanman to concern itself with affairs in the Central Plains. None at all.”
I did not know whether the thought that came to me then was merely a misunderstanding. But one thing was certain: something about his words felt strange and out of place to me.

Baeksang was the great chieftain of the Bai people, who possessed Nanman’s second-largest faction and the second-largest population. And yet he was trying to ignore an event unfolding right beside him.
I watched him for a moment, then spoke.
“What if the Blood Monk is heading south?”
The chieftains who grasped my meaning widened their eyes. Baeksang answered without a trace of hesitation.
“Nanman isn’t the only place bordering Guizhou. Beyond Guangxi lies the open sea. With a favorable wind, one can sail to Hainan in ten days.”
“So you think it’s unlikely the Blood Monk will enter Nanman?”
“Why would he come all the way here? Rather than face venomous beasts, ferocious beasts, and countless Nanman warriors, he could go through Guangxi to the sea...”
“There is a reason. One clear reason. But...”
I forcefully cut him off before he could continue, fixing Baeksang with a grave, steady gaze as I went on.
“Strangely enough, you seem to be the only one who doesn’t know it.”
“What?”
“Or did you agree with someone to pretend you didn’t know from the start?”
At that moment—
Fwoosh. Whoomph.
The wavering torchlight went out.
In the darkness that fell over the vast hall, a pair of eyes radiated a piercing chill.
“You have finally crossed the line.”
Whoosh!
“Well.”
An immense wave of qi bore down on me from every direction, squeezing my entire body. I spoke calmly.
“I think you’re the one crossing it.”

Minor means the small ones come up, too.
—...That matter is way too small, though.
—How else are thirty-two tribes supposed to live together in harmony?
They settle things one by one when everyone’s gathered.
It lets them clear up old grudges.
Crash!
“You son of a bitch!”
“Is this bastard out of his mind...?”
“You think your martial arts are that strong?
Shut up and come outside.”
The two chieftains arguing over the cows had finally grabbed each other by the collars.
Yohi looked at them and added:
—Of course, there are exceptions.
—It’ll be settled soon.
The real grand council starts after that.
“Ah, give me the land.
I said give it to me.”
“Oh, you Thousand-Year Spider bastard.”
“Come to think of it, a thousand years ago, our ancestors...”
“Stop!
Stoooop!”
It’ll be settled soon, she said.
Hmm.
I had my doubts.
Are these people really just a bunch of barbarians...?
I kept that thought to myself.
But just as Yohi had said, the chaos began to subside, one dispute at a time, and new matters came up.
“Thirty Man warriors were wounded and twenty-two were killed in this year’s ferocious-beast hunt.
The beasts seem to have become especially rampant lately, so before the losses grow any larger, we request that the Inner Palace take action...”
“Sudden torrential rain caused a flood.
The pasture and around fifty nearby homes were submerged...”
“I report that the dispute between the Huang and Dong tribes has been resolved.
Both sides have drawn up an official written agreement and will maintain peace for the next ten years...”
Ferocious-beast hunts.
Floods.
Tribal disputes.
The appetizers were over.
Now the main dishes were coming out.
And among those reports was something that deserved serious attention.
“They say a strange figure has appeared in the northeast.”
A strange figure?
As the question arose in my mind, the Beast Miao King—who until then had merely nodded along with short replies—straightened his posture and spoke.
“A strange figure.
This is the first I have heard of it.”
“W-well...”
The chieftain who had raised the matter looked uncertain.
“The information hasn’t been confirmed, so I can’t speak with confidence...”
“Where did it come from?”
“Three days ago, we captured a Han Chinese man who crossed the northeastern border.
He told us an unidentified man had appeared out of nowhere and was leaving a trail of blood through Guizhou.”
Guizhou was a border region touching Nanman, along with Sichuan and Guangxi.
With a little exaggeration, it was practically close enough to trip and bump your nose against.
But some strange man suddenly appeared in Guizhou?
Something felt off.
More than off—it nagged at me.
And I wasn’t the only one who sensed there was more to this than the stranger’s unknown identity.
“Tell me more.”
The chieftain swallowed at the sight of the Beast Miao King’s frown.
“Neither his name nor his age is known.
They say he’s bald like a monk from the Central Plains and carries a Zen staff.
He’s beaten several hundred people to death in Guizhou alone.
That’s apparently why they call him the Blood Monk.”
“The Blood Monk?”
“Yes.
The Han Chinese man we captured seemed to be a fairly skilled martial artist himself, but he couldn’t hide his fear when he spoke of him.”
The sobriquet was grim enough.
Its owner had to possess astonishing martial arts.
Guizhou is orthodox faction territory.
The Murim Alliance wouldn’t have just stood by.
Yet the Blood Monk had killed several hundred people and made a name for himself.
Without at least Supreme Peak-level martial prowess, that would have been impossible.
It also bothered me that he’d appeared in Guizhou, right beside Nanman.
Could it be...?
An unidentified man appearing at such a strange time.
Strong enough to rampage alone through Guizhou, a stronghold of the orthodox faction.
I couldn’t help thinking of Dark Heaven.
He might not be a major figure on the Southern Heaven Demon Empress’s level, but the possibility was there.
The Blood Lord and the Western Heaven Demon Lord had commanded Supreme Peak masters like the Yin-Yang Twin Ghosts and the Qilian Three Fiends.
And what if the Blood Monk is headed for Nanman?
For the first time, I spoke to the chieftain.
“Do you know where the Blood Monk is going?”
“I wanted to ask him myself, but there’s no way to know now.”
“What do you mean?”
The chieftain shook his head with a faint sigh.
“The man died.”
“What?”
“He died before I could ask anything else.
He was badly injured to begin with, and I don’t think he adapted to the sudden change in environment.
Then the heavy rain brought a flood, and we couldn’t take proper measures.”
The Blood Monk’s appearance.
And the death of our only witness.
Silence settled over the hall.
Then someone who had said nothing since the council began spoke up.
“Injury, endemic disease, and death.
They happen often enough.”
Everyone turned toward the voice.
Baeksang.
“The Slaughter Saint appearing in the Central Plains is no different.
Han Chinese have always been that way.
Though they are one people, they’ve kept their world going by killing one another.
In short...”
His tone and expression remained perfectly calm.
His voice was cold.
“There’s no reason for Nanman to concern itself with affairs in the Central Plains.
None at all.”
I did not know whether the thought that came to me then was merely a misunderstanding.
But one thing was certain: something about his words felt strange and out of place to me.
Baeksang was the great chieftain of the Bai people, who possessed Nanman’s second-largest faction and the second-largest population.
And yet he was trying to ignore an event unfolding right beside him.
I watched him for a moment, then spoke.
“What if the Blood Monk is heading south?”
The chieftains who grasped my meaning widened their eyes.
Baeksang answered without a trace of hesitation.
“Nanman isn’t the only place bordering Guizhou.
Beyond Guangxi lies the open sea.
With a favorable wind, one can sail to Hainan in ten days.”
“So you think it’s unlikely the Blood Monk will enter Nanman?”
“Why would he come all the way here?
Rather than face venomous beasts, ferocious beasts, and countless Nanman warriors, he could go through Guangxi to the sea...”
“There is a reason.
One clear reason.
But...”
I forcefully cut him off before he could continue, fixing Baeksang with a grave, steady gaze as I went on.
“Strangely enough, you seem to be the only one who doesn’t know it.”
“What?”
“Or did you agree with someone to pretend you didn’t know from the start?”
At that moment—
Fwoosh.
Whoomph.
The wavering torchlight went out.
In the darkness that fell over the vast hall, a pair of eyes radiated a piercing chill.
“You have finally crossed the line.”
Whoosh!
“Well.”
An immense wave of qi bore down on me from every direction, squeezing my entire body.
I spoke calmly.
“I think you’re the one crossing it.”

chapters.title: Chapter 645
paragraphs: Who had crossed the line first?
Me? Or Baeksang?
And of the words we’d exchanged, which were true and which were lies?
Questions flashed through my mind, but they no longer mattered. From here on, we would settle the matter as martial artists did: with force.
Whoosh!
A sharp sound cut through the air. Before it reached my ears, I tilted my head aside, dodging the Finger Qi flying toward me. Without hesitation, I planted a hand on the stone table in front of me.
Boom!
The table, carved from a massive boulder, shuddered. Thirty-three wine cups sprang into the air. I reached out and sent several of them toward one person alone.
Tung.
Baeksang.
Whoosh-whoosh-whoosh!
They were crude cups, roughly carved from wood. Filled with the internal energy I’d sent into them, they became deadly weapons—faster than arrows, with enough force to shatter stone.
But Baeksang was calm. More importantly, he was strong.
Whoomph! Slash!
He swept his straightened hand blade sideways. Invisible qi cut across the air and split the cups apart.
Before the fragments could hit the floor, Baeksang surged from his seat. His figure blurred.
Papapat!

White robes fluttered like a ghost through the darkness over the hall. In an instant, he had crossed the stone table and closed the five zhang between us. His fist came down toward the crown of my head.
“You’re crossing the line again.”
I muttered the words and drove my palm upward.
Fwoosh!
Flame Divine Palm.
Flames consumed the darkness and met Baeksang’s fist, which blazed with Force. White and blue energies mingled, bursting into a flash that shook the hall.
Boom! Rumble-rumble!
A descending fist and an upward palm. An old man and a young man. A collision of raw strength.
The impact rocked the hall.
Whoooosh!
Beyond the light exploding from the point where our attacks met, I saw Baeksang’s eyes widen.
Baeksang’s eyes, which had always shone with a cool light, held unmistakable surprise.
How?
I knew the look. Most of the people I’d faced had worn it.

Before my name and sobriquet had begun spreading through the Murim, and even afterward, people sometimes seemed to forget that and underestimate me too soon—because I was young, came from an insignificant family, or was an inexperienced brat who had never experienced war.
Whenever that happened, I kindly set them straight.
Not with words, but with force.
Just like now.
Along with the mutter that never escaped my lips, I drew up the energy filling my entire body even more forcefully.
Whoooosh!

The tremendous internal energy of no less than three jiazi stirred to life and stretched. The terrible heat of my Scorching Yang Qi evaporated the moisture around us, and red heat haze rose into the air.
Tsss-tsss-tsss!
Baeksang’s fist began to give way against my open palm. His trembling eyes flicked from his burning white robes to my calm face.
A cool voice emerged from between his heat-cracked lips.
“You bastard...”
Remarkable composure. Usually, people in his position went straight to fucking bastard, son of a bitch, or crazy bastard.

But whether he had been tempered by a hundred battles or because he was the Great Chieftain leading tens of thousands of tribespeople, Baeksang’s emotions might have surged, but they never overflowed, and his martial prowess was far greater than I had expected.
Swish!
A blackened collar brushed against my forearm. At some point, the fist he had clenched tightly had spread open like an eagle’s talons and shot toward my wrist with lightning speed.
It would have caught me, too, if I hadn’t moved faster and hit harder.
Crack!
I caught his wrist instead and squeezed with strength far beyond human limits. Pain made his brow twitch, and a short groan escaped him.
“Hng!”
I seized the opening.
Now.
I twisted his wrist aside, blocking his other hand and throwing him off balance. Then I drove my free palm into his flank.
Bang!
I released his wrist before the heavy report of the strike reached my ears.
In front of dozens of watching chieftains, Baeksang flew backward. He twisted in midair and landed on the stone table.
Swish.
He touched down so lightly he made no sound. His expression was anything but light.
He fixed me with a heavy stare and started to move again.
“Enough.”
The voice was not loud, but it held a deep resonance and authority. The Beast Miao King had risen from his seat and opened his mouth with a hard expression.
“Stand down. Both of you.”
Baeksang’s figure wavered. I shrugged.
“I didn’t move.”
That was an undeniable fact. I had pulled my chair back a little, but Baeksang had been the one to charge first. I had exchanged moves with him while remaining seated.
And the result? Well, the other chieftains were staring at me as if they’d seen a ghost. Their faces said it all.
“Jin Taekyung.”
I did need to show some propriety. This was Nanman, not my home ground, and Baeksang was the Great Chieftain of the Bai people.
At the Beast Miao King’s reproachful call, I raised both hands.
“I’m sorry. It was a situation where I couldn’t help using my hands. I just acted without thinking.”
I still needed to make that clear. Even if I conceded that I’d started the trouble, Baeksang had used an attack that could have killed me.
Perhaps he understood. The Beast Miao King sighed softly and turned to the other man.
“Baeksang, do not act rashly.”
Conflict flickered through Baeksang’s cold eyes. He kept staring at me without answering the Beast Miao King behind him, then looked around the hall.
More than thirty chieftains watched us. Some shifted in their seats as if ready to rush me. Others fought back smiles. Still others looked half dazed by what they’d just seen.
There were factions within the Nanman Beast Palace. And in front of all of them, Baeksang’s standing and Fame had taken a blow that would not be easily erased.
At the hands of a Han Chinese brat from the Central Plains, no less.
Baeksang knew it. He pressed his lips together and bowed his head to the Beast Miao King.
“I apologize for causing a disturbance. I will see you again after I have calmed my mind.”
Then he left the hall, his scorched robes fluttering behind him.
Yohi rose and followed as if it were the most natural thing in the world. Heugung hurried after them, and nearly half the chieftains got up as well, watching one another for cues.
“Palace Lord, forgive me, but I...”
“L-let’s go together.”
They were probably the pro-Baeksang faction. Unlike the ordinary moderates, they were fiercely opposed to Nanman joining the Murim Alliance.
As roughly half of the thirty-two chieftains filed out, Yayul Mok frowned in anger. The Beast Miao King spoke wearily.
“So it’s finally come to this.”
I glanced at him before speaking.
“I’m sorry. Feels like this happened because of me.”
“Hoo. You have nothing to apologize for. It was bound to happen sooner or later.”
“Oh, good. That’s what I thought, too.”
The remaining chieftains, Yayul Mok, and the Beast Miao King all gave me the same flat look.
—It is because of you, you bastard.
What was that? I must be hearing things. It definitely wasn’t Sound Transmission.
I tilted my head at the strange phenomenon, then asked, “The Tribal Grand Council isn’t over, is it?”
“The Tribal Grand Council runs for three days, alongside the festival. You were told that before you attended.”
“I was. Just checking.”
The Beast Miao King shook his head at my shameless answer.
“Did you really have to take it that far?”
“It felt too suspicious to let it go. I wanted to see his real reaction, too.”

“That curiosity has made enemies of more than ten thousand Bai people. Add Yohi and Heugung, the two Great Chieftains who follow Baeksang, and the others, and it would be no exaggeration to say that half of Nanman is against you.”
Hmm. Half of Nanman.
“That’s not as bad as I expected.”
“What?”
“Two days ago, all of Nanman was against me. I was about to get thrown out before the Tribal Grand Council even started.”
The Beast Miao King gave a hollow laugh and turned to the chieftains who remained.
“Chief Jang. Chief Go.”
“Yes.”
“This time, I will need your help. First, organize a scouting party of fast-moving warriors and have them watch the area toward Guizhou.”
“Because of the Blood Monk?”
The Beast Miao King nodded.
“Both Baeksang and Jin Taekyung have a point. The man has no particular reason to come to Nanman. But if he belongs to Dark Heaven, we should be prepared.”
“We will obey your command, Palace Lord.”
“As you command.”
If the chieftains who had left were Baeksang’s people, most of those still here were loyal to the Beast Miao King or were moderates favorably disposed toward him.
The two chiefs, each the leader of a mid-sized tribe, accepted their orders without protest. The Beast Miao King’s expression eased a little.
“Tonight, we will erect a memorial for those who died and hold a banquet in their honor. The Tribal Grand Council will resume afterward. You may withdraw for now.”
“What happened?”
Namho came rushing over the moment we returned to our quarters.
“You didn’t cause another incident, did you?”
His voice brimmed with suspicion. I was about to answer when Hyuk Mujin burst out indignantly.
“Old man Nam! What do you take our Captain for?”
“What else? A lunatic.”
“Now, now. Even if our Captain is a lunatic, that’s going too far! Do you seriously think he’d cause trouble at a meeting that important?”
“Yes. Easily.”
Is it normal to feel guilty right now?
I hesitated, then opened my mouth. Or tried to.
That was when Ju Hwaran joined in.
“Elder Namho, that’s too harsh. How can you call our Pavilion Master a lunatic?”
If Taishan was the reason Namho was aging so quickly, Ju Hwaran was his one weakness. The man who had been so sure of himself a moment ago scratched his thinning crown.
“Well, I...”

“Our Pavilion Master came here representing the Murim Alliance. He can be a little rough around the edges, but he knows how important it is to secure Nanman’s entry into the alliance. He would never cause a disturbance at the Tribal Grand Council.”
Please kill me.
My conscience had gone past pricking me. It hurt.
Meanwhile, Ju Hwaran was canvassing the others like an enthusiastic campaigner.
“What do you all think? Why isn’t anyone answering?”
The usually quiet Song Ilseom smacked his lips.
“Hmm. Young Bureau Head, perhaps we ought to hear from the man himself first...”
“Extra bonus.”
“On second thought, you’re right. The Pavilion Master would never do such a thing.”
Money-crazed bastard—out.
“Why aren’t the other two saying anything?”
“Taishan. Hungry...”
“I heard there’s a banquet tonight.”
“Taishan. Strongly agrees with Young Lady Ju.”
“...I agree as well.”
Glutton—out. Ex-fiancé I could chew to bits and still not feel satisfied—out.
Her petition gathered signatures with the speed of Quick Attack. Then Ju Hwaran turned eyes sparkling like the Milky Way on me.
“Pavilion Master, say something. So, have you decided to join the alliance?”
One second felt like an hour.
After a long silence, I spoke.
“Um. Everyone. Well. There was... a minor problem.”
Ju Hwaran froze. Namho nodded as if he’d known all along.
“See? Crazy Pavilion Master.”
“Did you kill someone?”
“No.”
“Then you hit someone.”
“Who? Some chieftain who picked a fight without knowing better? Or someone who said something you didn’t like? Surely not the Great Chieftain of the Bai people.”
“Ah.”
“Pavilion Master?”
“...Pavilion Master?”
As Ju Hwaran’s voice grew faint, I kept my mouth shut and stared toward a distant mountain.
Namho chuckled.
“See? Crazy bastard.”
