Ex-fiancé I could chew to bits and still not feel satisfied—out.
Her petition gathered signatures with the speed of Quick Attack.
Then Ju Hwaran turned eyes sparkling like the Milky Way on me.
“Pavilion Master, say something.
So, have you decided to join the alliance?”
One second felt like an hour.
After a long silence, I spoke.
“Um.
Everyone.
Well.
There was... a minor problem.”
Ju Hwaran froze.
Namho nodded as if he’d known all along.
“See?
Crazy Pavilion Master.”
“Did you kill someone?”
“No.”
“Then you hit someone.”
“Who?
Some chieftain who picked a fight without knowing better?
Or someone who said something you didn’t like?
Surely not the Great Chieftain of the Bai people.”
“Ah.”
“Pavilion Master?”
“...Pavilion Master?”
As Ju Hwaran’s voice grew faint, I kept my mouth shut and stared toward a distant mountain.
Namho chuckled.
“See?
Crazy bastard.”

chapters.title: Chapter 646
paragraphs: If this continued, I was liable to be branded a traitor guilty of high treason, so in the end, I had to explain everything that had happened at the Tribal Grand Council from beginning to end.
And answer every question that came up along the way.
“More than half the chieftains accepted you?”
“Yes. They even gave me cupped-fist salutes. Thanked me for saving their tribespeople and families.”

“My goodness. You were gone so long that I had a feeling something had happened... But an outsider—especially a Han Chinese person—attending the Tribal Grand Council must be a first in Nanman’s history. No, in Murim history.”
At Ju Hwaran’s surprise, Namho, who stood beside her, added with a warm smile.
“Of course it’s a first. An outsider attending the Tribal Grand Council was a first, and that outsider getting into a fight with the Great Chieftain of the Bai people was a first too. Yes, indeed.”
“Hoho. I’m laughing because I’m so very proud and happy. Don’t mind me. Go on.”
It was hard not to mind him, but I went on.
“Anyway, the council started, and...”
Ju Hwaran’s eyes widened as she listened.
“The Blood Monk?”

“Yes. Apparently, he’s rampaging through Guizhou right now. I heard he’s already beaten several hundred people to death and is running wild. This was the first time I’d heard that sobriquet, so I was wondering if Young Lady Ju had ever heard of him.”

The Yongbong Escort Bureau was based in Sichuan, which bordered Guizhou to the southeast. And though the bureau’s fortunes had declined for a time, it had once been among the foremost Escort Bureaus in the world. Its intelligence network was considerable.
Young Lady Ju might know something.
But my hopes faded when I told her what little I knew about the Blood Monk and she shook her head.
“I’m sorry. A few sobriquets vaguely come to mind, but none of them belonged to a master of that caliber. Besides, there’s no specific sketch or description of his appearance.”
“Hmm. I see.”
I was a little disappointed, but I tried not to show it. As she’d said, picking one man out from a handful of characteristics, without even a proper description of his face, was difficult.
All I’d been able to tell her was that he was probably middle-aged, his martial arts were likely at the Supreme Peak level, and his signature weapon was a Zen staff.
Murim’s a big place.

Not just in terms of land. There were plenty of people, too. Men with cheap swords made of scrap iron gave themselves names like Soaring Dragon Guest and Sword Demon, then strutted around as if they were somebody.
I might as well search an endless beach for one grain of sand.
I was smacking my lips when Ju Hwaran, who still looked apologetic, seemed to remember something.
“Oh, but Captain Song would know more about this than I would. Wouldn’t you, Captain Song?”
Oh. Right.
Every eye in the room, including mine, turned toward Song Ilseom. As usual, he’d been keeping quiet.
“Hmm. I don’t know.”
Like hell you don’t.
I’d figured him out by now. I tossed him a silver nyang.
“Hey, Soul-Chasing Guest. If you know something, let’s hear it.”

He might call himself a mere escort these days, but Song Ilseom was a martial arts prodigy of Guangdong Chen Family blood. At a startlingly young age, he’d won more than a hundred life-and-death duels and become a legend among wandering martial artists.
In some ways, there were few professions more sensitive to people and rumors than wandering martial artists. Their lives could depend on it from one day to the next.
Clack.
Song Ilseom snatched the silver out of the air and frowned.
“You think I’m obsessed with money?”
“Yes.”
“So, you don’t like it?”
“I don’t dislike it.”
“What if I give you more?”
“I’d like that even better.”
“Here. Have some more silver, you money-crazed bastard.”
Whoosh. Clack.
“...Somehow, this feels even worse.”
Having secured a generous bonus, Song Ilseom began, looking vaguely uncomfortable. “Middle-aged, and he uses a Zen staff?”
“Yeah. Steel, from what I heard.”
“What does he look like?”
“I don’t know much beyond the bald head and lack of a beard. The survivor who made it all the way to Nanman died after telling them that much.”
“A complete mess, then. Still, three people come to mind. Not many martial artists use a Zen staff as their signature weapon.”
“Oh, three?”
“There’s just one problem...”
“That’s fine. Tell me.”
With all of us watching him expectantly, Song Ilseom spoke.
“He’s dead.”
“Huh?”
“More precisely, I killed him. Took a commission and happened to meet him on a battlefield.”
“Hmm... Well, that happens. What about the other two?”
“What do you mean, the other two?”
“You just said you killed one.”
“I killed all three.”
“Two on battlefields, one in a life-and-death duel. The last was the strongest.”
A heavy silence fell. Then Namho muttered what everyone was thinking.
“So there’s another crazy bastard.”
I didn’t know who the other crazy bastard was supposed to be, but I couldn’t agree more.
I glared at Song Ilseom, who stood there blankly. Should I take back the silver first and then beat him up? Or beat him up first and then take back the silver?
That was when I noticed someone else giving him a look of utter contempt.
“Hey, unorthodox grunt.”
“...Unorthodox grunt?”
“Yeah. Know anything?”
Sama Pyo, Young Sect Leader of the Black Dragon Demon Gate—the most powerful unorthodox faction in the world today, and self-proclaimed ruler of Gansu—knitted his brows.

“I have three things to say. First, I am not an unorthodox grunt. Second, Gansu and Guizhou are nearly a thousand li apart, so travel between them is difficult. And third, why would you think I’d know?”
“Because you’re part of the unorthodox faction.”
“Bad guys all know each other, don’t they?”
“Well, maybe not.”
I waved a hand at Sama Pyo, who had gone stiff as a statue, and turned to the other, enormous unorthodox grunt beside him.
Before I could say a word, I got a booming answer.
Grrrrowl. Grrrrrrrrowl.
What the fuck?
This wasn’t the World Cup final, yet a vuvuzela was blaring in the middle of Nanman. Namho burst out laughing.
“Hoho! That bastard. If only I’d learned martial arts, I’d cut that goddamn belly open. Hahaha!”
Given how much he’d been laughing, he seemed about halfway out of his mind. Hyuk Mujin stared at him in fear, then turned to me.
“Captain.”
“Head to the floor.”
“What?”
“Ah, sorry. That was just a habit. But if you start talking nonsense like the others in this situation, I’ll kill you.”
“No, that’s not it. This Blood Monk or whatever he’s called... Isn’t there too little information about him for a martial artist?”
It was the most sensible thing anyone had said since Ju Hwaran spoke. I scratched the back of my head in frustration and smacked my lips.
“That’s true. How fucking old is he, anyway? How is there not a single person who knows him?”
Namho, who’d been shooting Taishan a murderous glare, cut in.

“Speaking as someone who’s old enough to know, I’ve never heard of him either. There was a fiend called the Killing Buddha during the Great Faction War, but he doesn’t sound much like this Blood Monk. The man was ancient even then. I doubt he’s still alive.”
If Namho had been just some old man from another tribe, that might not have meant much. But he’d held a fairly important post in the Hidden Shadow Pavilion. Chances were he was right.
Then who the hell is this guy? He sounds like some hidden master.
If even Namho, a man from the distant past, and the Fire Dragon Pavilion members of the current generation had never heard of him, then he was truly a freak.
But what mattered most wasn’t the Blood Monk’s identity. It was who stood behind him—and what he wanted.
Namho tapped his knees, as if he’d read my mind.
“We can’t be sure yet, but there’s a strong chance Dark Heaven is behind the Blood Monk.”
“I agree. I said as much at the Tribal Grand Council.”
“What do the Beast Miao King and the other chieftains think?”
“We decided to send some scouts and warriors toward Guizhou first, but before that... Baeksang’s reaction bothered me.”
“He told you not to concern yourselves with affairs in the Central Plains, I suppose.”
“Huh?”

“He’s done it often enough. Ever since the Great Faction War, Baeksang has bristled at anything to do with the Central Plains. Even the few trade routes Nanman had were closed after the Bai people and several other tribes opposed them. What I wonder now is...”
Namho sighed quietly before continuing.
“Does his hostility come from the grief of losing his only child in a war between Han Chinese? Or did something that happened then leave him with a grudge against the orthodox faction?”
“Hmm.”
“If it’s the former, it may end with a bereaved father’s resentment. But if it’s the latter...”
Ju Hwaran, who had been listening in silence, murmured, “Betrayal. Enough to put all of Nanman in danger.”
“Yes. If he’s joined hands with Dark Heaven, this could spiral beyond anyone’s control.”
An enemy within was more dangerous than one outside. Even an impregnable fortress was no better than a sandcastle in the surf if it crumbled from the inside.
And if the traitor was the Great Chieftain who, alongside the Beast Miao King, held sway over half of Nanman—
We’re finished.
I had to uncover the plot taking shape inside Nanman and stop it. I also had to find out where the Blood Monk was headed as he made his way onward from distant Guizhou.
But even the System that had brought me from an F-rank Hunter to where I stood now couldn’t split me in two.
In that case...
I raised my head and slowly looked over everyone around me.
I recalled their martial arts, characteristics, and personalities one by one as I considered who was best suited for the task. Who could return alive from an unknown danger?
I was deep in thought, with no end to it in sight, when someone spoke.
“I’ll go.”
“Please send me. I will complete the mission and return without fail.”
I was startled twice: first that she’d understood what I was thinking without a word from me, and then that the person who’d spoken was Ju Hwaran.
My answer came out as if I’d settled on it from the start.
“No.”
“Why? Do you think that old monster, the Blood Monk, will hurt me?”
“That’s...”
“My martial arts may be meager compared to yours, Pavilion Master, but I believe I am strong enough to protect myself.”
“Young Lady Ju.”

“I know what you’re worried about. Of course I couldn’t take on the Blood Monk. But warriors handpicked by the Nanman Beast Palace will be with us, and some of our members will come, too. Tell me if I’m wrong.”
I pressed my lips together instead of answering. She wasn’t wrong.

I’d planned to send some Fire Dragon Pavilion members with the scouting party that would soon depart. They would find out who the Blood Monk was and what he wanted, and I’d accounted for the possibility of a fight.
What I hadn’t considered was Ju Hwaran volunteering.
“Pavilion Master. No—Benefactor.”
Benefactor.
That was what she’d first called me months ago, just after we’d settled the Yongbong Escort Bureau’s affairs in Sichuan.
For a moment, I could almost smell the flowers in the Fire Courtyard, where we’d taken our last walk before leaving. The eyes that had been wet beneath the moonlight then now shone with firm resolve.
“Please send me. Send me.”
“I can do it.”
A thought came to me.
I would never be able to refuse a request made with those eyes and that voice. Not now, not ever.
Whew.
The wind was hot. My mouth tasted bitter.
I let out a small sigh and finally nodded.
Ju Hwaran’s face lit up. In the distance, music announcing the start of the banquet was already playing.

chapters.title: Chapter 647
paragraphs: The banquet was being held in a large training ground inside the Inner Palace.
The place was large enough to accommodate more than a thousand warriors. Every kind of delicacy had been laid out, and the grounds were packed with people, including the tribal chieftains.
And at the most honored seat in the training ground, someone was waiting for me.
“You’ve arrived.”
The Beast Miao King spotted me from his high-backed chair adorned with tiger skin and beckoned me over.
“Come sit. I had a place prepared for you.”
The seat assigned to me was directly beside the Beast Miao King, on his left.
It was exceptional treatment for an outsider, but given my status and what I’d done the previous night, it wasn’t all that strange.
That didn’t mean every member of the Fire Dragon Pavilion was getting the same treatment, of course.
“I’ve prepared places for all of you at this banquet as well. Eat, drink, and enjoy your—”
“Taishan! Meat!”
Grab! Chomp, chomp, chomp!
Taishan swept up the meat on the table in front of him. The Beast Miao King stared at me, baffled.
“...What in the world is that fellow?”
“...He’s just insane. Don’t pay him too much attention.”

At a glance from me, Taishan’s mom—no, Sama Pyo—let out a long sigh, grabbed Taishan, and dragged him away. Namho, who’d been watching for an opening like an assassin, snatched up a nearby wine bottle and smashed it against the top of Taishan’s head.
Crash!
Water Style without any water...?
He’d really put his back into that one.
But Taishan drank from the fountain of wine bursting over his head and cried out happily.
“Namho! Thank you! Taishan was thirsty!”
“Die. Please, just die...!”
The Beast Miao King watched them, then turned an uneasy look on me.
“Hmm. Your subordinates get along well.”
“They do. So well that one could die and the other wouldn’t notice.”
“Is that why you didn’t send them?”
I paused before answering. “You heard about that? News travels fast.”
“I don’t involve myself in every matter, but I hear about them all. That is the position of Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace.”
He had a point. Since outsiders had joined the scouts, it wouldn’t have been strange for a report to have already reached him through the great chieftains.
I thought of the three people who should be heading somewhere northeast by now and muttered inwardly.
Will they be all right?
After a great deal of thought, I’d chosen three people: Ju Hwaran, Song Ilseom, and Hyuk Mujin.
Regardless of my concerns, Ju Hwaran possessed exceptional martial prowess and experience compared to other young prodigies. Song Ilseom needed no explanation, and the last member, Hyuk Mujin, was...
Whatever else you could say about him, the man has the survival instincts of a cockroach.
Despite how he looked, Hyuk Mujin had survived countless battlefields alongside me, from Shanxi Province to the present day, escaping death at every turn.
He was so good at wriggling his way out of danger that Jeok Cheongang had once said,
How has someone so weak and cowardly survived this long?
I’d answered:
Because he’s weak and cowardly.
It was true that Hyuk Mujin’s martial arts fell short of the others’. Calling him cowardly wasn’t wrong, either.
But you could also call it caution.
He has an uncanny knack for avoiding the worst danger. And when he can’t avoid it, he fights for his life.
No wonder he always came back alive. I might as well change his nickname to Hyukroach.
“They’ll do well. No matter what happens.”
I muttered that with a personal wish behind it, then glanced over the Beast Miao King’s shoulder.
“By the way, there are a lot of empty seats for a banquet that’s already started.”
“They’ll be here soon.”
He said it casually, but the Beast Miao King’s eyes had grown heavy and dark. This was especially true whenever he looked at the empty seat directly to his right.
Baeksang.
The chieftains who had left the main hall following him were already seated, but Baeksang, Yohi, and Heugung had yet to return.
The Beast Miao King stared at their empty seats for a while before silently tilting the wine bottle.
Drip.
The sun had long since set behind the western mountains, yet the Nanman Beast Palace glowed against the darkness. Festivities were taking place everywhere.

The Tribal Grand Council, held only once a year, was also an occasion for unity, and the countless tribespeople who had poured into the streets were laughing and talking with bright faces as they enjoyed themselves.
Or, at least, they probably were. I couldn’t see them from here, but the cheers and firecracker explosions drifting over from the Outer Palace were more than enough to tell me.
Whoosh! Boom!
Waaaaaaah!
If I only listened to the noise, I would have thought it was at least a Samba Festival.
“So, um... Is this really okay?”
“What do you mean?”
“You know. Everyone seems to have amnesia. They all know what happened at Ailao Mountain barely a day ago.”
He didn’t seem concerned. “They do. That’s why the festival is even grander.”
“Because of that?”

“Yes. Every one of them was a brave warrior who fought and died for Nanman. So they believe that each of them has returned to the arms of the god their tribe worships. Though they died in this world, they believe they were reborn as warriors of their god.”
I’d heard something like that before.
It brought to mind the Middle Eastern terrorist group I’d beaten up before logging in.
They aren’t Crusaders or ancient Vikings.
All kinds of superstitions ran rampant in the Central Plains as well, but Nanman was clearly different. Perhaps it was because so many indigenous faiths existed here.
As someone born and raised in the twenty-first century, though, I couldn’t understand it.
“Do you believe that too, Great Hero Yayul?”
At my question, the Beast Miao King, who had been about to raise his wine cup, let out a short laugh.
“Interesting.”
“What is?”
“Isn’t it only natural? You asked that question of an old Miao man born and raised in Nanman—and of the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, at that.”
“Oh.”
“But that isn’t why I laughed. It reminded me that someone else asked me the same thing a very long time ago.”
I had a pretty good idea who. “My Old Master—no, my master?”
“Old Jeok? No. He had no interest in whether the local gods existed. He did tell me to call him if those Demonic Cult bastards ever set Nanman on fire. He said he’d gladly come help, at least once.”
That old man hated leaving home, yet he’d volunteered to travel here for some killing. His grudge over Mount Jiuhua must have gone right down to the bone.
I nodded reflexively. “Then who asked you?”
His answer was simple, clear, and baffling.
“God.”
“Sorry? What?”
As I stood there, momentarily dumbfounded by the incomprehensible answer, the Beast Miao King continued while stroking his full wine cup.

“The Martial God. Someone whose name, age, and even face are not properly known. A divine man who was born human and became something beyond humanity. That person asked me whether I truly believed my god existed.”
“So I answered, ‘Honestly, I don’t know. But I think I’m looking at one right now.’”
The crescent moon reflected in his wine cup rippled. The Beast Miao King downed the wine and moon together, then burst into laughter.

“It was a foolish answer, but what else could I say? That day, the Martial God single-handedly defeated five fiends who had reached the Supreme Peak realm and five hundred members of the Blood Ghost Squad. When I first met him, he had a snow-white beard that fluttered like an immortal’s. At our second and final meeting, he looked like a young boy.”
“More than fifty years have passed, but I still remember that day as clearly as ever.”
I listened with my mouth hanging open, unable to speak.
The Blood Ghost Squad. I knew the name. It came up whenever Jeok Cheongang launched into one of his “back in my day” stories.

The Blood Ghost Squad had been the Demonic Cult’s premier strike force, sweeping across the Central Plains at the head of a hundred thousand demonic troops. Every single member was said to have been a Peak master.
Five hundred Peak masters. And five fiends at the Supreme Peak realm on top of that.
The Martial God had wiped out that entire force alone.
Even coming from the Beast Miao King, I would have dismissed the story as nonsense if not for those two words: Martial God.
...Just how powerful was he?
Jeok Cheongang. Mungyeong. Mae Jonghak. And others.
I had heard stories about the Martial God until my ears bled from people who deserved to be called giants in the long history of the Murim.
And yet I still didn’t know. What kind of realm had that master reached? No—was he even human at all?
And why had someone so extraordinary suddenly vanished without a trace? Where was he now, and what was he doing?
One thought led to another. Then, without warning, someone’s name came to mind.
...Wait.
The fingers tapping against the table stopped dead.
My eyes flew open, but they were not looking at the banquet hall before me. Nor were they looking at the Murim.
They were looking beyond the hot, heavy air blowing in from far away—beyond some unknown realm that could not be explained in words—to another world and the person who existed there.
Cheon Taemin.
The savior who’d rescued humanity from the Demon King Asmodeus. An immortal legend, called a living god by his followers.
A man who had one day been cut off from the world and fallen into a deep sleep.
I knew exactly why I’d thought of him.
He’s like the Martial God.

It could have been a coincidence, but they had too much in common to dismiss it so easily. The Martial God’s exploits in the Great Faction War and Cheon Taemin’s in the Great Cataclysm—even their actions immediately afterward.
No way. No. No, that’s impossible.
I couldn’t follow the thought any further. The musicians had stopped playing, the dancers had stopped moving, and every eye was on the man climbing the stairs.
“Welcome, little brother.”
Baeksang, flanked by great chieftains as though he were the Palace Lord himself, answered the Beast Miao King’s greeting.
“I’m late, Palace Lord.”
I came out of my thoughts and finally met his gaze, cold enough to freeze everything around him.
The banquet has begun.
Security in the Outer Palace has been reinforced.
About two hundred elite warriors from the Inner Palace are moving through the North Gate.
As the Sound Transmissions from her subordinates pierced the darkness one after another, someone buried in the shadows rose from her seat.
Final report. What is the target?

The Blood Monk of Guizhou. The targets are moving for reconnaissance and possible combat. At Jin Taekyung’s order, the group includes Ju Hwaran, the Young Bureau Head of the Yongbong Escort Bureau; Song Ilseom, the Soul-Chasing Guest; and Hyuk Mujin of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
It would have been surprising for anyone to know Song Ilseom’s past, known to only a select few. Not for the shadow and her subordinates.
“Ha.”
After letting out a quiet laugh, the shadow turned around in one smooth motion.
Snap.
Fingers struck together in the darkness. A strand of flame sprang up, casting light around it.
Fwoosh.
The flame was a dark, ominous reddish brown. Watching it flicker, the Southern Heaven Demon Empress smiled.

Despite how he looked, Hyuk Mujin had survived countless battlefields alongside me, from Shanxi Province to the present day, escaping death at every turn.
He was so good at wriggling his way out of danger that Jeok Cheongang had once said,

Because he’s weak and cowardly.
It was true that Hyuk Mujin’s martial arts fell short of the others’.
Calling him cowardly wasn’t wrong, either.

chapters.title: Chapter 648
paragraphs: It was as though the world had stopped.
The music cut off all at once, as if on cue. People froze in place.
In the sudden silence, the Beast Miao King spoke, breaking Baeksang’s cold stare.
“Little brother, take your seat.”
Baeksang’s gaze slowly left me. Perhaps he had changed in the meantime; his sleeves were now snow-white as he resumed his climb.
“Very well.”
Step. Step.

His clothes were neat and his voice calm, just as they had been in the main hall, as though nothing had happened. He climbed the stairs with two great chieftains flanking him, and bitterness seemed to cloud the Beast Miao King’s eyes as he watched.
I suppose that’s understandable.
One called him little brother. The other answered, “Palace Lord.”
They weren’t related by blood, but I’d heard they had grown up together as sworn brothers. Yet I had never once heard Baeksang call the Beast Miao King hyung.
A thought occurred to me.
What was the Beast Miao King to Baeksang?
A sworn elder brother he still felt some affection for?
Or merely the Palace Lord of the Nanman Beast Palace, someone above him in the hierarchy?
Or perhaps...
An enemy whose involvement in the Great Faction War had cost him his only son?
I didn’t know. But I had a feeling I would find out soon enough, one way or another.
I hoped it would go well. The Beast Miao King seemed to hope so too.
“It’s been a long time since this foolish elder brother filled your cup.”
Baeksang looked silently at the wine bottle in the Beast Miao King’s hand, then answered in a dry voice.
“I’ve kept away from wine and women for decades. I must respectfully decline.”

The Nanman Beast Palace might be a tribal society governed through a kind of divided rule, but the Palace Lord’s authority was considerable. Only Baeksang could have refused him like that. Before he was the Great Chieftain of the Bai people, he was the Beast Miao King’s sworn younger brother.
“You liked fruit wine when you were young. Won’t you even accept a drink poured by me now? I made this wine myself for you.”
“Baeksang.”
At the quiet call, tinged with hurt and bitterness, Baeksang slowly closed his eyes, opened them again, and raised his cup.
“If you insist, I suppose I have no choice.”
“Then...”
“I’ll accept the cup, at least.”
The Beast Miao King’s face brightened. He filled Baeksang’s cup to the brim, then whispered softly enough that only Baeksang and I could hear.
“I hope you’ll both forget what happened in the main hall. You each wronged the other. There’s no use blaming either of you alone.”
Baeksang was still suspicious, and I still didn’t like him. But I wasn’t stupid enough to hit the gas now.
“All right. I did go a little too far.”
Baeksang gave me an unreadable look, then nodded slightly.
“I apologize for my unseemly behavior, Palace Lord.”
It was a surprisingly compliant answer.

The Beast Miao King smiled with satisfaction. Turning to the crowd, he called out, “Today is a joyous occasion for every tribe of Nanman and our honored guests who have traveled all the way from the Central Plains. Eat and drink to your hearts’ content!”
His voice rang across the quiet training ground. The music started again, and the men and women dancing picked up where they had left off.
At last, the mood began to ease.
Then a Sound Transmission reached my ear, hard as stone.
—Honored guests from the Central Plains, are we? How amusing.
Aha. I knew that had gone too smoothly.

I scratched the bridge of my nose and glanced at the Beast Miao King. He had risen and was encouraging the chieftains around him and the warriors they had brought, unaware of what was happening behind him.
—Leave. There is no place for you in this land.
I drained my cup in one gulp and moved my lips.
—Our great chieftain isn’t very generous, is he? I know you hate the Han Chinese, but how many people did I rescue at Ailao Mountain last night?
—I’ll pay you.
—What?
—What do you want? Gold? Silver? Name it. I’ll give you gold and silver treasures heavier than your own body.
The sweet fragrance of the fruit wine turned bitter, just like my mood.
Gold and silver treasures.
I’d expected a cold reception, but this felt far worse than I’d imagined. I refilled my cup and sent another Sound Transmission.
—I didn’t do it for a reward. Do people in Nanman put a price on human lives?
—Of course not. The life of a tribesman is beyond price. But it’s different when the other party is Han Chinese.
—Why?
—Because you people...
The Sound Transmission trailed off. Baeksang stared at his full cup with gloomy gray eyes, then shook his head.
—I’ve said too much. Stop arguing and leave.
—If you stop there, I won’t sleep tonight. Why not tell me what’s bothering you, and we can look for a way to settle it?
—A way to settle it?
He gave a short laugh.
It was the first time I’d seen Baeksang laugh, and there was no mistaking the contempt and mockery in it.
Clink—crash!
The sound was nearly lost beneath the banquet, but I saw and heard it clearly. His porcelain cup struck the ground and shattered, sending wine splashing in every direction.
Trickle. Drip.
As the spilled fruit wine soaked the stone steps and dripped from one to the next, Baeksang’s Sound Transmission reached me again.
—It is already too late to turn things back. Just like those.
—Hmm.
Too late? Is it really?
I studied the broken cup, then reached out.
Fwoosh!

A thread of internal energy flowed from my fingertips and swept gently across the ground. As though time had turned backward, the pieces that had lost their shape moments ago rose and flew into my open hand.
Sss. Tick, tick!
Dozens of fragments drew together like magnets. I used internal energy to bind their broken edges until they formed a cup again.
A murmur rippled through the onlookers. I subtly turned my head to look around. The reactions of those who had been watching us from earlier were quite a sight.
Namho and Heugung stood frozen with their mouths hanging open. A strange light flashed through Sama Pyo and Yohi’s eyes. Taishan had even forgotten to chew his meat and was staring blankly.
Not bad. My control over internal energy really has gotten finer since I opened my Middle Dantian.
If nothing else, stopping Taishan from eating was an achievement worth celebrating.
“Hmm, good. That’s some excellent Seizing an Object Through Empty Space.”
Baeksang watched me praise myself and spoke in an even voice.
“Was that meant to show off your martial arts? It’s a pitiful cup for all your effort.”
“Pitiful?”
“It can’t hold anything. The wine will leak out before you can pour it in.”

He wasn’t entirely wrong. I wasn’t a god. Short of turning back time, I couldn’t restore the cup perfectly. I must have missed some fragments, because hairline cracks ran all through it. Even I couldn’t recover the wine that had already soaked into the ground and the steps.
But...
“You’re so damn picky. Just drink it.”

I picked up the bottle and poured without hesitation—not merely filling the cup, but letting the wine overflow. Then I wrapped my whole hand around it to cover the places where it leaked and tipped it into my mouth.
Gulp.
My throat burned as if I’d swallowed fire. When I spoke, my voice came out heated, carrying the fragrant scent of fruit wine.
“What’s the big deal? Cracked or broken, if you can put something in it and drink from it, it’s a cup.”
Baeksang’s gaze darkened.
—And what will you do about the wine spilled on the ground long ago?
Anyone else hearing that might have wondered what on earth he was talking about. But it sounded different to me after our earlier exchange of Sound Transmissions.
The cup is trust. The spilled wine is people.

During the Great Faction War, the Nanman Beast Palace had been forced to lose countless tribespeople. Afterward, because of some matter he did not even want to mention, Baeksang had completely lost his trust in the Central Plains.
By putting the shattered cup back together, I’d tried to show him what I meant.
I don’t know whether he’ll take this as a plea to trust once more or as a final warning...
Either way, I’d made my meaning clear.
I looked across the training ground, where the banquet was in full swing. At the center of the countless cheering people stood the Beast Miao King, watching me with profound eyes.
Whoa. That man doesn’t miss a thing.
I felt like a high school kid caught causing trouble. I gave him a deliberate shrug, rose, and ambled off.
“Where are you going?” Baeksang asked behind me.
I threw back a brief answer in a deep voice.
“To take a piss!”
That fruit wine was surprisingly strong.
“Kh... urk!”
He was a bear of a man. But his towering, eight-cheok frame and more than a jiazi’s worth of internal energy weren’t enough to save him from the death before him.
Crunch!
“Urk... Y-you. Who are you?”
A hand held his throat in an unyielding grip. Blood ran from the crown of his head, and between that and the lack of air, his vision had gone red and blurry.
He drew on every last bit of strength he had to speak.
“P-please... s-save me...”
He wanted to live. Desperately. But the strange man gripping his throat had other ideas.
Crack!
Bone broke, and the whites of the man’s eyes showed. When the life left him and his body went limp, the stranger released his grip.
Thud!
The heavy body rolled onto the ground. Without a moment’s hesitation over the life he had taken, the stranger thought, Ah. Was that the last one?
Only half a shichen had passed since enemies suddenly appeared at both ends of the gorge and shouted:
“I’ll tear you apart and kill you to avenge my martial brothers and friends!”
“Kill him!”
That was how the one-against-many battle had begun. After killing the men who rushed him from every direction without pause, he’d lost count.
About two hundred, I’d say.
They had gathered quite a force. The outcome had been all but decided from the start, though.
A sea of corpses and blood.
Only those four characters could describe the sight. The stranger, having once again left his mark on an unnamed gorge in Guizhou, picked up the weapon he had left leaning against a rock.
Clang. Clatter.
His Zen staff rattled as it swayed.
Stepping through a pool of blood, he headed somewhere to the south.

“Then...”
“I’ll accept the cup, at least.”
The Beast Miao King’s face brightened.
He filled Baeksang’s cup to the brim, then whispered softly enough that only Baeksang and I could hear.
“I hope you’ll both forget what happened in the main hall.
You each wronged the other.
There’s no use blaming either of you alone.”
Baeksang was still suspicious, and I still didn’t like him.
But I wasn’t stupid enough to hit the gas now.
“All right.
I did go a little too far.”
Baeksang gave me an unreadable look, then nodded slightly.
“I apologize for my unseemly behavior, Palace Lord.”
It was a surprisingly compliant answer.
The Beast Miao King smiled with satisfaction.
Turning to the crowd, he called out, “Today is a joyous occasion for every tribe of Nanman and our honored guests who have traveled all the way from the Central Plains.
Eat and drink to your hearts’ content!”
His voice rang across the quiet training ground.
The music started again, and the men and women dancing picked up where they had left off.
At last, the mood began to ease.
Then a Sound Transmission reached my ear, hard as stone.
—Honored guests from the Central Plains, are we?
How amusing.
Aha.
I knew that had gone too smoothly.
I scratched the bridge of my nose and glanced at the Beast Miao King.
He had risen and was encouraging the chieftains around him and the warriors they had brought, unaware of what was happening behind him.
—Leave.
There is no place for you in this land.
I drained my cup in one gulp and moved my lips.
—Our great chieftain isn’t very generous, is he?
I know you hate the Han Chinese, but how many people did I rescue at Ailao Mountain last night?
—I’ll pay you.
—What?
—What do you want?
Gold?
Silver?
Name it.
I’ll give you gold and silver treasures heavier than your own body.
The sweet fragrance of the fruit wine turned bitter, just like my mood.
Gold and silver treasures.
I’d expected a cold reception, but this felt far worse than I’d imagined.
I refilled my cup and sent another Sound Transmission.
—I didn’t do it for a reward.
Do people in Nanman put a price on human lives?
—Of course not.
The life of a tribesman is beyond price.
But it’s different when the other party is Han Chinese.
—Why?
—Because you people...
The Sound Transmission trailed off.
Baeksang stared at his full cup with gloomy gray eyes, then shook his head.
—I’ve said too much.
Stop arguing and leave.
—If you stop there, I won’t sleep tonight.
Why not tell me what’s bothering you, and we can look for a way to settle it?
—A way to settle it?
He gave a short laugh.
It was the first time I’d seen Baeksang laugh, and there was no mistaking the contempt and mockery in it.
Clink—crash!
The sound was nearly lost beneath the banquet, but I saw and heard it clearly.
His porcelain cup struck the ground and shattered, sending wine splashing in every direction.
Trickle.
Drip.
As the spilled fruit wine soaked the stone steps and dripped from one to the next, Baeksang’s Sound Transmission reached me again.
—It is already too late to turn things back.
Just like those.
—Hmm.
Too late?
Is it really?
I studied the broken cup, then reached out.
Fwoosh!
A thread of internal energy flowed from my fingertips and swept gently across the ground.
As though time had turned backward, the pieces that had lost their shape moments ago rose and flew into my open hand.
Sss.
Tick, tick!
Dozens of fragments drew together like magnets.
I used internal energy to bind their broken edges until they formed a cup again.
A murmur rippled through the onlookers.
I subtly turned my head to look around.
The reactions of those who had been watching us from earlier were quite a sight.
Namho and Heugung stood frozen with their mouths hanging open.
A strange light flashed through Sama Pyo and Yohi’s eyes.
Taishan had even forgotten to chew his meat and was staring blankly.
Not bad.
My control over internal energy really has gotten finer since I opened my Middle Dantian.
If nothing else, stopping Taishan from eating was an achievement worth celebrating.
“Hmm, good.
That’s some excellent Seizing an Object Through Empty Space.”
Baeksang watched me praise myself and spoke in an even voice.
“Was that meant to show off your martial arts?
It’s a pitiful cup for all your effort.”
“Pitiful?”
“It can’t hold anything.
The wine will leak out before you can pour it in.”
He wasn’t entirely wrong.
I wasn’t a god.
Short of turning back time, I couldn’t restore the cup perfectly.
I must have missed some fragments, because hairline cracks ran all through it.
Even I couldn’t recover the wine that had already soaked into the ground and the steps.
But...
“You’re so damn picky.
Just drink it.”
I picked up the bottle and poured without hesitation—not merely filling the cup, but letting the wine overflow.
Then I wrapped my whole hand around it to cover the places where it leaked and tipped it into my mouth.
Gulp.
My throat burned as if I’d swallowed fire.
When I spoke, my voice came out heated, carrying the fragrant scent of fruit wine.
“What’s the big deal?
Cracked or broken, if you can put something in it and drink from it, it’s a cup.”
Baeksang’s gaze darkened.
—And what will you do about the wine spilled on the ground long ago?
Anyone else hearing that might have wondered what on earth he was talking about.
But it sounded different to me after our earlier exchange of Sound Transmissions.
The cup is trust.
The spilled wine is people.
During the Great Faction War, the Nanman Beast Palace had been forced to lose countless tribespeople.
Afterward, because of some matter he did not even want to mention, Baeksang had completely lost his trust in the Central Plains.
By putting the shattered cup back together, I’d tried to show him what I meant.
I don’t know whether he’ll take this as a plea to trust once more or as a final warning...
Either way, I’d made my meaning clear.
I looked across the training ground, where the banquet was in full swing.
At the center of the countless cheering people stood the Beast Miao King, watching me with profound eyes.
Whoa.
That man doesn’t miss a thing.
I felt like a high school kid caught causing trouble.
I gave him a deliberate shrug, rose, and ambled off.
“Where are you going?” Baeksang asked behind me.
I threw back a brief answer in a deep voice.
“To take a piss!”
That fruit wine was surprisingly strong.
“Kh... urk!”
He was a bear of a man.
But his towering, eight-cheok frame and more than a jiazi’s worth of internal energy weren’t enough to save him from the death before him.
Crunch!
“Urk...
Y-you.
Who are you?”
A hand held his throat in an unyielding grip.
Blood ran from the crown of his head, and between that and the lack of air, his vision had gone red and blurry.
He drew on every last bit of strength he had to speak.
“P-please... s-save me...”
He wanted to live.
Desperately.
But the strange man gripping his throat had other ideas.
Crack!
Bone broke, and the whites of the man’s eyes showed.
When the life left him and his body went limp, the stranger released his grip.
Thud!
The heavy body rolled onto the ground.
Without a moment’s hesitation over the life he had taken, the stranger thought, Ah.
Was that the last one?
Only half a shichen had passed since enemies suddenly appeared at both ends of the gorge and shouted:
“I’ll tear you apart and kill you to avenge my martial brothers and friends!”
“Kill him!”
That was how the one-against-many battle had begun.
After killing the men who rushed him from every direction without pause, he’d lost count.
About two hundred, I’d say.
They had gathered quite a force.
The outcome had been all but decided from the start, though.
A sea of corpses and blood.
Only those four characters could describe the sight.
The stranger, having once again left his mark on an unnamed gorge in Guizhou, picked up the weapon he had left leaning against a rock.
Clang.
Clatter.
His Zen staff rattled as it swayed.
Stepping through a pool of blood, he headed somewhere to the south.

chapters.title: Chapter 649
paragraphs: Magic and machines.
Compared to the modern world, with all its technological conveniences, the Murim was a difficult place to live.
Its unpaved roads could wreck your hips and back even if all you did was sit in a carriage.

Smartphones and Wi-Fi were out of the question, and there wasn’t any electricity. The only way to get some was to take a direct lightning strike, but trading your life for electricity was terrible value for money.
Still, I’d managed to live without any of it.
No—my life had been so precarious that I’d never had time to worry about it. After that, things had been more or less fine.
They say food, clothing, and shelter are the three essentials of life. By that measure, I’d lived pretty luxuriously as the Third Young Master of the Jin Family of Taiyuan.
Except for one thing.
I fixed a grave stare on the non-Han servant from the Inner Palace. Even being generous, he looked no older than a middle schooler.
“I’m going to ask you one thing. Think carefully before you answer.”
“Yes?”
“Are you looking down on me because I’m Han Chinese?”
His eyes went round, and he waved his hands.
“N-no, sir. How could this lowly one dare...”
“Then why did you bring me to this shithole? I’m pretty sure I asked you to take me to the latrine.”
“T-this is the latrine, sir.”
“I told you to think carefully. Lie to me again, and I’ll fill your house with shit. You’ve heard of the Beggars’ Sect in the Central Plains, right?”
“Yes? Yes. Isn’t that the sect made up of beggars?”

“Exactly. One word from me, and I can bring several thousand beggars here... Well, maybe not thousands. About a hundred. One of them, Gung Gibang, smells absolutely monstrous. They’ll shit-dismember you and all nine generations of your family. So take me to a proper latrine!”
The servant flinched at my roar, his eyes filling with tears.
“I-I’m sorry. I’m truly sorry, but this is the cleanest latrine we have.”
Damn it. I’d hoped I was wrong, but this shithole really was the latrine.
The truth I didn’t want to face made my vision go dark. Even the Central Plains hadn’t been this bad.
“These savages...”
“Sir?”
“Never mind. You can go.”
I sent the innocent servant away, stared into the narrow space full of a hideous stench, and carefully set one foot inside.
Creeeak.
The plank beneath me shrieked. Once I shut the door, I felt like I’d stepped into a chemical-warfare chamber built for one. Grim-faced, I muttered to myself.
Did Baeksang dig this trap for me?
I’d seen it plenty of times in martial-arts novels: some incredible master gets assassinated in a latrine, or something like that.
But after I checked the gaps between the planks, even that suspicion vanished. No matter how dedicated an assassin was, I couldn’t imagine one hiding down there.
Please. God. Buddha. Namu Amitabha, Guanyin, amen...
Every second felt like ten years.
It was just as I had accepted reality and was holding my breath while doing my business.
Whoosh—thud!
It happened in an instant.
I reached out on reflex and caught the object that had punched through the old door with a sharp whistle.
An arrow?
The moment I recognized it, I shot into motion like lightning.
Boom!
The door shattered, and fresh night air greeted me. But that was all.
There was nothing around me. Nothing except the cheers and musical instruments I could hear from somewhere not too far away.
Still...
Southeast.
At my level, working out where the arrow had come from wasn’t difficult. I kicked off the ground without hesitation.
Boom! Whoosh!
Wind swept over me. I sprang off a wall and landed atop the highest pavilion, with the Inner Palace spread out below.
Torches lit the grounds. People enjoyed the banquet at the training ground. Warriors stood guard everywhere.
Who the hell was it?
Even someone in the Supreme Peak realm had limits. The Inner Palace was too vast to search at a glance, and several times more people than usual were moving through it.
Unfortunately for me, the Nanman Beast Palace warriors on alert for trouble took their duties seriously.
“Southwest! On the pavilion!”
“Who goes there?”
Peeeep!
At the sharp blast of a whistle, the warriors patrolling the Inner Palace swarmed toward me like ants.
Something else arrived first.
Whoooosh! Boom!
Hmm. This has gotten a little complicated.
I looked at the arrow and spear embedded near my feet, then checked the arrow in my hand again. It was identical to the new arrivals in size and shape.
But there was one important difference I’d missed.
This is...
A small leather bundle hung from its fletching.
The moment I realized it was there, dozens of torches flared to life beneath the pavilion where I stood.
“You’re surrounded!”
“Identify yourself and surrender immediately!”
Perfect timing.
After a brief moment’s thought, I silently gave a command.
Open Inventory. Store.
Ding.
At the System’s clear chime, the arrow vanished from my hand as if it had never existed.
Unable to make out what had happened in the darkness, the warriors of the Inner Palace shouted again.
“This is your final warning! Disarm yourself and surrender!”
“Put both hands over your head! Otherwise, I’ll put an arrow through your skull!”
That was a pretty savage script. Was this what they called a local patch?
I smacked my lips at the Nanman version of the NYPD and raised both hands as instructed. Once they knew who I was, the misunderstanding would clear up quickly. A few excuses, and that would be that.
Making more trouble would only make things harder for me...
Why are they looking at me like that?
They look as though they’ve seen a ghost.
Then I realized.
Fwoosh.
A breeze blew in from somewhere. My lower half felt unusually cool tonight.
Fwoosh.
“Good heavens...!”
Dozens of torches shone on me like spotlights.
As the warriors forgot their duties long enough to gasp, I had one thought.
I’m really fucked.
I’d forgotten to pull up my pants.
“I’m asking because I genuinely want to know.”
Namho, whom I met about half a shichen later, spoke with perfect composure.
“You bastard. Are you Dark Heaven?”
“You keep doing this because you’re Dark Heaven, don’t you? Huh?”

“Of course you are. What else could you be? Why would a Murim Alliance pavilion master come all the way to Nanman, punch a Great Chieftain in the solar plexus, then climb onto a pavilion in the middle of the night with his lower half on display? You came here determined to wreck the alliance admission from the start, didn’t you? Am I wrong?”
Taishan, who was sitting at the table chewing something, shot up a hand.
“Namho, what is Dark Heaven? Taishan is curious.”
Namho gave Taishan a long, searching look before turning to Sama Pyo.
“I’m asking you from the bottom of my heart. How do I put a padlock on that goddamn bastard’s mouth?”
“Hmm.”
After a moment’s thought, Sama Pyo stood.
“I’ll get more food.”
“Good idea. But as an agent of the Hidden Shadow Pavilion with a keen eye, let me add this: don’t bring the food here. Take him to it. If I hear one more word of his bullshit, I might go insane.”
Namho was prickly even on a good day. Today, he was all sharp edges. Even oblivious Taishan looked frightened enough to apologize.
“Taishan... was wrong...”
Namho shot him a murderous glare, then steadied his breathing.
I knew my turn was coming and spoke first.
“Well... there’s been a bit of a misunderstanding.”
“A misunderstanding? What kind of dogshit misunderstanding?”
“Could you not put it like that? Just hear me out...”
“I heard everything! I heard every last bit of it! There are even witnesses! More than two hundred people saw it! Did you send Young Lady Ju here for this? Is that your thing?”
“Wow, come to think of it, it would’ve been awful if Young Lady Ju had been there. Thank God she wasn’t...”
“You little baaastard!”
Boom! Crack!
That old man was over eighty, but he sure was strong. He had smashed apart that sturdy table with one blow.
I barely stopped myself from applauding. One more provocation, and Namho looked liable to die of rage.
“Elder Nam, calm down. Calm down,” Sama Pyo said.
“Huff. Hah.”
“Deep breath in, then out. Good. Just like that.”
After soothing Namho with a look of concern that hardly suited a man of the unorthodox faction, Sama Pyo turned to me.
“Anyway, Pavilion Master, is what you just said true?”
“Yeah, damn it. There was a small misunderstanding I can’t exactly tell other people about...”
“Did you really send Young Lady Ju here for this?”
“You fucking bastard.”
How had things ended up like this? At this rate, my nickname would change to the Naked Divine Dragon.
I stared at the ceiling in despair, then finally managed to speak.
“That’s not it. I was attacked before any of that happened.”
“What?”
“Attacked?”
“Oh. Taishan knows what an attack is.”
All three of them focused on me at once. Namho’s eyes widened.
“When? Where?”

“In the latrine. I was doing my business when an arrow came flying in from outside. I ran out to find whoever shot it, and that’s how I ended up like this. I didn’t even have time to pull up my pants.”
“Then the culprit! Did you catch him?”
“Do you think I did? It was shot from far away, and there were so many people in the Inner Palace that I failed to find him.”
A dagger or poisoned needle would have made things easier. Hidden weapons like those had a much shorter range.
A bow could strike from quite a distance. That made the culprit much harder to find.
“Then why didn’t you say so from the start?” Namho demanded. “If you’d been attacked, you could have reported it to the Palace Lord immediately and had the culprit hunted down.”
He had a point. I’d considered telling them the truth. It would have been better than letting everyone think I was a pervert wandering around at night with his pants off.
But...
“Someone did shoot an arrow at me. I just don’t think it was an attack.”
“What?”
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
“Taishan knows attacks. Taishan does not know attacks that are not attacks. Explain it to Taishan.”
“Die. Please die.”
Having shut Taishan down, Namho frowned at me.
“It wasn’t an attack?”
“Yes.”
“Then there was something hidden. Tell me in more detail.”
“I didn’t notice until later, but there was something strange attached to the arrow.”
As I answered, I spread my Qi Sense over a wide area. Once I was sure no one else was nearby, I silently gave another command.
Open Inventory. Summon.
Ding.

Something settled into my hand. I drew the hand I’d kept tucked inside my robes back out, bringing with it the arrow that had flown into the latrine. Then I untied the small leather pouch hanging from its fletching.
The rolled-up leather unfurled across the table. Smaller than a child’s palm, it bore letters as tiny as sesame seeds.
Today. Insi. West Gate.
It was a missive—an invitation from someone whose identity I didn’t know.

Having shut Taishan down, Namho frowned at me.
“It wasn’t an attack?”
“Yes.”
“Then there was something hidden.
Tell me in more detail.”
“I didn’t notice until later, but there was something strange attached to the arrow.”
As I answered, I spread my Qi Sense over a wide area.
Once I was sure no one else was nearby, I silently gave another command.
Open Inventory.
Summon.
Ding.
Something settled into my hand.
I drew the hand I’d kept tucked inside my robes back out, bringing with it the arrow that had flown into the latrine.
Then I untied the small leather pouch hanging from its fletching.
The rolled-up leather unfurled across the table.
Smaller than a child’s palm, it bore letters as tiny as sesame seeds.
Today.
Insi.
West Gate.

chapters.title: Chapter 650
paragraphs: The banquet held in the Inner Palace alongside the Tribal Grand Council that day didn’t begin to wind down until nearly the Ox hour.
For me, that was a relief. Otherwise, I’d have had to endure the stares and whispers coming from every direction all night.
“That Han Chinese fellow—wasn’t he up on a pavilion with his pants off?”
“What? What are you talking about?”
“My wife’s nephew is with the Inner Palace guard. Apparently, that brief alert a shichen ago was because of him.”
“Now that you mention it, I did hear a whistle... But wasn’t that when he said he was going to take a leak?”
“Maybe he didn’t go take a leak. Maybe he wanted to show everyone something else. People have all kinds of tastes, you know. Could be a Central Plains custom.”
“Good heavens. I had no idea the Central Plains had such a barbaric custom.”
“Barbaric as it gets. But separate from that, he does seem pretty impressive.”
“What does?”
“You know. That.”
“According to my nephew, they nearly attacked him because they thought he was holding a weapon. Until they shone a torch on him, they thought it was a spear.”
“What? How could anyone mistake it for a spear?”
“Come now. Do you think ‘dragon’ was added to his sobriquet for no reason? A dragon is a dragon.”
“Whaaaaaat!”
System Rumors about you are spreading far and wide! - A considerable number of influential figures are reacting to the rumors! - Fame has increased slightly! - Fame has increased slightly!
Please stop. And why did my Fame have to go up again?
My fucking life...
I did my best to ignore the whispers around me as I tipped back the last of my drink. Seeing me like that, the Beast Miao King laughed heartily and patted me on the shoulder.
“Don’t take it so hard. These things happen to a man.”
“When you put it like that, it sounds like I did it on purpose. It was an accident. I was in such a hurry to get out that I forgot to fasten my trousers...”
“Hm? Why were you in such a hurry?”
“Ah, well...”
Damn it. That had slipped out.
I still hadn’t told even the Beast Miao King about the missive from the unidentified sender. After a brief silence, I gave up.
“Actually, I did do it on purpose.”
“Oh my.”
“I’ve been like that since I was young. Still do it now and then.”
“Good grief.”
“It’s my hobby and my special talent. You thought I only used one spear? I actually use two.”
“Whaaaaaat...”
If I died in Nanman, it wouldn’t matter how it happened. The cause of death would be humiliation.
But I couldn’t tell him the truth. Whoever had contacted me this way wanted to meet in secret, which meant I wasn’t supposed to tell anyone else.
At the very least, no one in the Nanman Beast Palace can know.
I trusted the Beast Miao King. But nowhere were trust and faith cheaper words than in Murim. No one knew what might happen.
Besides, if the Beast Miao King found out, someone else might notice.
That man, for instance.
I met Baeksang’s impassive gaze. The longer I looked at him, the less I could read in his eyes.
He had spent the entire banquet sitting without lifting a finger to touch the food or alcohol. Now, after meeting my gaze, he smoothed his immaculate white robes, rose from his seat, and spoke.
“Palace Lord, it is already late. Let us end the banquet here.”
“Hm. Let us.”
The Beast Miao King nodded without hesitation. The Tribal Grand Council would continue tomorrow, after all.
Of course, since everyone present was a Peak master who practiced martial arts, none of them would suffer from a hangover. Even so, drinking in an atmosphere like this was bound to dull the mind.
Drip. Drip.
The Beast Miao King expelled the alcohol through his fingertips. His face clear again, he announced the end of the banquet, drawing disappointed murmurs from around the room.
Not any of them, then. The appointed time is nearly here, and they’re disappointed the banquet’s ending.
After quickly checking the faces of those who looked disappointed, I spoke to the Beast Miao King.
“Sir Yayul, I should head in too.”
“Of course. Which pavilion will you be going to this time?”
Seriously?
He took one look at my face, slapped his knee, and laughed. I sighed and left with Namho and the rest of the unorthodox faction underlings.
By then, the night had deepened, and the time had entered Insi.
It was time to meet whoever had sent the missive.
“Are you sure you’ll be all right going alone? It could be a trap.”
On the way to the quarters assigned to the Fire Dragon Pavilion, I reassured the worried-looking Namho.
“I’ll be fine. Besides, Elder Nam, you’d only be a burden if you came.”
“Were you thinking of following me?”
“I’ve lived a fairly long life, but I have no desire to die like a stray dog.”
“Then stay in the quarters with the other two deadweights.”
Taishan, as usual, gave it little thought. Sama Pyo was less pleased to be called deadweight when he was one of the unorthodox faction’s finest young prodigies, but my next words shut him up.
“If you don’t like it, reach Supreme Peak.”
“I can somehow survive, but you two can’t. Keep watch around the quarters until I return. And swing your swords at least one more time while you’re at it.”
We went inside together as though nothing were amiss. Fifteen minutes later, I slipped out unnoticed and disappeared into the darkness.
Around Insi. The West Gate, right?
I had no idea whether the contents of the missive tied to the arrow were a trap or an attempt to make contact in order to share information. I could only go and find out for myself.
Whoosh, whoosh!
I kept out of sight of the patrolling warriors as I moved. Before long, the cheers and clamor that had echoed faintly in the distance grew louder.
Fwoosh! Boom!
“Waaaaaaah!”
The banquet in the Inner Palace was over, but the night’s festivities in the Outer Palace were still going strong. They would go on tomorrow and the day after, too.
The ordinary tribespeople—neither the chieftains attending the Tribal Grand Council nor the warriors standing guard—were completely immersed in the festival atmosphere.
So that’s why the meeting place is in the Outer Palace. It’s more crowded now than at any other time of year.
I slipped into the crowd. The streets were packed with people wearing animal masks, and no one gave me a second look in the tiger mask I’d worn before.
The West Gate... Is that over there?
The Outer Palace was in a festive mood, but its guards hadn’t let their vigilance slip. I avoided the warriors stationed along the way and soon reached the West Gate.
Or, more precisely, somewhere near it. The area was just as crowded as the rest of the Outer Palace.
I came where the missive told me to, but...
There were too many people here, and plenty of guards besides. If I stood around like a Great General guardian post, I was bound to draw attention.
What now?
I was looking around when someone called out.
“Hey, tiger-mask fellow. If you’ve got nothing better to do, come have a bowl of somyeon before you go.”
I turned toward the voice and met the eyes of a middle-aged man at a nearby food stall. His face and eyes were unremarkable, and he was painfully thin. He grinned and raised the bowl in front of him.
“I don’t usually talk to strangers, but the broth here is incredible.”
I wasn’t sure the broth was the only incredible thing here.
I studied him for the briefest moment, then nodded and sat beside him. At last, I sent a thread of Sound Transmission to the unexpected contact.
—Funny. You’ve lost a lot of weight in a short time. You seemed to be eating plenty at the banquet.
Clatter!
His thin body flinched and trembled. I picked up the chopsticks he had dropped and continued the Sound Transmission.
—So what brings the Great Chieftain of the Yi people here?
Heugung’s eyes widened at the Sound Transmission in his ear.
Heugung was clearly shocked that I’d recognized him so quickly, but I was no less surprised.
He sent the missive?

We hadn’t met often or spent much time together, but I’d already formed an opinion of him: a pathetic man so besotted with Yohi’s beauty that he’d hand over his liver and gallbladder, and a spineless puppet who followed Baeksang’s lead.

Perhaps that was why this surprised me so much. Neither his appearance nor his behavior matched the man I thought I knew. And that magnificent spare tire you could have made a pilgrimage around? Gone without a trace.
If not for the System, he’d have fooled me completely.
I marveled inwardly and put the chopsticks back in his hand, adding a casual remark for anyone who might be watching.
“Why’d you drop these all of a sudden? Feeling weak?”
Heugung came to his senses and hurriedly composed himself.
“Ah, thank you.”
Only the two of us knew that Sound Transmissions were passing beneath our ordinary conversation.
“Sir, one bowl of somyeon, please.”
I placed my order, then moved my lips.
—You sent the missive tied to the arrow, didn’t you?
When the hunched old owner didn’t stir, Heugung pounded on the stall.
“Sir! One bowl of somyeon!”
He grinned at me.
“You’ll have to excuse him. He’s over ninety, and his hearing isn’t what it used to be.”
—...Yes, I sent it. But I changed my appearance with the Bone-Shrinking Technique. How did you recognize me at a glance?
Ah. The Bone-Shrinking Technique.
That answered one question about his sudden transformation.

Jeok Cheongang had once told me it was a martial art that could stretch and shrink bone and flesh like rubber bands. Learning it was so difficult and painful that almost no one in the Central Plains practiced it.
I doubt it’s common in Nanman either.
I still had plenty of questions. While I waited for the somyeon, I spoke aloud.
“I was craving some hot broth anyway. This worked out nicely.”
—How I recognized you doesn’t matter. Why send that missive?
Heugung made sure I had chopsticks as he answered.
“If nothing else, the broth is excellent. He’s been running this stall almost as long as he’s been alive.”
—I had information I absolutely needed to tell you.
“Oh, really? Then I’ll look forward to it.”
—Were you trying to kill me or tell me something? I nearly ended up with an arrow through my head.
—I thought you’d dodge it. Even Great Chieftain Baeksang couldn’t get the better of you. Surely you could dodge one arrow.
Did he have any idea that arrow was how I’d become the Naked Divine Dragon?
I considered smacking him over the head, but generously restrained myself.
—So, what is this information you absolutely had to tell me?
Heugung stared at the bowl steaming in front of him. His lips moved with difficulty.
—Great Chieftain Baeksang... has colluded with Dark Heaven.
Crack.
My grip tightened before I knew it, and the chopsticks snapped in my hand.
